[{:db/id 17592186412202 :question/problem "Find the volume of the solid $R,$ given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 4,\,4\le z\le 8-x,\,0\le y\le 2-\frac{x}{2}\}.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186281288 :question/problem "Find the volume of the solid $R,$ given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-2\le x\le 2,\,0\le z\le \sqrt{2-{x}^{2}},\,0\le y\le 2z\}.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186281287 :question/problem "Find the volume of the solid $R,$ given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,1\le z\le 3,\,0\le x\le 2z\operatorname{sin}⁡y\}.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186281300 :question/worked-solution "![](images/a7/a7261baec0c907779f5b1f5ff669ca826d4b93c5dd1b9a389e0989fe34756a6e.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type I region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,y)\in D,\,\,0\le z\le 4-x-2y\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le 1\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](images/65/65c61ad7dc2964cd0de9a6bbdf259fcf3388e25da4eaabf155d58ff0c05c8d55.png)

Hence, the type I representation of $R$ is

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 4-x-2y\}
$$

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{4-x-2y}dz\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}[z]_{z=0}^{z=4-x-2y}\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(4-x-2y)-0\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}4-x-2y\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[(4-x)y-{y}^{2}]_{y=0}^{y=1}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}4-x-1\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}3-x\,dx \\  & ={[3x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =(6-2)-0 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186412209 :question/worked-solution "![](images/c4/c4cf12ec9b53282620c1730f824c96d98e0b9dbabee0478bf258cf6c2741da81.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type II region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,0\le x\le 1+y+z\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 1\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane, shown below.

![](images/b4/b497e6ef73b5b16e11baa08819e9628d3b5e1f2ee4d05fbafec48f73e087cbf1.png)

Hence, the type II representation of $R$ is

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 1,\,\,0\le x\le 1+y+z\}
$$

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1+y+z}dx\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}[x]_{x=0}^{x=1+y+z}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(1+y+z)-0\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}1+y+z\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[(1+y)z+\frac{{z}^{2}}{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}1+y+\frac{1}{2}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{2}+y\,dy \\  & ={[\frac{3}{2}y+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =(\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{2})-0 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186412194 :question/worked-solution "![](images/7c/7c1738e97bc16a32f86d6901136afc4d9e288035d170fcd640db340ad36d19c5.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type II region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,0\le x\le 2-\frac{1}{3}y-\frac{1}{2}z\},
$$

where $D$ is the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane.

To find the top boundary curve of $D$ in the form $z=z(y),$ we substitute $x=1$ into the equation $x=2-\frac{1}{3}y-\frac{1}{2}z:$

$$
1=2-\frac{1}{3}y-\frac{1}{2}z\,⟹\,z=2-\frac{2}{3}y
$$

Then, we have

$$
D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 3,\,\,0\le z\le 2-\frac{2}{3}y\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/ea/ea8b8397163309a11aa478fcc21ab53ee293c19f0d77a93b5c3d3472bb0eba70.png)

Hence, the type II representation of $R$ is

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 3,\,\,0\le z\le 2-\frac{2}{3}y,\,\,0\le x\le 2-\frac{1}{3}y-\frac{1}{2}z\}.
$$

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2-2y/3}{\int }_{0}^{2-y/3-z/2}dx\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2-2y/3}[x]_{x=0}^{x=2-y/3-z/2}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2-2y/3}(2-\frac{y}{3}-\frac{z}{2})-0\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2-2y/3}2-\frac{y}{3}-\frac{z}{2}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[(2-\frac{y}{3})z-\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}]}_{z=0}^{z=2-2y/3}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}((2-\frac{y}{3})(2-\frac{2y}{3})-\frac{1}{4}{(2-\frac{2y}{3})}^{2})-0\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(2-\frac{2y}{3})((2-\frac{y}{3})-\frac{1}{4}(2-\frac{2y}{3}))\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(2-\frac{2y}{3})(\frac{3}{2}-\frac{y}{6})\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}3-\frac{4y}{3}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}\,dy \\  & ={[3y-\frac{2{y}^{2}}{3}+\frac{{y}^{3}}{27}]}_{y=0}^{y=3} \\  & =(3(3)-\frac{2(3)^{2}}{3}+\frac{{3}^{3}}{27})-0 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186412207 :question/worked-solution "![](images/59/599b5392add89a6a22eb6c2232fedbdd26704ebf849bb05d7de52a6d81dcfb6a.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type III region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,0\le y\le 3-\frac{x}{2}-z\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le z\le 2\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $xz$-plane, shown below.

![](images/9e/9e7c6fad45d9d85bad5ca16a2000e4d44a1739ab70797e41ae94945a4ffb02ef.png)

Hence, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le z\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le 3-\frac{x}{2}-z\}
$$

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3-x/2-z}dy\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}[y]_{y=0}^{y=3-x/2-z}\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(3-\frac{x}{2}-z)-0\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}3-\frac{x}{2}-z\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[(3-\frac{x}{2})z-\frac{{z}^{2}}{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=2}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}((3-\frac{x}{2})(2)-\frac{{2}^{2}}{2})-0\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}4-x\,dx \\  & ={[4x-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =(8-2)-0 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186281292 :question/worked-solution "Notice that our solid can be written as a type I region: 

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le 2,\,\,0\le z\le 4-{x}^{2}\}
$$

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{4-{x}^{2}}\,dz\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}[z]_{z=0}^{z=4-{x}^{2}}\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}4-{x}^{2}\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(4-{x}^{2})[y]_{y=0}^{y=2}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(4-{x}^{2})(2-0)\,dx \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2}4-{x}^{2}\,dx \\  & =2{[4x-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =2(4(2)-\frac{1}{3}({2}^{3}))-0 \\  & =2(\frac{16}{3}) \\  & =\frac{32}{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186412193 :question/worked-solution "Notice that our solid can be written as a type II region: 

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,-1\le z\le 2,\,\,-{z}^{2}\le x\le \sqrt{y}\}
$$

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-{z}^{2}}^{\sqrt{y}}dx\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{2}[x]_{x=-{z}^{2}}^{x=\sqrt{y}}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{2}\sqrt{y}-(-{z}^{2})\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{2}\sqrt{y}+{z}^{2}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[z\sqrt{y}+\frac{1}{3}{z}^{3}]}_{z=-1}^{z=2}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2-(-1))\sqrt{y}+\frac{1}{3}({2}^{3}-(-1)^{3})\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}3\sqrt{y}+3\,dy \\  & ={[2\sqrt{{y}^{3}}+3y]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =2\sqrt{{1}^{3}}+3(1)-0 \\  & =2+3 \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186281293 :question/worked-solution "Notice that our solid can be written as a type II region: 

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,1\le y\le 2,\,\,0\le z\le 1,\,\,1-y\le x\le y+1\}
$$

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1-y}^{y+1}\,dx\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}[x]_{x=1-y}^{x=y+1}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}y+1-(1-y)\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}2y\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}2y[z]_{z=0}^{z=1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}2y\,dy \\  & =[{y}^{2}]_{y=1}^{y=2} \\  & ={2}^{2}-{1}^{2} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129703 :question/worked-solution "Notice that our solid can be written as a type I region: 

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\}
$$

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{y\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,dz\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{1}[z]_{z=0}^{z=y\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{1}y\operatorname{cos}⁡x-0\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{1}y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x(\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}-0)\,dx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,dx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\operatorname{sin}⁡x]_{x=0}^{x=\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(1-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186412199 :question/worked-solution "Notice that our solid can be written as a type I region: 

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-1\le x\le 0,\,\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le x+y+2\}
$$

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x+y+2}\,dz\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}[z]_{z=0}^{z=x+y+2}\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}x+y+2\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{[(x+2)y+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}x+2+\frac{1}{2}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}x+\frac{5}{2}\,dx \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+\frac{5}{2}x]}_{x=-1}^{x=0} \\  & =0-(\frac{1}{2}(-1)^{2}+\frac{5}{2}(-1)) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{5}{2} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186412206 :question/worked-solution "First, we need to determine the projection of the intersection of our surfaces onto the $yz$-plane. So, let's find where they intersect.

$$
\begin{aligned}5{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =9-4{y}^{2} \\ 9{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =9\end{aligned}
$$

So, the projection of the intersection in the $yz$-plane is an ellipse.

Notice that our solid can be written as a type II region: 

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,5{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le x\le 9-4{y}^{2}\},
$$

where $D$ is the interior of the ellipse $9{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=9.$ 

As a result, the volume of $R$ is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{5{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}^{9-4{y}^{2}}\text{d}x]\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(9-4{y}^{2})-(5{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}9-9{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the boundary of $D$ consists of 

- the lower part $z=-\sqrt{9-9{y}^{2}},$ and

- the upper part $z=\sqrt{9-9{y}^{2}},$

for $-1\le y\le 1.$ 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}9-9{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-\sqrt{9-9{y}^{2}}}^{\sqrt{9-9{y}^{2}}}\,9-9{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}\,dz\,dy.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}+f & ={(-\sqrt{9-9{y}^{2}})}^{2}+{(\sqrt{9-9{y}^{2}})}^{2}+(9-9{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}) \\  & =(9-9{y}^{2})+(9-9{y}^{2})+(9-9{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}) \\  & =27-27{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186412196 :question/worked-solution "First, we need to determine the projection of the intersection of our surfaces onto the $xy$-plane. So, let's find where they intersect.

$$
\begin{aligned}2+3{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2} & =4+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} \\ 2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the projection of the intersection in the $xy$-plane is an ellipse.

Notice that our solid can be written as a type I region: 

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,y)\in D,\,\,2+3{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}\le z\le 4+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\},
$$

where $D$ is the interior of the ellipse $2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=2.$ 

As a result, the volume of $R$ is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{2+3{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}}^{4+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\text{d}z]\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})-(2+3{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2-2{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the boundary of $D$ consists of 

- the lower part $y=-\sqrt{2-2{x}^{2}},$ and

- the upper part $y=\sqrt{2-2{x}^{2}},$

for $-1\le x\le 1.$ 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2-2{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-\sqrt{2-2{x}^{2}}}^{\sqrt{2-2{x}^{2}}}\,2-2{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\,dy\,dx.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}+f & ={(-\sqrt{2-2{x}^{2}})}^{2}+{(\sqrt{2-2{x}^{2}})}^{2}+(2-2{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}) \\  & =(2-2{x}^{2})+(2-2{x}^{2})+(2-2{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}) \\  & =6-6{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186235411 :question/worked-solution "First, we need to determine the projection of the intersection of our surfaces onto the $xy$-plane. So, let's find where they intersect.

$$
\begin{aligned}1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =3-3{x}^{2}-{y}^{2} \\ 4{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2} & =2 \\ 2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So, the projection of the intersection in the $xy$-plane is an ellipse.

Notice that our solid can be written as a type I region: 

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,y)\in D,\,\,1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le z\le 3-3{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\},
$$

where $D$ is the interior of the ellipse $2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1.$ 

As a result, the volume of $R$ is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}^{3-3{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}\text{d}z]\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3-3{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})-(1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2-4{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the boundary of $D$ consists of 

- the lower part $y=-\sqrt{1-2{x}^{2}},$ and

- the upper part $y=\sqrt{1-2{x}^{2}},$

for $-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\le x\le \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.$ 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2-4{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-\sqrt{2}/2}^{\sqrt{2}/2}{\int }_{-\sqrt{1-2{x}^{2}}}^{\sqrt{1-2{x}^{2}}}\,2-4{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}\,dy\,dx.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}+f & ={(-\sqrt{1-2{x}^{2}})}^{2}+{(\sqrt{1-2{x}^{2}})}^{2}+(2-4{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}) \\  & =(1-2{x}^{2})+(1-2{x}^{2})+(2-4{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}) \\  & =4-8{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186235409 :question/worked-solution "First, we need to determine the projection of the intersection of our surfaces onto the $xz$-plane. So, let's find where they intersect.

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2} & =1-2{z}^{2} \\ 4{x}^{2}+2{z}^{2} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So, the projection of the intersection in the $xz$-plane is an ellipse.

Notice that our solid can be written as a type III region: 

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,4{x}^{2}\le y\le 1-2{z}^{2}\},
$$

where $D$ is the interior of the elipse $4{x}^{2}+2{z}^{2}=1.$ 

As a result, the volume of $R$ is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{4{x}^{2}}^{1-2{z}^{2}}\text{d}y]\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-2{z}^{2})-(4{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}1-2{z}^{2}-4{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the boundary of $D$ consists of 

- the lower part $z=-\sqrt{\frac{1-4{x}^{2}}{2}},$ and

- the upper part $z=\sqrt{\frac{1-4{x}^{2}}{2}},$

for $-\frac{1}{2}\le x\le \frac{1}{2}.$ 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}1-2{z}^{2}-4{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}{\int }_{-\sqrt{(1-4{x}^{2})/2}}^{\sqrt{(1-4{x}^{2})/2}}\,1-2{z}^{2}-4{x}^{2}\,dz\,dx.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}+f & ={(-\sqrt{\frac{1-4{x}^{2}}{2}})}^{2}+{(\sqrt{\frac{1-4{x}^{2}}{2}})}^{2}+(1-2{z}^{2}-4{x}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1-4{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{1-4{x}^{2}}{2}+(1-2{z}^{2}-4{x}^{2}) \\  & =2-8{x}^{2}-2{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186235407 :question/worked-solution "First, we need to determine the projection of the intersection of our surfaces onto the $yz$-plane. So, let's find where they intersect.

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2} & =1-{y}^{2} \\ 4{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2} & =1 \\ {y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the projection of the intersection in the $yz$-plane is a circle.

Notice that our solid can be written as a type II region: 

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,3{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2}\le x\le 1-{y}^{2}\},
$$

where $D$ is the interior of the circle ${y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=\frac{1}{4}.$ 

As a result, the volume of $R$ is given by 

$$

for $-\frac{1}{2}\le y\le \frac{1}{2}.$

$$

Which of the figures above is a parallelogram?" :question/worked-solution "First, recall the hierarchy diagram of quadrilaterals, where each shape below another is a specific type of the one above it.

![](images/1d/1dbe4c3e8ea97c0ac077c37143802366c5817d86965ab1dbc5abf54cd01d27c3.png)

Remember that a parallelogram is a quadrilateral with $2$ pairs of parallel sides.

With that in mind, let's look at each shape in turn.

- The shape $P$ is a parallelogram since it has $2$ pairs of parallel sides.

- The shape $Q$ is a square. Therefore, its opposite sides are parallel, so it is a parallelogram.

- The shape $R$ is a rhombus. Since the opposite sides of a rhombus are parallel, it is a parallelogram.

- The shape $S$ is a kite. It has no pairs of opposite sides that are parallel, therefore, it is not a parallelogram.

Therefore, shapes $P,$ $Q,$ and $R$ are parallelograms. The shape $S$ is not parallelogram." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b42fb396-a4b8-5570-82e5-99d092314e89"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} How much water is in the tank?" :question/worked-solution "To solve this problem, we can use the formula:

$$
\text{part}=\text{percentage}\times \text{whole}
$$

In our case, the whole is the capacity of the tank, which is $5,000$ liters. The percentage is $42.5%,$ and the part is the amount of water in the tank.

**Method 1**

First, we convert the percentage to a decimal:

$$
42.5%=42.5÷100=0.425
$$

Applying our formula, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{part} & =\text{percentage}\times \text{whole} \\  & =42.5%\times 5,000 \\  & =0.425\times 5,000 \\  & =2,125\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $42.5%$ of $5,000$ is $2,125.$ Thus, there are $2,125$ liters of water in the tank.

**Method 2**

First, we convert the percentage to a fraction:

$$
42.5%=\frac{42.5}{100}
$$

Applying our formula, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{part} & =\text{percentage}\times \text{whole} \\  & =42.5%\times 5,000 \\  & =\frac{42.5}{100}\times 5,000 \\  & =42.5\times \frac{5,000}{100} \\  & =42.5\times 50 \\  & =2,125\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $42.5%$ of $5,000$ is $2,125.$ Thus, there are $2,125$ liters of water in the tank." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields So the ratio of triangles to hexagons is $2:10.$

We can simplify this ratio by dividing both numbers by $2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,2 &  & : & \,\,\,\, & \,\,\,10 &  \\ \,\,↓÷\,\,2 &  &  &  & \,\,\,↓÷\,\,2 &  \\ \,\,1 &  & : &  & \,\,\,5 & \end{aligned}
$$

This means that $1:5$ is equivalent to $2:10.$

"The ratio of triangles to hexagons is $1:5$ because there is $1$ triangle for every $5$ hexagons."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields - $5$ is a rational number. It can be written as $\frac{5}{1}.$

- For the number $523,$ we have that 

$$
52-2(3)=52-6=46
$$

which is not divisible by $7.$ Therefore, $523$ is not divisible by $7.$

- For the number $532,$ we have that 

$$
53-2(2)=53-4=49
$$

which is divisible by $7.$ Therefore, $532$ is divisible by $7.$

- For the number $501,$ we have that 

$$
50-2(1)=50-2=48
$$

which is not divisible by $7.$ Therefore, $501$ is not divisible by $7.$

Find the arc length of the polar curve $r={2}^{\theta }$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}$ (shown in blue in the diagram above)." :question/worked-solution "The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={2}^{\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }={2}^{\theta }\operatorname{ln}⁡2.
$$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6}\sqrt{{(3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6}\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +9{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6}\sqrt{9}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6}3\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6} \\  & =3(\frac{5\pi }{6}-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}

"25541256-5bc3-5680-8cfb-415ab2841d24" :question/math-academy-id "q-2343" :question/problem "Find the values of $c$ that satisfy the mean value theorem for 
 $f(x)=2\sqrt{x}$ on the interval $[0,4].$" :question/worked-solution "The function $f(x)$ is continuous on $[0,4]$ and differentiable on $(0,4),$ hence we can apply the mean value theorem. 

So, the mean value theorem states that there exists a $c\in (0,4)$ such that

$$
{f}^{′}(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}.
$$

Plugging in $a=0$ and $b=4$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(c) & =\frac{f(4)-f(0)}{4-0} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{4}-2\sqrt{0}}{4} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt{x})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{f}^{′}(c)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{c}}.
$$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{c}} & =1 \\ \sqrt{c} & =1 \\ c & =1.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c188be5e-98c5-59a5-b9d1-5475ca041c52"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id </tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $f(y)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}+{y}_{2}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}+{y}_{2}^{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{y}_{1} & 1 \\ 1 & 2{y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${y}_{0}=y({x}_{0})=[\begin{aligned}2(1) \\ 1-3(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $y$ with respect to $x$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}(2{x}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}(2{x}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{2}-3{x}_{1}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{2}-3{x}_{1})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x)){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 9 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-3703a9d4-39d0-52e0-b2bc-ee344c22c3a9" "answer-field-488426ab-dda7-531e-996c-ff2ec4f75627" \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $f(y)\in {R}^{3}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}^{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}^{2}{y}_{2}^{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}^{2}{y}_{2}^{3})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{y}_{1} & 0 \\ 2{y}_{1} & 1 \\ 2{y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{3} & 3{y}_{1}^{2}{y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${y}_{0}=y({x}_{0})=[\begin{aligned}1\cdot (-1) \\ -{1}^{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $y$ with respect to $x$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}{x}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}{x}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}(-{x}_{1}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}(-{x}_{1}^{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & {x}_{1} \\ -2{x}_{1} & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x)){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 \\ -8 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0c22a089-927d-5420-ba5b-9d5a307d76f3" "answer-field-fa3ff81f-7b33-5955-80fb-a94bca6abd34" $$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $f(y)\in {R}^{3}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}{y}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}{y}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{2}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{2}^{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}+{y}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}+{y}_{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{y}_{2} & {y}_{1} \\ 0 & 2{y}_{2} \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${y}_{0}=y({x}_{0})=[\begin{aligned}-1\cdot 1 \\ -1-1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ 0 & -4 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

$$

Evaluating at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x)){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ 0 & -4 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ -4 & 4 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

:question/math-academy-id "q-269827" :question/problem "For $x,y,z\in {R}^{2},$ consider the following functions:

$$

What is $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(z(y(x)))$ evaluated at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]?$" :question/worked-solution "Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(z(y(x)))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}z}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $z\in {R}^{2}$ by multiplying it by $C$ and outputs a vector $f(z)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}z}=C.
$$

- The function $z$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $z(y)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{z}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{z}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{z}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{z}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ {y}_{2} & {y}_{1}\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].

$$

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c755d686-d2d4-566f-b38a-59bbea939df7"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "For $x,y,z\in {R}^{2},$ consider the following functions: 

$$
\begin{aligned} & y(x)=Ax\,\text{where}\,A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 3 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & z(y)=[\begin{aligned}5{y}_{1}-3{y}_{2} \\ 4{y}_{1}+6{y}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & f(z)=Cz\,\text{where}\,C=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

What is $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(z(y(x)))$ evaluated at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]?$" :question/worked-solution "Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(z(y(x)))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}z}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $z\in {R}^{2}$ by multiplying it by $C$ and outputs a vector $f(z)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}z}=C.
$$

- The function $z$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $z(y)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{z}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{z}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{z}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{z}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ 4 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

Evaluating at ${y}_{0}=A{x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}5 & 3 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ 4 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{2}$ by multiplying it by $A$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=A.
$$

Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(z(y(x))){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}z}{|}_{{z}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ 4 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 & 3 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & 21 \\ -2 & -24\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 & 3 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}28 & 63 \\ -82 & -102\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-9995b9e8-664d-5abc-9320-d2d470edb6d8"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id ![](images/af/afa5940765a9d39d7f8ab5aeefd4b550434adc0497b1b65845b00e30dd83d1f5.svg)

which is a vector-valued function of a variable $x.$ 

In a previous lesson, we saw that the derivative of $f(\mathbf{y}(x))$ with respect to $x$ is given by the multivariable chain rule.

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d}x}= \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y_1} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y_1}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y_2} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y_2}{\partial x} + \dots + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y_n} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y_n}{\partial x}
$$

This can be written as a product of matrices as follows:

![](images/14/1482285b6db08d8b944fd98871736ffebd912d78842ceac6fbad959b9b9e9e6d.svg)

Now, notice that this can be written as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d}x}
= \underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}\mathbf y}}_{1\times n} \cdot \underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf y}{\textrm{d}x}}_{n\times 1}
$$

where

- $\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}\mathbf y}$ is the *total derivative* of $f$ with respect to $\mathbf y$, which is a row vector of size $1\times n$, and

- $\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf y}{\textrm{d}x}$ is the *total derivative* of $\mathbf y$ with respect to $x$, which is a column vector of size $n\times 1.$

$$

\cdot
\underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf{y}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}}}_{q \times n}.
$$

Here, the dot denotes matrix multiplication. The inner matrix dimensions match, so this is a valid matrix product.

**Watch Out!** When applying the chain rule for total derivatives, the *order of multiplication matters!* For example, if we swap the order of the matrix products, we'd get an incorrect result:

:question/math-academy-id "q-332746" :question/problem "Consider the following inhomogeneous system of linear differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{2} & -\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2} & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}]x(t)+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

A complementary solution to this system is given by

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+{c}_{2}(t[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]){e}^{2t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Then, the general solution of the system can be written as 
$x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t),$
where ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution. Determine the form of the particular solution ${x}_{p}(t).$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

The forcing term

$$
[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

of the inhomogeneous system of ODEs is constant. Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also constant, i.e.

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

where ${a}_{1},{a}_{2}$ are constants that are to be determined." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-9383c075-7b49-5325-9b5c-cd8dcad979f2"] <td align="center"></td>

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

The forcing term

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2}+t+3 \\ -{t}^{2}+2t\end{aligned}]
$$

of the inhomogeneous system of ODEs is polynomial of degree $2.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also polynomial of degree $2,$ i.e.

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}{t}^{2}+{b}_{1}t+{c}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}{t}^{2}+{b}_{2}t+{c}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{aligned}]{t}^{2}+[\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]t+[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

where ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{c}_{1},{c}_{2}$ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the derivative of ${x}_{p}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{x}_{p}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ 2{a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the unknown constants, we substitute ${x}_{p}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}$ into our system:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}2{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ 2{a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}{t}^{2}+{b}_{1}t+{c}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}{t}^{2}+{b}_{2}t+{c}_{2}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2}+t+3 \\ -{t}^{2}+2t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ 2{a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-({a}_{2}{t}^{2}+{b}_{2}t+{c}_{2}) \\ {a}_{1}{t}^{2}+{b}_{1}t+{c}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2}+t+3 \\ -{t}^{2}+2t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0{t}^{2}+2{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ 0{t}^{2}+2{a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}(-{a}_{2}+2){t}^{2}+(-{b}_{2}+1)t+(-{c}_{2}+3) \\ ({a}_{1}-1){t}^{2}+({b}_{1}+2)t+{c}_{1}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding coefficients of like powers of $t,$ we get the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-{a}_{2}+2=0 \\ -\,{b}_{2}+1=2{a}_{1} \\ -\,{c}_{2}+3={b}_{1} \\ {a}_{1}-1=0 \\ {b}_{1}+2=2{a}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}={b}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first and fourth equations, we get

$$
{a}_{2}=2,\,{a}_{1}=1.
$$

Substituting these into the second and fifth equations, and solving for ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2},$ we get

$$
{b}_{2}=-1,\,{b}_{1}=2.
$$

Finally, substituting these last values into the third and sixth equations, and solving for ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we have

$$
{c}_{2}=1,\,{c}_{1}=-1.
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}+2t-1 \\ 2{t}^{2}-t+1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{t}^{2}+[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]t+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-2933141c-2169-5b87-8fb5-b8ed2e025c9c" "answer-field-f3dc74ec-4f14-5ce0-aef2-9920a7e3da3c" $$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

The forcing term

$$
{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]
$$

of the inhomogeneous system of ODEs is exponential. Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also exponential, i.e.

$$
{x}_{p}(t)={e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}],
$$

where $a,b$  are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the derivative of ${x}_{p}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{x}_{p}^{′}(t)=-3{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the unknown constants, we substitute ${x}_{p}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}$ into our system:

$$
\begin{aligned}-3{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot {e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]+{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\ -3[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-3a \\ -3b\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2b \\ 2a\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-3a \\ -3b\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2b+1 \\ 2a+5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-2b+1=-3a \\ 2a+5=-3b\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get 

$$
-2b+1=-3a\,⇒\,a=\frac{2b-1}{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $b,$ we have

$$
2(\frac{2b-1}{3})+5=-3b\,⇒\,4b-2+15=-9b\,⇒\,b=-1.
$$

So,

$$
a=\frac{2(-1)-1}{3}=\frac{-2-1}{3}=-1.
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{x}_{p}(t)={e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-6c17466c-b8ca-50c3-9f75-a6a53610a6c3" "answer-field-79975f54-a6ab-5d67-8f15-fd4af267d146"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-6c17466c-b8ca-50c3-9f75-a6a53610a6c3" :answer-field/id #uuid "6c17466c-b8ca-50c3-9f75-a6a53610a6c3" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-731aa6f4-9b42-511b-99eb-f375784ef6ae" :answer-field/choices ["answer-731aa6f4-9b42-511b-99eb-f375784ef6ae"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-731aa6f4-9b42-511b-99eb-f375784ef6ae" :answer/id #uuid "731aa6f4-9b42-511b-99eb-f375784ef6ae" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "e^{-3t}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-79975f54-a6ab-5d67-8f15-fd4af267d146" :answer-field/id #uuid "79975f54-a6ab-5d67-8f15-fd4af267d146" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-26d00d5e-9f6b-5691-9183-ca640417b15f" :answer-field/choices ["answer-26d00d5e-9f6b-5691-9183-ca640417b15f"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-26d00d5e-9f6b-5691-9183-ca640417b15f" :answer/id #uuid "26d00d5e-9f6b-5691-9183-ca640417b15f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167169 :question/problem "Consider the following inhomogeneous system of linear differential equations:

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2t+1\end{aligned}]
$$

of the inhomogeneous system of ODEs is polynomial of degree $1.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also polynomial of degree $1,$ i.e.

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{aligned}]t+[\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

where ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{b}_{1},{b}_{2}$  are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the derivative of ${x}_{p}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{x}_{p}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the unknown constants, we substitute ${x}_{p}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}$ into our system:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]([\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{aligned}]t+[\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}])+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2t+1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}+3{a}_{2} \\ {a}_{1}-{a}_{2}\end{aligned}]t+[\begin{aligned}{b}_{1}+3{b}_{2} \\ {b}_{1}-{b}_{2}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2t+1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0t+{a}_{1} \\ 0t+{a}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}({a}_{1}+3{a}_{2})t+({b}_{1}+3{b}_{2}+1) \\ ({a}_{1}-{a}_{2}-2)t+({b}_{1}-{b}_{2}+1)\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}+3{a}_{2}=0 \\ {a}_{1}-{a}_{2}-2=0 \\ {b}_{1}+3{b}_{2}+1={a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}-{b}_{2}+1={a}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first two equations, we get 

$$
{a}_{1}=\frac{3}{2},\,{a}_{2}=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

 
Substituting these into the third and fourth equations, and solving for ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2},$ we have

$$

:question/math-academy-id "q-362710" :question/problem "![](images/3d/3dbd6e325acdddddfb0bdcca5eef77fc3e75df2ccf946592780a0e1043ee1b01.png)

Consider the region bounded by the curve $x=-\sqrt{y}+y$ and the $y$-axis from $y=0$ to $y=1$ (shown in the picture). Using the shell method, calculate the volume of the solid generated when that region is rotated about the $x$-axis.

$V=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The region is enclosed between the $y$-axis, the curve $x=-\sqrt{y}+y$, and the lines $y=0$ and $y=1.$ So, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=1.$ 

Since the region lies to the left of the $y$-axis, the width of the cylindrical shells is given by $f(y)=0-(-\sqrt{y}+y)=\sqrt{y}-y.$ Using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}yf(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y(\sqrt{y}-y)\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{3/2}-{y}^{2})\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi ({\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{3/2}\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =2\pi ({\frac{2{y}^{5/2}}{5}|}_{0}^{1}-{\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{1}) \\  & =2\pi ((\frac{2}{5}-0)-(\frac{1}{3}-0)) \\  & =2\pi (\frac{2}{5}-\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{15}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0682446c-0c6a-5d39-8e65-0e1157e67525"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-0682446c-0c6a-5d39-8e65-0e1157e67525" :answer-field/id #uuid "0682446c-0c6a-5d39-8e65-0e1157e67525" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-85964491-e360-5d94-bffc-8e0d1ef8230f" :answer-field/choices ["answer-85964491-e360-5d94-bffc-8e0d1ef8230f"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-85964491-e360-5d94-bffc-8e0d1ef8230f" :answer/id #uuid "85964491-e360-5d94-bffc-8e0d1ef8230f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2\pi}{15}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-2d1d4e63-93d8-5dc2-a21f-3d16bb6f6063" :question/id #uuid "2d1d4e63-93d8-5dc2-a21f-3d16bb6f6063" :question/math-academy-id "q-352098" :question/problem "![](images/7d/7d6ef1d9a58af96b51152ce354ec85c616921187ed467273e8c41c4fe93fc19c.png)

Consider the region bounded by the curve $x={y}^{2}-5{y}^{4}$ and the $y$-axis (shown in the picture). Using the shell method, calculate the volume of the solid generated when that region is rotated about the $x$-axis. Do not round the answer.

$V=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we determine the points where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-5{y}^{4} & =0 \\ {y}^{2}(1-5{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ y & =0\,\text{or}\,{y}^{2}=\frac{1}{5} \\ y & =0\,\text{or}\,y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions are $y=0$ and $y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}.$ So, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}.$ 

Using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}yf(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1/\sqrt{5}}y({y}^{2}-5{y}^{4})\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1/\sqrt{5}}({y}^{3}-5{y}^{5})\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi ({\int }_{0}^{1/\sqrt{5}}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y-5{\int }_{0}^{1/\sqrt{5}}{y}^{5}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =2\pi (\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}\,{|}_{0}^{1/\sqrt{5}}-\frac{5}{6}{y}^{6}\,{|}_{0}^{1/\sqrt{5}}\,) \\  & =2\pi (\frac{1}{4}(\frac{1}{25}-0)-\frac{5}{6}(\frac{1}{125}-0)) \\  & =2\pi (\frac{1}{100}-\frac{1}{150}) \\  & =2\pi (\frac{1}{300}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{150}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d7d44499-1aa4-52d0-a15f-ec7d8581275c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d7d44499-1aa4-52d0-a15f-ec7d8581275c" :answer-field/id #uuid "d7d44499-1aa4-52d0-a15f-ec7d8581275c" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-0db6ee6f-edbb-5e5c-b2d1-764a2ea9a097" :answer-field/choices ["answer-0db6ee6f-edbb-5e5c-b2d1-764a2ea9a097"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0db6ee6f-edbb-5e5c-b2d1-764a2ea9a097" :answer/id #uuid "0db6ee6f-edbb-5e5c-b2d1-764a2ea9a097" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{150}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-7e282fab-f673-50f6-9e1f-aaa485da50b0" :question/id #uuid "7e282fab-f673-50f6-9e1f-aaa485da50b0" :question/math-academy-id "q-352100" :question/problem "![](images/69/69dbf7a007980f1f1a9c2531ad398237e22d28f329afc619e05b8372afe970d4.png)

Consider the region bounded by the curve $x={y}^{2}-2{y}^{3}$ and the $y$-axis (shown in the picture). Using the shell method, calculate the volume of the solid generated when that region is rotated about the $x$-axis. Do not round the answer.

$V=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we determine the points where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-2{y}^{3} & =0 \\ {y}^{2}(1-2y) & =0 \\ y & =0\,\text{or}\,1-2y=0 \\ y & =0\,\text{or}\,y=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions are $y=0$ and $y=\frac{1}{2}.$ So, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=\frac{1}{2}.$ 

Using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}yf(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1/2}y({y}^{2}-2{y}^{3})\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1/2}({y}^{3}-2{y}^{4})\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi ({\int }_{0}^{1/2}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y-2{\int }_{0}^{1/2}{y}^{4}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =2\pi (\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}\,{|}_{0}^{1/2}-\frac{2}{5}{y}^{5}\,{|}_{0}^{1/2}\,) \\  & =2\pi (\frac{1}{4}(\frac{1}{16}-0)-\frac{2}{5}(\frac{1}{32}-0)) \\  & =2\pi (\frac{1}{64}-\frac{1}{80}) \\  & =2\pi (\frac{1}{320}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{160}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-2c795d78-7949-57ee-a8d5-8e5d26c90629"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-2c795d78-7949-57ee-a8d5-8e5d26c90629" :answer-field/id #uuid "2c795d78-7949-57ee-a8d5-8e5d26c90629" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-2e920f28-4383-54cc-9cc9-d78d86338f95" :answer-field/choices ["answer-2e920f28-4383-54cc-9cc9-d78d86338f95"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2e920f28-4383-54cc-9cc9-d78d86338f95" :answer/id #uuid "2e920f28-4383-54cc-9cc9-d78d86338f95" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\pi}{160}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-2fefe340-5c6b-584d-b7e8-9e9204c610ea" :question/id #uuid "2fefe340-5c6b-584d-b7e8-9e9204c610ea" :question/math-academy-id "q-126111" :question/problem "![](images/28/287bde55681f44bd4132fdd5b4777a66d3dba7b16708533d755379c41f35b797.png)

Calculate the volume of the solid generated when this region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "First, we determine the points where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-3+4y-{y}^{2} & =0 \\ {y}^{2}-4y+3 & =0 \\ (y-1)(y-3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions are $y=1,$ and $y=3.$ So, we need to integrate from $y=1$ to $y=3.$ 

Using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}yf(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{3}y(-3+4y-{y}^{2})\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{3}(-3y+4{y}^{2}-{y}^{3})\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi (-3{\int }_{1}^{3}y\,\text{d}y+4{\int }_{1}^{3}{y}^{2}\text{d}y-{\int }_{1}^{3}{y}^{3}\text{d}y) \\  & =2\pi (-3\cdot {\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}|}_{1}^{3}+4\cdot {\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}|}_{1}^{3}-{\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}|}_{1}^{3}) \\  & =2\pi (-3(\frac{9}{2}-\frac{1}{2})+4(\frac{27}{3}-\frac{1}{3})-(\frac{81}{4}-\frac{1}{4})) \\  & =2\pi (-12+\frac{104}{3}-20) \\  & =\frac{16\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1289d38d-0117-531f-a4f5-10acc347ae1c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-1289d38d-0117-531f-a4f5-10acc347ae1c" :answer-field/id #uuid "1289d38d-0117-531f-a4f5-10acc347ae1c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-3b94c6a5-9527-5477-a1a3-7f03234197e5" :answer-field/choices ["answer-03592d71-01c8-5c8e-8dc1-555c9e33cf9a" "answer-3b94c6a5-9527-5477-a1a3-7f03234197e5" "answer-7732a064-ce3b-5465-88a9-cfdd49f7a517" "answer-432c08ab-5b41-5def-a73b-e813b7482639" "answer-0c15f7c1-4bcc-5b00-9a47-f77a64d0f457"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-03592d71-01c8-5c8e-8dc1-555c9e33cf9a" :answer/id #uuid "03592d71-01c8-5c8e-8dc1-555c9e33cf9a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{14\pi }{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3b94c6a5-9527-5477-a1a3-7f03234197e5" :answer/id #uuid "3b94c6a5-9527-5477-a1a3-7f03234197e5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{16\pi }{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7732a064-ce3b-5465-88a9-cfdd49f7a517" :answer/id #uuid "7732a064-ce3b-5465-88a9-cfdd49f7a517" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{16\pi }{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-432c08ab-5b41-5def-a73b-e813b7482639" :answer/id #uuid "432c08ab-5b41-5def-a73b-e813b7482639" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{18\pi }{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0c15f7c1-4bcc-5b00-9a47-f77a64d0f457" :answer/id #uuid "0c15f7c1-4bcc-5b00-9a47-f77a64d0f457" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{8\pi }{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-69689ccc-dfd4-5812-991b-d48dbc7eafee" :question/id #uuid "69689ccc-dfd4-5812-991b-d48dbc7eafee" :question/math-academy-id "q-363229" :question/problem "Consider the finite region bounded by the curve $x=5y-5{y}^{4}$ and the $y$-axis. Calculate the volume $V$ of the solid generated when this region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis. Do not round the answer.

$V=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we determine the points where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}5y-5{y}^{4} & =0 \\ 5y(1-{y}^{3}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions are $y=0$ and $y=1.$ So, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=1.$ 

Using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}yf(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y(5y-5{y}^{4})\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(5{y}^{2}-5{y}^{5})\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi (5{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y-5{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{5}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =2\pi (\frac{5}{3}{y}^{3}\,{|}_{0}^{1}-\frac{5}{6}{y}^{6}\,{|}_{0}^{1}\,) \\  & =2\pi (\frac{5}{3}(1-0)-\frac{5}{6}(1-0)) \\  & =2\pi (\frac{5}{3}-\frac{5}{6}) \\  & =2\pi \cdot \frac{5}{6} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a692812a-555a-5732-b8c5-43f45d5cfb92"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-a692812a-555a-5732-b8c5-43f45d5cfb92" :answer-field/id #uuid "a692812a-555a-5732-b8c5-43f45d5cfb92" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-1b2bc8ac-9cce-5432-82e4-a0d93044820f" :answer-field/choices ["answer-1b2bc8ac-9cce-5432-82e4-a0d93044820f"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1b2bc8ac-9cce-5432-82e4-a0d93044820f" :answer/id #uuid "1b2bc8ac-9cce-5432-82e4-a0d93044820f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5\pi}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069988 :tutorial/content "Consider the plane region enclosed by the curve $x=f(y),$ the $y$-axis, and the horizontal lines $y=c$ and $y=d,$ as shown below. If we rotate this region $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis, we get a solid of revolution.

![](images/19/1927064dcef318f2c0490ff071532b024da30a328b2752c28e197171eeec6b5f.png)

One way of computing the volume of the solid is to divide the interval from $y=c$ to $y=d$ on the $y$-axis to get horizontal slices. This approach is called the **shell method**.

Consider one such slice of height $\Delta{y},$ as shown in the picture below (on the left). When this rectangle is rotated about the $x$-axis, it forms a solid **shell** (i.e., the skin of a cylinder).

![](images/25/2561448ab909594dda427b76860fcdda5147f8966fec9e20958d1c5fca11b536.png)

Since we assume that $\Delta{y}$ is very small, the outer radius of the shell approximately equals the inner radius $y.$ The thickness of the shell is $\Delta{y}$ and its height is $x=f(y)$.

Imagine we cut this shell and unfold it to obtain a rectangular solid, as shown below. Its width is $x=f(y)$, its thickness is $\Delta{y},$ and its height is $2\pi y$ (the circumference of the shell).

![](images/03/03030fb80f0aa51c637e6d39b4f763e8d7fc89abd111a012d3e560a952cfba99.png)

The volume of the shell approximately equals the volume of the rectangular solid:

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{shell}} & ≈{V}_{\text{rec}} \\  & =2\pi y\cdot x\cdot Δy \\  & =2\pi yf(y)Δy\end{aligned}
$$

The sum over all the shells will approximate the total volume that we want. This approximation becomes more accurate as $\Delta{y} \to 0$. Therefore, the volume $V$ of the solid is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}yx\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}y\,f(y)\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069989 :tutorial/content "One of the advantages of using the shell method versus other methods is that the resulting integral can be much simpler to evaluate. This is often true when we want to rotate a curve of the form $x = f(y)$ about the $x$-axis.

For example, suppose we want to compute the volume generated when the region below is rotated about the $x$-axis:

![](images/1d/1d23dde2cdd557feb50f82f72f4ff09174d5fb9a0c94e7810a6c06acb95a13d0.png)

According to the shell method, the volume $V$ is given by the following straightforward integral: 

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}yf(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y(2y-2{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}-2{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now compare this to the disc method.

To determine this volume using the disc method, we'd first need to express our curve as two separate functions of $x,$ one for the lower part and one for the upper part, as follows:

![](images/d9/d957a8e263db8ddd8ad3e5fa37f63b0cdbb47e706c367350c3ff6b8ff90294ff.svg)

![](images/f4/f416ab43297265aec4836eca2020d8f08976852cc025ad4d3a0766023187adef.png)

The required volume is equal to the difference between the volumes generated when the upper and lower curves are rotated about the $x$-axis. Thus, according to the disc method, the required volume is given by

$$
V = \pi \int_{0}^{1/2} \left( \left[ \dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{1-2x} \right]^2 - \left[ \dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{1-2x} \right]^2 \right) \textrm{d}x.
$$

As we can see, this integral is a lot more complicated than the one we obtained using the shell method!" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068950 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069746 :step/math-academy-id 643617 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069749 :step/math-academy-id 643618 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069748 :step/math-academy-id 643621 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069747 :step/math-academy-id 643622 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068713 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-fbb8ab84-c16d-554a-bf88-2b57aaa4afbf" "question-2377eeaf-5209-5b0e-a180-97a6667f01fb" "question-8fea67f7-ec4c-5ab9-8c67-4d43507c8b87"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068481 :question/worked-solution "The point of intersection consists of the coordinates $(x,y)$ that satisfy both equations $y=5x+3$ and $y=x-1.$ So, we need to solve the system of equations consisting of the two lines:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=5x+3 \\ y=x-1\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the substitution method to solve the system. Substituting the first equation $y=5x+3$ into the second equation $y=x-1$ gives an equation that we can solve for $x\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}5x+3 & =x-1 \\ 5x & =x-4 \\ 4x & =-4 \\ x & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

This is the $x$-coordinate of the point of intersection. To find the $y$-coordinate, we substitute $x = -1$ back into one of the equations, say $y=x-1,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =x-1 \\  & =-1-1 \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system is $x=-1, \, y=-2.$ So, the coordinates of the intersection point are $(-1,-2).$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068714 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-0e71161b-a139-5715-8ffb-5d9680416a1c" "question-3f0c0760-2f71-5da7-a09a-417c59aab4e2"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068482 :question/problem "Find the point of intersection of the lines $x + 2 y = 1$ and $2 x - y = 7.$" :question/worked-solution "We need to solve the system of equations consisting of the two lines:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x+2y=1 \\ 2x-y=7\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the elimination method to solve the system. Notice that if we multiply the second equation by $2,$ then we will get a $-2y$ term that can cancel with the $2y$ term in the first equation:

![](images/d2/d2cac87bca62cf4fa8cc6ad3c0bd289de7cb0f8c39e742dd6e7731cb90b0e354.svg)

Adding the two equations eliminates the $y$-variable and allows us to solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+\cancel{2y} & =1 \\ 4x-\cancel{2y} & =14 \\ (x+4x) & =(1+14) \\ 5x & =15 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $x=3$ into the equation $x+2y=1$ to solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{aligned}3x-1 & =-4x+6 \\ 3x & =-4x+7 \\ 7x & =7 \\ x & =1\end{aligned}

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4x+y=a \\ 7x+2y=-2\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=-2,\,y=b$ to obtain a new system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4(-2)+b=a \\ 7(-2)+2b=-2\end{aligned}
$$

The system simplifies as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-8+b=a \\ b=6\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we know that $b=6.$ Then, we can substitute $b=6$ into the first equation and solve for $a:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-8+b & =a \\ -8+6 & =a \\ -2 & =a\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $a=-2$ and $b=6.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-5ceb5866-3821-5721-8ddd-69dfc4a85ef3" "answer-field-7ad9b32b-e694-53a4-b684-a9c3d5526acf"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-5ceb5866-3821-5721-8ddd-69dfc4a85ef3" :answer-field/id #uuid "5ceb5866-3821-5721-8ddd-69dfc4a85ef3" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-8d79f727-28b1-5c7a-a40d-c1d970975032" :answer-field/choices ["answer-8d79f727-28b1-5c7a-a40d-c1d970975032"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8d79f727-28b1-5c7a-a40d-c1d970975032" :answer/id #uuid "8d79f727-28b1-5c7a-a40d-c1d970975032" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-7ad9b32b-e694-53a4-b684-a9c3d5526acf" :answer-field/id #uuid "7ad9b32b-e694-53a4-b684-a9c3d5526acf" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-1f9a098d-ebc1-504f-8f6e-6368dd1908a1" :answer-field/choices ["answer-1f9a098d-ebc1-504f-8f6e-6368dd1908a1"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1f9a098d-ebc1-504f-8f6e-6368dd1908a1" :answer/id #uuid "1f9a098d-ebc1-504f-8f6e-6368dd1908a1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-6f0810d4-95d5-5ec1-a80a-fff5b7ccd8fa" :question/id #uuid "6f0810d4-95d5-5ec1-a80a-fff5b7ccd8fa" :question/math-academy-id "q-215449" :question/problem "Find the parameters $a$ and $b$ given that the lines $y=-2x+2$ and $y=-5x-a$ intersect at the point $C$ with coordinates $(b,8).$

$$

$$

From the first equation, we know that $b=-3.$ Then, we can substitute $b=-3$ into the second equation and solve for $a:$

![](images/2b/2bf429fdfbe706521b81617f56a0f561171aa7fd48e0af89318225f1d328e667.png)

The point $P$ consists of the coordinates $(x,y)$ that satisfy both equations $y=x+2$ and $y=2x+1.$ So, to find the coordinates of $P$ we need to solve the system of equations consisting of the two lines:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=x+2 \\ y=2x+1\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this system by substitution. Substituting the first equation $y=x+2$ into the second equation $y=2x+1$ gives an equation that we can solve for $x\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2 & =2x+1 \\ x+1 & =2x \\ 1 & =x\end{aligned}
$$

This is the $x$-coordinate of the point of intersection. To find the $y$-coordinate, we substitute $x = 1$ back into one of the equations, say $y=x+2,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =x+2 \\  & =1+2 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system is $x=1, \, y=3.$ So, the point of intersection has the coordinates $(1,3).$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068945 :activity/expected-seconds {x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x(t)+\overset{f(t)}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}]}},\,Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t} & {e}^{2t} \\ 0 & -2{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the system of differential equations and the fundamental matrix of the corresponding homogeneous system above. Using the method of variation of parameters, compute ${Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)$ and the particular solution ${x}_{p}(t)$ of the system.

<td align="center"></td>

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t} & {e}^{2t} \\ 0 & -2{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{4t}\cdot (-2{e}^{2t})-0\cdot {e}^{2t}}[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{-{e}^{-6t}}{2}[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{-4t} & {e}^{-4t} \\ 0 & -{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}]. \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{-4t} & {e}^{-4t} \\ 0 & -{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{-4t} \\ -2{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}-{e}^{-4t} \\ -2{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int -{e}^{-4t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -2{e}^{-2t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-4t} \\ {e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t} & {e}^{2t} \\ 0 & -2{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-4t} \\ {e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{4} \\ -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-57ab610c-28ab-5d09-83f7-d68b274b353d" "answer-field-9aa355cf-d45f-5b54-bcec-6c9a1e489b0d"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-57ab610c-28ab-5d09-83f7-d68b274b353d" :answer-field/id #uuid "57ab610c-28ab-5d09-83f7-d68b274b353d" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-8535759b-fe73-52af-853f-f3486f41d48a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-8535759b-fe73-52af-853f-f3486f41d48a"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8535759b-fe73-52af-853f-f3486f41d48a" :answer/id #uuid "8535759b-fe73-52af-853f-f3486f41d48a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2e^{-2t}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-9aa355cf-d45f-5b54-bcec-6c9a1e489b0d" :answer-field/id #uuid "9aa355cf-d45f-5b54-bcec-6c9a1e489b0d" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-f89927db-d31d-51e0-b063-5d1318a6634f" :answer-field/choices ["answer-f89927db-d31d-51e0-b063-5d1318a6634f"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f89927db-d31d-51e0-b063-5d1318a6634f" :answer/id #uuid "f89927db-d31d-51e0-b063-5d1318a6634f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166936 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-59d9272b-7eb2-549a-868b-86d14c7fdef5"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-59d9272b-7eb2-549a-868b-86d14c7fdef5" :question/id #uuid "59d9272b-7eb2-549a-868b-86d14c7fdef5" :question/math-academy-id "q-336703" :question/problem "Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into the {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation." :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L2},$ and $\text{L3}.$ Let's substitute ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$ from $\text{L1}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into $\text{initial system of ODEs}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{pre-multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-dfeef9c0-222d-580e-9176-2a58212a74b2" "answer-field-e749236f-06ab-5ec0-b55c-1658240128bd" You are given the following conditional expectations:

$$
\textrm{E}[X \mid Y=u] = 6, \quad \textrm{E}[X \mid Y=v] = 9, \quad \textrm{E}[X \mid Y=w] = 3.
$$

What is $\textrm{E}[X]?$" :question/worked-solution "We are given the conditional expectations of $X$ given different values of another random variable $Y,$ along with the probabilities of those values. This is a direct application of the law of total expectation, which states:

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \sum_y \textrm{E}[X \mid Y = y] \cdot P(Y = y).
$$

In this problem, $Y$ takes three values:

- $Y = u$ with probability $0.2,$ and $\textrm{E}[X \mid Y = u] = 6$

- $Y = v$ with probability $0.5,$ and $\textrm{E}[X \mid Y = v] = 9$

- $Y = w$ with probability $0.3,$ and $\textrm{E}[X \mid Y = w] = 3$

So, we calculate our expected value as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =\text{E}[X∣Y=u]\cdot P(Y=u)+\text{E}[X∣Y=v]\cdot P(Y=v) \\  & \,+\text{E}[X∣Y=w]\cdot P(Y=w) \\  & =6\cdot 0.2+9\cdot 0.5+3\cdot 0.3 \\  & =1.2+4.5+0.9 \\  & =6.6\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186208561 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-87aec959-895e-5be8-8c69-b3c4045c5829" "question-e734511f-0834-5433-966a-4ae3851cf360" "question-cdbfe9c8-c3f2-5a6b-9ce7-99052b0abd68" "question-e0fafa34-8718-5c91-847f-90668c3f437e"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186208277 :question/problem "A wildlife researcher is sent to either Forest $1$ or Forest $2$ to record animal sightings. With probability $0.7,$ he is sent to Forest $1,$ where the expected number of sightings in a day is $6.2.$ With probability $0.3,$ he is sent to Forest $2,$ where the expected number is $3.8.$

What is the expected number of animal sightings in a day?" :question/worked-solution "We are asked to compute the expected number of animal sightings the researcher records daily. This is a classic application of the law of total expectation, which allows us to calculate an overall expected value by conditioning on a related variable — in this case, the forest where the researcher is stationed.

Let $X$ be the number of animal sightings in a day, and let $Y$ be the forest to which the researcher is assigned.

- $Y = 1$ with probability $0.7,$ and $\textrm{E}[X \mid Y = 1] = 6.2.$

- $Y = 2$ with probability $0.3,$ and $\textrm{E}[X \mid Y = 2] = 3.8.$

So, we calculate our expected value as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =\text{E}[X∣Y=1]\cdot P(Y=1)+\text{E}[X∣Y=2]\cdot P(Y=2) \\  & =6.2\cdot 0.7+3.8\cdot 0.3 \\  & =4.34+1.14 \\  & =5.48\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186208562 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-9a2b9353-2f5e-55ce-b33e-819639da3c0b" "question-eff3dc19-9675-582f-bb2d-ae75355788e9" "question-fde0d020-b26d-5edb-a043-de5b1f35d4a2"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186208278 :question/problem "Let $Y$ be a discrete random variable, and suppose $\textrm{E}[X \mid Y] = 3Y + 2.$ If $\textrm{E}[X] = 20,$ what is $\textrm{E}[Y]?$" :question/worked-solution "We are given an expression for $\textrm{E}[X \mid Y]$ in terms of $Y,$ and the value of $\textrm{E}[X].$ This is a direct application of the tower property, which states that

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \textrm{E}[\textrm{E}[X \mid Y]].
$$

So, we substitute the given expression for the inner expectation, which gives

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \textrm{E}[3Y + 2].
$$

Now, we apply the linearity of expectation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =\text{E}[3Y+2] \\  & =3\cdot \text{E}[Y]+2\end{aligned}
$$

We are told that $\textrm{E}[X] = 20,$ so we solve this equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}20 & =3\cdot \text{E}[Y]+2 \\ 18 & =3\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\ \text{E}[Y] & =6\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186208563 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d15a80b9-3b38-5de0-953c-45a827aaaf2b" "question-12dc9838-1006-5e99-98b8-8a2304014d14" "question-5923cf06-a8dd-57e8-81ff-5f4a640b9a2b"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186208279 :question/problem "In a fantasy card game, a random mana level $m$ is drawn uniformly from $1$ to $201.$ A player selects a random spell costing an integer amount of mana between $1$ and $m,$ chosen uniformly at random. What is the expected cost of the spell selected?" :question/worked-solution "This is a two-step random process: first, a mana level $m$ is chosen uniformly from $1$ to $201,$ and then a spell is chosen uniformly from $1$ to $m.$ We are asked to find the expected value of the mana cost selected in the second step.

- Let $Y$ be the first random number, the mana level drawn uniformly from $1$ to $201.$

- Let $X$ be the cost of the spell selected, uniformly from $1$ to $Y.$

We are asked to compute $\textrm{E}[X].$ Since the distribution of $X$ depends on $Y,$ we apply the tower property:

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \textrm{E}[\textrm{E}[X \mid Y]]
$$

Given $Y = m,$ the value of $X$ is uniformly distributed on $\{1, 2, \dots, m\},$ so

$$
\textrm{E}[X \mid Y = m] = \frac{m + 1}{2}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \textrm{E}\left[\frac{1 + Y}{2}\right].
$$

Now, we apply the linearity of expectation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \text{E}[1+Y] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (1+\text{E}[Y])\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Y$ is uniformly distributed on $\{1, 2, \dots, 201\},$ we compute

$$
\textrm{E}[Y] = \frac{1 + 201}{2} = 101.
$$

Substituting, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (1+101) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 102 \\  & =51.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-fb48c25d-7d3e-5c68-83ac-d6034fcc4a05" :question/id #uuid "fb48c25d-7d3e-5c68-83ac-d6034fcc4a05" :question/math-academy-id "q-275424" :question/problem "Let $X$ and $Y$ be discrete random variables, where $Y$ takes values $a$ and $b$ with probabilities $0.55$ and $0.45,$ respectively. You are given the following conditional expectations:

$$
\text{E}[X∣Y=a]=6,\,\text{E}[X∣Y=b]=4
$$

What is $\text{E}[X]?$" :question/worked-solution "We are asked to compute the expected value of $X,$ given conditional expectations of $X$ based on the value of another random variable $Y.$ This is a direct application of the law of total expectation, which states

$$
\text{E}[X]={\sum }_{y}\text{E}[X∣Y=y]\cdot P(Y=y).
$$

In this problem, $Y$ takes two values:

- $Y=a$ with probability $0.55,$ and $\text{E}[X∣Y=a]=6$

- $Y=b$ with probability $0.45,$ and $\text{E}[X∣Y=b]=4$

So, we calculate our expected value as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =\text{E}[X∣Y=a]\cdot P(Y=a)+\text{E}[X∣Y=b]\cdot P(Y=b) \\  & =6\cdot 0.55+4\cdot 0.45 \\  & =3.3+1.8 \\  & =5.1\end{aligned}

You are given the following conditional expectations:

$$
\text{E}[X∣Y=p]=8,\,\text{E}[X∣Y=q]=14,\,\text{E}[X∣Y=r]=10.
$$

What is $\text{E}[X]?$" :question/worked-solution "We are given the conditional expectations of $X$ given different values of another random variable $Y,$ along with the probabilities of those values. This is a direct application of the law of total expectation, which states:

$$
\text{E}[X]={\sum }_{y}\text{E}[X∣Y=y]\cdot P(Y=y).
$$

In this problem, $Y$ takes three values:

- $Y=p$ with probability $0.5,$ and $\text{E}[X∣Y=p]=8$

- $Y=q$ with probability $0.3,$ and $\text{E}[X∣Y=q]=14$

- $Y=r$ with probability $0.2,$ and $\text{E}[X∣Y=r]=10$

So, we calculate our expected value as follows:
