<tbody><tr>
<td align="center" height="40px" rowspan="2">$x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+$ {{field-1}} $\cdot \,\,$</td>
<td height="30px" width="5px"></td>
<td align="center">$-1$</td>
<td align="center" width="5px"></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td height="30px" width="5px"></td>
<td align="center">{{field-2}}</td>
<td align="center"></td>
</tr>
</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

The forcing term

$$
{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]
$$

of the inhomogeneous system of ODEs is exponential. Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also exponential, i.e.

$$
{x}_{p}(t)={e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}],
$$

where $a,b$  are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the derivative of ${x}_{p}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{x}_{p}^{′}(t)=-3{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the unknown constants, we substitute ${x}_{p}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}$ into our system:

$$
\begin{aligned}-3{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot {e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]+{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\ -3[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-3a \\ -3b\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2b \\ 2a\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-3a \\ -3b\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2b+1 \\ 2a+5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-2b+1=-3a \\ 2a+5=-3b\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get 

$$
-2b+1=-3a\,⇒\,a=\frac{2b-1}{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $b,$ we have

$$
2(\frac{2b-1}{3})+5=-3b\,⇒\,4b-2+15=-9b\,⇒\,b=-1.
$$

So,

$$
a=\frac{2(-1)-1}{3}=\frac{-2-1}{3}=-1.
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{x}_{p}(t)={e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-6c17466c-b8ca-50c3-9f75-a6a53610a6c3" "answer-field-79975f54-a6ab-5d67-8f15-fd4af267d146"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-6c17466c-b8ca-50c3-9f75-a6a53610a6c3" :answer-field/id #uuid "6c17466c-b8ca-50c3-9f75-a6a53610a6c3" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-731aa6f4-9b42-511b-99eb-f375784ef6ae" :answer-field/choices ["answer-731aa6f4-9b42-511b-99eb-f375784ef6ae"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-731aa6f4-9b42-511b-99eb-f375784ef6ae" :answer/id #uuid "731aa6f4-9b42-511b-99eb-f375784ef6ae" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "e^{-3t}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-79975f54-a6ab-5d67-8f15-fd4af267d146" :answer-field/id #uuid "79975f54-a6ab-5d67-8f15-fd4af267d146" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-26d00d5e-9f6b-5691-9183-ca640417b15f" :answer-field/choices ["answer-26d00d5e-9f6b-5691-9183-ca640417b15f"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-26d00d5e-9f6b-5691-9183-ca640417b15f" :answer/id #uuid "26d00d5e-9f6b-5691-9183-ca640417b15f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167169 :question/problem "Consider the following inhomogeneous system of linear differential equations:

$$

$$

The complementary solution to this system is given by

$$

Then, the general solution of the system is

<td align="center" height="40px" rowspan="2">$x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+\,\,$</td>

<td align="center" width="5px"></td>
<td align="center" height="40px" rowspan="2">$\,\,t+\,\,$</td>
<td height="30px" width="5px"></td>
<td align="center">{{field-1}}</td>
<td align="center" width="5px"></td>
<td align="center" height="40px" rowspan="2">.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td height="30px" width="5px"></td>
<td align="center">{{field-2}}</td>
<td align="center"></td>
<td height="30px" width="5px"></td>

<td align="center"></td>
</tr>
</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

The forcing term

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2t+1\end{aligned}]
$$

of the inhomogeneous system of ODEs is polynomial of degree $1.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also polynomial of degree $1,$ i.e.

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{aligned}]t+[\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

where ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{b}_{1},{b}_{2}$  are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the derivative of ${x}_{p}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{x}_{p}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the unknown constants, we substitute ${x}_{p}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}$ into our system:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]([\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{aligned}]t+[\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}])+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2t+1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}+3{a}_{2} \\ {a}_{1}-{a}_{2}\end{aligned}]t+[\begin{aligned}{b}_{1}+3{b}_{2} \\ {b}_{1}-{b}_{2}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2t+1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0t+{a}_{1} \\ 0t+{a}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}({a}_{1}+3{a}_{2})t+({b}_{1}+3{b}_{2}+1) \\ ({a}_{1}-{a}_{2}-2)t+({b}_{1}-{b}_{2}+1)\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}+3{a}_{2}=0 \\ {a}_{1}-{a}_{2}-2=0 \\ {b}_{1}+3{b}_{2}+1={a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}-{b}_{2}+1={a}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first two equations, we get 

$$
{a}_{1}=\frac{3}{2},\,{a}_{2}=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

 
Substituting these into the third and fourth equations, and solving for ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2},$ we have

$$
{b}_{1}=-1,\,{b}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

 

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=[\begin{aligned}3/2 \\ -1/2\end{aligned}]t+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1/2\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186164048 :answer-field/correct "answer-68397710-f20c-5389-86e2-ff7174f9153b" :answer-field/choices ["answer-68397710-f20c-5389-86e2-ff7174f9153b"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-68397710-f20c-5389-86e2-ff7174f9153b" :answer/id #uuid "68397710-f20c-5389-86e2-ff7174f9153b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186164047 :answer-field/correct "answer-168093fa-9a63-55ce-a515-83e652a3a0ce" :answer-field/choices ["answer-168093fa-9a63-55ce-a515-83e652a3a0ce"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-168093fa-9a63-55ce-a515-83e652a3a0ce" :answer/id #uuid "168093fa-9a63-55ce-a515-83e652a3a0ce" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167990 :tutorial/content "Consider an **inhomogeneous** linear system of ordinary differential equations in component form:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)={a}_{11}{x}_{1}(t)+{a}_{12}{x}_{2}(t)+{f}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)={a}_{21}{x}_{1}(t)+{a}_{22}{x}_{2}(t)+{f}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we can package the unknown functions into vectors
![](images/03/037289f6f3a779d750cef23dc18d149786604bd477565e3708d6470f2e3c2f7a.svg)

Then, the system can be written as
![](images/77/77fc846681e1f0a98675b06f962e42f4491fd07d9bb2eab291e69cd49e4dd5f9.svg)

Often, the **forcing functions** $f_1(t), f_2(t)$ are linear combinations of a few basic functions (such as $e^{3t},$ $t^2,$ or $\sin t$).
In that case, it is useful to write $\mathbf{g}(t)$ as a sum of those basic functions times constant vectors.

For example, let's write down the system of linear ODEs below in matrix form.

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=4{x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t)+8{e}^{3t} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-3{x}_{1}(t)+5{x}_{2}(t)+10{e}^{4t}\end{aligned}
$$

First, let's rewrite our system, highlighting the coefficients:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=4\cdot {x}_{1}(t)+2\cdot {x}_{2}(t)+{e}^{3t}\cdot 8+{e}^{4t}\cdot 0 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=(-3)\cdot {x}_{1}(t)+5\cdot {x}_{2}(t)+{e}^{3t}\cdot 0+{e}^{4t}\cdot 10\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can write the system in matrix form:
![](images/47/47fb751641455ab4cf85756166fa8811bd8fe3ddc6bcb6005c8e6be8c31b6fe1.svg)
where ![](images/f4/f47e1272123fb8f4a5f54931929b9492f54e9d78d590b2ee28394bf29976ce44.svg)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186065571 :answer-field/choices 17592186065572] [:db/retract 17592186065571 :answer-field/choices 17592186065573] [:db/retract 17592186065571 :answer-field/choices 17592186065574] [:db/retract 17592186065571 :answer-field/choices 17592186065575] [:db/retract 17592186065571 :answer-field/choices 17592186065576] {:db/id 17592186068816 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-dfd26745-ef58-57dc-ac34-552acd1f12bb" "question-95c12fb3-5acd-5573-a477-4562c842d9b2" "question-5e9d38c5-007b-59fb-ae42-189521635fd6" "question-ba5c4320-47ed-5bb0-ac9c-df1a49799343"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068658 :question/worked-solution "First, we determine the points where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}4y-{y}^{2} & =0 \\ y(4-y) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions are $y=0, \, 4.$ So, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=4.$ 

Using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}yf(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{4}y(4y-{y}^{2})\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068815 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-a00b0b94-53a1-5e23-84f6-859ac793fc56" "question-2d1d4e63-93d8-5dc2-a21f-3d16bb6f6063" "question-7e282fab-f673-50f6-9e1f-aaa485da50b0" "question-2fefe340-5c6b-584d-b7e8-9e9204c610ea" "question-69689ccc-dfd4-5812-991b-d48dbc7eafee"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068657 :question/worked-solution "First, we determine the points where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2y-2{y}^{2} & =0 \\ 2y(1-y) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions are $y=0,$ and $y=1.$ So, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=1.$

Using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}yf(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y(2y-2{y}^{2})\text{d}y \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{2}-{y}^{3})\text{d}y \\  & =4\pi ({\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{3}\text{d}y) \\  & =4\pi ({\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{1}-{\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}|}_{0}^{1}) \\  & =4\pi ((\frac{1}{3}-0)-(\frac{1}{4}-0)) \\  & =4\pi (\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-dfd26745-ef58-57dc-ac34-552acd1f12bb" :question/id #uuid "dfd26745-ef58-57dc-ac34-552acd1f12bb" :question/math-academy-id "q-126096" :question/problem "![](images/93/9312e042b08ce1aae28eab8bb64aff176fc734c38184d781e348dc5ec6058bfa.png)

Consider the region bounded by the curve $x=-\sqrt{y}+y$ and the $y$-axis from $y=0$ to $y=1$ (shown in the picture). Using the shell method, calculate the volume of the solid generated when that region is rotated about the $x$-axis.

$V=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The region is enclosed between the $y$-axis, the curve $x=-\sqrt{y}+y$, and the lines $y=0$ and $y=1.$ So, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=1.$ 

Since the region lies to the left of the $y$-axis, the width of the cylindrical shells is given by $f(y)=0-(-\sqrt{y}+y)=\sqrt{y}-y.$ Using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}yf(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y(\sqrt{y}-y)\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{3/2}-{y}^{2})\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi ({\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{3/2}\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =2\pi ({\frac{2{y}^{5/2}}{5}|}_{0}^{1}-{\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{1}) \\  & =2\pi ((\frac{2}{5}-0)-(\frac{1}{3}-0)) \\  & =2\pi (\frac{2}{5}-\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{15}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0682446c-0c6a-5d39-8e65-0e1157e67525"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-0682446c-0c6a-5d39-8e65-0e1157e67525" :answer-field/id #uuid "0682446c-0c6a-5d39-8e65-0e1157e67525" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-85964491-e360-5d94-bffc-8e0d1ef8230f" :answer-field/choices ["answer-85964491-e360-5d94-bffc-8e0d1ef8230f"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-85964491-e360-5d94-bffc-8e0d1ef8230f" :answer/id #uuid "85964491-e360-5d94-bffc-8e0d1ef8230f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2\pi}{15}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-2d1d4e63-93d8-5dc2-a21f-3d16bb6f6063" :question/id #uuid "2d1d4e63-93d8-5dc2-a21f-3d16bb6f6063" :question/math-academy-id "q-352098" :question/problem "![](images/7d/7d6ef1d9a58af96b51152ce354ec85c616921187ed467273e8c41c4fe93fc19c.png)

$V=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we determine the points where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-5{y}^{4} & =0 \\ {y}^{2}(1-5{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ y & =0\,\text{or}\,{y}^{2}=\frac{1}{5} \\ y & =0\,\text{or}\,y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions are $y=0$ and $y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}.$ So, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}.$ 

Using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}yf(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1/\sqrt{5}}y({y}^{2}-5{y}^{4})\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1/\sqrt{5}}({y}^{3}-5{y}^{5})\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi ({\int }_{0}^{1/\sqrt{5}}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y-5{\int }_{0}^{1/\sqrt{5}}{y}^{5}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =2\pi (\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}\,{|}_{0}^{1/\sqrt{5}}-\frac{5}{6}{y}^{6}\,{|}_{0}^{1/\sqrt{5}}\,) \\  & =2\pi (\frac{1}{4}(\frac{1}{25}-0)-\frac{5}{6}(\frac{1}{125}-0)) \\  & =2\pi (\frac{1}{100}-\frac{1}{150}) \\  & =2\pi (\frac{1}{300}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{150}\end{aligned}

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1289d38d-0117-531f-a4f5-10acc347ae1c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-1289d38d-0117-531f-a4f5-10acc347ae1c" :answer-field/id #uuid "1289d38d-0117-531f-a4f5-10acc347ae1c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-3b94c6a5-9527-5477-a1a3-7f03234197e5" :answer-field/choices ["answer-03592d71-01c8-5c8e-8dc1-555c9e33cf9a" "answer-3b94c6a5-9527-5477-a1a3-7f03234197e5" "answer-7732a064-ce3b-5465-88a9-cfdd49f7a517" "answer-432c08ab-5b41-5def-a73b-e813b7482639" "answer-0c15f7c1-4bcc-5b00-9a47-f77a64d0f457"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-03592d71-01c8-5c8e-8dc1-555c9e33cf9a" :answer/id #uuid "03592d71-01c8-5c8e-8dc1-555c9e33cf9a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{14\pi }{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3b94c6a5-9527-5477-a1a3-7f03234197e5" :answer/id #uuid "3b94c6a5-9527-5477-a1a3-7f03234197e5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{16\pi }{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7732a064-ce3b-5465-88a9-cfdd49f7a517" :answer/id #uuid "7732a064-ce3b-5465-88a9-cfdd49f7a517" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{16\pi }{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-432c08ab-5b41-5def-a73b-e813b7482639" :answer/id #uuid "432c08ab-5b41-5def-a73b-e813b7482639" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{18\pi }{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0c15f7c1-4bcc-5b00-9a47-f77a64d0f457" :answer/id #uuid "0c15f7c1-4bcc-5b00-9a47-f77a64d0f457" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{8\pi }{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-69689ccc-dfd4-5812-991b-d48dbc7eafee" :question/id #uuid "69689ccc-dfd4-5812-991b-d48dbc7eafee" :question/math-academy-id "q-363229" :question/problem "Consider the finite region bounded by the curve $x=5y-5{y}^{4}$ and the $y$-axis. Calculate the volume $V$ of the solid generated when this region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis. Do not round the answer.

$V=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we determine the points where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}5y-5{y}^{4} & =0 \\ 5y(1-{y}^{3}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions are $y=0$ and $y=1.$ So, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=1.$ 

Using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}yf(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y(5y-5{y}^{4})\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(5{y}^{2}-5{y}^{5})\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi (5{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y-5{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{5}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =2\pi (\frac{5}{3}{y}^{3}\,{|}_{0}^{1}-\frac{5}{6}{y}^{6}\,{|}_{0}^{1}\,) \\  & =2\pi (\frac{5}{3}(1-0)-\frac{5}{6}(1-0)) \\  & =2\pi (\frac{5}{3}-\frac{5}{6}) \\  & =2\pi \cdot \frac{5}{6} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a692812a-555a-5732-b8c5-43f45d5cfb92"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-a692812a-555a-5732-b8c5-43f45d5cfb92" :answer-field/id #uuid "a692812a-555a-5732-b8c5-43f45d5cfb92" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-1b2bc8ac-9cce-5432-82e4-a0d93044820f" :answer-field/choices ["answer-1b2bc8ac-9cce-5432-82e4-a0d93044820f"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1b2bc8ac-9cce-5432-82e4-a0d93044820f" :answer/id #uuid "1b2bc8ac-9cce-5432-82e4-a0d93044820f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5\pi}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069988 :tutorial/content "Consider the plane region enclosed by the curve $x=f(y),$ the $y$-axis, and the horizontal lines $y=c$ and $y=d,$ as shown below. If we rotate this region $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis, we get a solid of revolution.

![](images/19/1927064dcef318f2c0490ff071532b024da30a328b2752c28e197171eeec6b5f.png)

One way of computing the volume of the solid is to divide the interval from $y=c$ to $y=d$ on the $y$-axis to get horizontal slices. This approach is called the **shell method**.

Consider one such slice of height $\Delta{y},$ as shown in the picture below (on the left). When this rectangle is rotated about the $x$-axis, it forms a solid **shell** (i.e., the skin of a cylinder).

![](images/25/2561448ab909594dda427b76860fcdda5147f8966fec9e20958d1c5fca11b536.png)

Since we assume that $\Delta{y}$ is very small, the outer radius of the shell approximately equals the inner radius $y.$ The thickness of the shell is $\Delta{y}$ and its height is $x=f(y)$.

Imagine we cut this shell and unfold it to obtain a rectangular solid, as shown below. Its width is $x=f(y)$, its thickness is $\Delta{y},$ and its height is $2\pi y$ (the circumference of the shell).

![](images/03/03030fb80f0aa51c637e6d39b4f763e8d7fc89abd111a012d3e560a952cfba99.png)

The volume of the shell approximately equals the volume of the rectangular solid:

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{shell}} & ≈{V}_{\text{rec}} \\  & =2\pi y\cdot x\cdot Δy \\  & =2\pi yf(y)Δy\end{aligned}
$$

The sum over all the shells will approximate the total volume that we want. This approximation becomes more accurate as $\Delta{y} \to 0$. Therefore, the volume $V$ of the solid is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}yx\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}y\,f(y)\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069989 :tutorial/content "One of the advantages of using the shell method versus other methods is that the resulting integral can be much simpler to evaluate. This is often true when we want to rotate a curve of the form $x = f(y)$ about the $x$-axis.

For example, suppose we want to compute the volume generated when the region below is rotated about the $x$-axis:

![](images/1d/1d23dde2cdd557feb50f82f72f4ff09174d5fb9a0c94e7810a6c06acb95a13d0.png)

According to the shell method, the volume $V$ is given by the following straightforward integral: 

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}yf(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y(2y-2{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}-2{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now compare this to the disc method.

To determine this volume using the disc method, we'd first need to express our curve as two separate functions of $x,$ one for the lower part and one for the upper part, as follows:

![](images/d9/d957a8e263db8ddd8ad3e5fa37f63b0cdbb47e706c367350c3ff6b8ff90294ff.svg)

![](images/f4/f416ab43297265aec4836eca2020d8f08976852cc025ad4d3a0766023187adef.png)

The required volume is equal to the difference between the volumes generated when the upper and lower curves are rotated about the $x$-axis. Thus, according to the disc method, the required volume is given by

$$
V = \pi \int_{0}^{1/2} \left( \left[ \dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{1-2x} \right]^2 - \left[ \dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{1-2x} \right]^2 \right) \textrm{d}x.
$$

As we can see, this integral is a lot more complicated than the one we obtained using the shell method!" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068950 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069746 :step/math-academy-id 643617 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069749 :step/math-academy-id 643618 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069748 :step/math-academy-id 643621 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069747 :step/math-academy-id 643622 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068713 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-fbb8ab84-c16d-554a-bf88-2b57aaa4afbf" "question-2377eeaf-5209-5b0e-a180-97a6667f01fb" "question-8fea67f7-ec4c-5ab9-8c67-4d43507c8b87"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068481 :question/worked-solution "The point of intersection consists of the coordinates $(x,y)$ that satisfy both equations $y=5x+3$ and $y=x-1.$ So, we need to solve the system of equations consisting of the two lines:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=5x+3 \\ y=x-1\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the substitution method to solve the system. Substituting the first equation $y=5x+3$ into the second equation $y=x-1$ gives an equation that we can solve for $x\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}5x+3 & =x-1 \\ 5x & =x-4 \\ 4x & =-4 \\ x & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

This is the $x$-coordinate of the point of intersection. To find the $y$-coordinate, we substitute $x = -1$ back into one of the equations, say $y=x-1,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =x-1 \\  & =-1-1 \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system is $x=-1, \, y=-2.$ So, the coordinates of the intersection point are $(-1,-2).$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068714 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-0e71161b-a139-5715-8ffb-5d9680416a1c" "question-3f0c0760-2f71-5da7-a09a-417c59aab4e2"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068482 :question/problem "Find the point of intersection of the lines $x + 2 y = 1$ and $2 x - y = 7.$" :question/worked-solution "We need to solve the system of equations consisting of the two lines:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x+2y=1 \\ 2x-y=7\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the elimination method to solve the system. Notice that if we multiply the second equation by $2,$ then we will get a $-2y$ term that can cancel with the $2y$ term in the first equation:

![](images/d2/d2cac87bca62cf4fa8cc6ad3c0bd289de7cb0f8c39e742dd6e7731cb90b0e354.svg)

Adding the two equations eliminates the $y$-variable and allows us to solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+\cancel{2y} & =1 \\ 4x-\cancel{2y} & =14 \\ (x+4x) & =(1+14) \\ 5x & =15 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $x=3$ into the equation $x+2y=1$ to solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2y & =1 \\ 3+2y & =1 \\ 2y & =-2 \\ y & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system is $x=3, \, y=-1.$ So the coordinates of the point of intersection are $(3,-1).$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068715 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-1afc104b-55b0-5a4c-8495-1467f6f4a4e0" "question-6f0810d4-95d5-5ec1-a80a-fff5b7ccd8fa"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068483 :question/problem "The lines $y = -3 x + a$ and $y = x - 1$ intersect at the point $C$ with coordinates $(b, -4).$ Find the parameters $a$ and $b.$" :question/worked-solution "Since $(b,-4)$ is the point of intersection of the two lines, the values $x=b, \, y=-4$ must solve the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=-3x+a \\ y=x-1\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=b, \, y=-4$ to obtain a new system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-4=-3b+a \\ -4=b-1\end{aligned}
$$

In the second equation, we can solve for $b\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-4 & =b-1 \\ -3 & =b\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we can substitute $b=-3$ into the first equation and solve for $a\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-4 & =-3b+a \\ -4 & =-3(-3)+a \\ -4 & =9+a \\ -13 & =a\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $a = -13$ and $b = -3.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-fbb8ab84-c16d-554a-bf88-2b57aaa4afbf" :question/id #uuid "fbb8ab84-c16d-554a-bf88-2b57aaa4afbf" :question/math-academy-id "q-12341" :question/problem "Find the point of intersection of the lines $y=-3x+4$ and $y=3x-2.$" :question/worked-solution "The point of intersection consists of the coordinates $(x,y)$ that satisfy both equations $y=-3x+4$ and $y=3x-2.$ So, we need to solve the system of equations consisting of the two lines:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=-3x+4 \\ y=3x-2\end{aligned}
$$

 

We can solve this system by substitution. Substituting the first equation $y=-3x+4$ into the second equation $y=3x-2$ yields an equation that we can solve for $x:$   

$$
\begin{aligned}-3x+4 & =3x-2 \\ -6x & =-6 \\ x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This is the $x$-coordinate of the point of intersection. To find the $y$-coordinate, we substitute $x=1$ back into one of the equations, say $y=3x-2,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3(1)-2 \\  & =3-2 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system is $x=1,\,y=1.$ So, the coordinates of the intersection point are  $(1,1).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields :question/worked-solution "The point of intersection consists of the coordinates $(x,y)$ that satisfy both equations $y=4x+3$ and $y=-x-2.$ So, we need to solve the system of equations consisting of the two lines:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=4x+3 \\ y=-x-2\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this system by substitution. Substituting the first equation $y=4x+3$ into the second equation $y=-x-2$ yields an equation that we can solve for $x:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}4x+3 & =-x-2 \\ 5x & =-5 \\ x & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

This is the $x$-coordinate of the point of intersection. To find the $y$-coordinate, we substitute $x=-1$ back into one of the equations, say $y=-x-2,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-x-2 \\  & =-(-1)-2 \\  & =1-2 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system is $x=-1$ and $y=-1.$ So, the coordinates of the intersection point are $(-1,-1).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-3570d971-4147-56ab-ae02-49d2d0cf3575"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-3570d971-4147-56ab-ae02-49d2d0cf3575" :answer-field/id #uuid "3570d971-4147-56ab-ae02-49d2d0cf3575" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-979be2e5-b995-5f79-92bc-1452bf76979d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-979be2e5-b995-5f79-92bc-1452bf76979d" "answer-e605f897-7836-56eb-9e13-386de276895a" "answer-04a54877-c197-56e8-954f-97fa34f640d6" "answer-a8935a5c-80c0-5239-b637-2aac33da488b" "answer-d03bf538-f673-50d4-bccb-b6bd89abd7f6"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-979be2e5-b995-5f79-92bc-1452bf76979d" :answer/id #uuid "979be2e5-b995-5f79-92bc-1452bf76979d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(-1,-1)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e605f897-7836-56eb-9e13-386de276895a" :answer/id #uuid "e605f897-7836-56eb-9e13-386de276895a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(-1,1)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-04a54877-c197-56e8-954f-97fa34f640d6" :answer/id #uuid "04a54877-c197-56e8-954f-97fa34f640d6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(1,-1)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a8935a5c-80c0-5239-b637-2aac33da488b" :answer/id #uuid "a8935a5c-80c0-5239-b637-2aac33da488b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(1,1)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d03bf538-f673-50d4-bccb-b6bd89abd7f6" :answer/id #uuid "d03bf538-f673-50d4-bccb-b6bd89abd7f6" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "No intersection" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069112 :question/problem "The point of intersection of the lines $y=3x-1$ and $y=-4x+6$ has coordinates

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-1 & =-4x+6 \\ 3x & =-4x+7 \\ 7x & =7 \\ x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This is the $x$-coordinate of the point of intersection. To find the $y$-coordinate, we substitute $x=1$ back into one of the equations, say $y=3x-1,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3x-1 \\  & =3(1)-1 \\  & =3-1 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system is $x=1,\,y=2.$ So, the coordinates of the intersection point are $(\,1,2\,).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186066106 :answer-field/correct "answer-43d86f66-2db2-5d8f-b88c-c725aa3c7f93" :answer-field/choices ["answer-43d86f66-2db2-5d8f-b88c-c725aa3c7f93"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-43d86f66-2db2-5d8f-b88c-c725aa3c7f93" :answer/id #uuid "43d86f66-2db2-5d8f-b88c-c725aa3c7f93" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186066105 :answer-field/correct "answer-116be24f-5fd6-5889-ac0f-f72b509821b0" :answer-field/choices ["answer-116be24f-5fd6-5889-ac0f-f72b509821b0"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-116be24f-5fd6-5889-ac0f-f72b509821b0" :answer/id #uuid "116be24f-5fd6-5889-ac0f-f72b509821b0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-8fea67f7-ec4c-5ab9-8c67-4d43507c8b87" :question/id #uuid "8fea67f7-ec4c-5ab9-8c67-4d43507c8b87" :question/math-academy-id "q-215406" :question/problem "The point of intersection of the lines $y=5x+2$ and $y=-2x-5$ has coordinates

$$

{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t} & {e}^{2t} \\ 0 & -2{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{4t}\cdot (-2{e}^{2t})-0\cdot {e}^{2t}}[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{-{e}^{-6t}}{2}[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{-4t} & {e}^{-4t} \\ 0 & -{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}]. \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{-4t} & {e}^{-4t} \\ 0 & -{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{-4t} \\ -2{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}-{e}^{-4t} \\ -2{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int -{e}^{-4t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -2{e}^{-2t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-4t} \\ {e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t} & {e}^{2t} \\ 0 & -2{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-4t} \\ {e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{4} \\ -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-57ab610c-28ab-5d09-83f7-d68b274b353d" "answer-field-9aa355cf-d45f-5b54-bcec-6c9a1e489b0d"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-57ab610c-28ab-5d09-83f7-d68b274b353d" :answer-field/id #uuid "57ab610c-28ab-5d09-83f7-d68b274b353d" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-8535759b-fe73-52af-853f-f3486f41d48a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-8535759b-fe73-52af-853f-f3486f41d48a"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8535759b-fe73-52af-853f-f3486f41d48a" :answer/id #uuid "8535759b-fe73-52af-853f-f3486f41d48a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2e^{-2t}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-9aa355cf-d45f-5b54-bcec-6c9a1e489b0d" :answer-field/id #uuid "9aa355cf-d45f-5b54-bcec-6c9a1e489b0d" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-f89927db-d31d-51e0-b063-5d1318a6634f" :answer-field/choices ["answer-f89927db-d31d-51e0-b063-5d1318a6634f"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f89927db-d31d-51e0-b063-5d1318a6634f" :answer/id #uuid "f89927db-d31d-51e0-b063-5d1318a6634f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166936 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-59d9272b-7eb2-549a-868b-86d14c7fdef5"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-59d9272b-7eb2-549a-868b-86d14c7fdef5" :question/id #uuid "59d9272b-7eb2-549a-868b-86d14c7fdef5" :question/math-academy-id "q-336703" :question/problem "Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into the {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation." :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L2},$ and $\text{L3}.$ Let's substitute ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$ from $\text{L1}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into $\text{initial system of ODEs}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{pre-multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-dfeef9c0-222d-580e-9176-2a58212a74b2" "answer-field-e749236f-06ab-5ec0-b55c-1658240128bd" You are given the following conditional expectations:

$$
\textrm{E}[X \mid Y=u] = 6, \quad \textrm{E}[X \mid Y=v] = 9, \quad \textrm{E}[X \mid Y=w] = 3.
$$

variables, and suppose $\text{E}[X∣Y]=\sqrt{3}\,Y+1.$ If $\text{E}[Y]=\sqrt{3},$ what is $\text{E}[X]?$" :question/worked-solution "We are given an expression for $\text{E}[X∣Y]$ in terms of $Y,$ and The arm then randomly picks one of these $n$ items and scans its position number (from $1$ to $n,$ each value equally likely).

What is the expected position number scanned?

The expected position number scanned is
{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "This is a two-step random process: first, a box is selected containing $n$ items uniformly from $1$ through $150,$ and then an item is chosen uniformly in one of the positions numbered $1$ through $n.$

- Let $Y$ be the number of items in the box. Since this is an integer selected uniformly from $1$ to $150,$ we have $Y∼U\{1,2,…,150\}.$

- Let $X$ be the position number scanned, an integer selected uniformly from $1$ to $Y.$

We are asked to compute $\text{E}[X].$ Since the distribution of $X$ depends on $Y,$ we apply the tower property:

$$
\text{E}[X]=\text{E}[\text{E}[X∣Y]]
$$

Given $Y=n,$ the number $X$ is chosen uniformly from $1$ to $n.$ So, we have that

$$
\text{E}[X∣Y=n]=\frac{n+1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\text{E}[X]=\text{E}[\frac{Y+1}{2}].
$$

Now, we apply the linearity of expectation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \text{E}[Y+1] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (\text{E}[Y]+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Y$ is uniformly distributed on $\{1,2,…,150\},$ we use the formula for the mean of the first $n$ integers:

$$
\text{E}[Y]=\frac{150+1}{2}=75.5
$$

Substituting, we finally get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (\text{E}[Y]+1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (75.5+1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 76.5 \\  & =38.25.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f05f3dbe-00ff-5d9e-ab0d-54ff37d66045"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-f05f3dbe-00ff-5d9e-ab0d-54ff37d66045" :answer-field/id #uuid "f05f3dbe-00ff-5d9e-ab0d-54ff37d66045" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-9cc71da5-b68e-5e22-b93f-45f1f89b8b2b" :answer-field/choices ["answer-9cc71da5-b68e-5e22-b93f-45f1f89b8b2b"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9cc71da5-b68e-5e22-b93f-45f1f89b8b2b" :answer/id #uuid "9cc71da5-b68e-5e22-b93f-45f1f89b8b2b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "38.25" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-12dc9838-1006-5e99-98b8-8a2304014d14" :question/id #uuid "12dc9838-1006-5e99-98b8-8a2304014d14" :question/math-academy-id "q-275576" :question/problem "In a puzzle game, a room's difficulty level $n$ is selected randomly from $1$ to $120,$ with each value equally likely. Then, a player is asked to guess an integer uniformly and randomly from $1$ to $n.$ What is the expected value of the player’s guess?" :question/worked-solution "This is a two-step random process: first, an integer $n$ is chosen uniformly from $1$ to $301,$ and then a number is chosen uniformly from $1$ to $n.$ We are asked to find the expected value of the number selected in the second step.

- Let $Y$ be the first random number, an integer selected uniformly from $1$ to $301.$

- Let $X$ be the player’s guess, an integer selected uniformly from $1$ to $Y.$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\text{E}[Y]=\frac{1+301}{2}=151.
$$

Substituting, we finally get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (1+\text{E}[Y]) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (1+151) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 152 \\  & =76.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186205421 :answer-field/correct 17592186205425 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186208946 :question/problem "A video game randomly selects a level difficulty $d$ from $1$ to $500,$ with each value equally likely. Once the difficulty is chosen, a treasure chest is placed in one of $d$ zones within the level, numbered from $1$ to $d,$ with each zone equally likely to receive the chest.

What is the expected number of the zone where the chest appears?

The expected number of the zone where the chest appears is
{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "This is a two-step random process: first, a level difficulty is selected uniformly from the integers $1$ through $500,$ and then a treasure chest is placed uniformly in one of the zones numbered $1$ through $d,$ where $d$ is the selected difficulty.

- Let $Y$ be the difficulty level of the chosen level. Since the difficulty is chosen uniformly from $1$ to $500,$ we have $Y∼U\{1,2,…,500\}.$

- Let $X$ be the number of the zone where the chest is placed, which is chosen uniformly from $1$ to $Y.$

We are asked to compute $\text{E}[X].$ Since $X$ depends on $Y,$ we apply the tower property:

$$
\text{E}[X]=\text{E}[\text{E}[X∣Y]]
$$

Given $Y=d,$ the zone is selected uniformly from $1$ to $d.$ So, we have that

$$
\text{E}[X∣Y=d]=\frac{d+1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\text{E}[X]=\text{E}[\frac{Y+1}{2}].
$$

Now, we apply the linearity of expectation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \text{E}[Y+1] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (\text{E}[Y]+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Y$ is uniformly distributed on $\{1,2,…,500\},$ we compute

$$
\text{E}[Y]=\frac{1+500}{2}=250.5.
$$

Substituting, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (250.5+1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 251.5 \\  & =125.75.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186205427 :answer-field/correct "answer-630c2241-afa1-5bd5-9578-2f06d9c7212c" :answer-field/choices ["answer-630c2241-afa1-5bd5-9578-2f06d9c7212c"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-630c2241-afa1-5bd5-9578-2f06d9c7212c" :answer/id #uuid "630c2241-afa1-5bd5-9578-2f06d9c7212c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "125.75" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186209887 :tutorial/content "Recall that if $X$ is a discrete random variable, the expected value of $X$ is given by

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \sum_{x} x\cdot P(X = x).
$$

There is an alternative method for computing $\textrm{E}[X],$ which allows us to compute the expected value of a random variable by conditioning on another variable.  

Suppose another discrete random variable $Y$ takes on a set of possible values. If we know $\textrm{E}[X \mid Y = y]$ for each value $y,$ then the **law of total expectation** states

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \sum_{y} \textrm{E}[X \mid Y = y] \cdot P(Y = y).
$$

 

Conceptually, this tells us that $\textrm{E}[X]$ is just a weighted average of the conditional expectations $\textrm{E}[X \mid Y = y],$ where each weight is the probability $P(Y = y).$  

In many problems, directly computing $\textrm{E}[X]$ from the definition can be difficult. It turns out that breaking $\textrm{E}[X]$ up into conditional pieces often simplifies things. The law of total expectation is especially useful when $X$ depends on an underlying condition $Y,$ and each conditional case is easier to analyze than the full distribution of $X.$

Let’s see how this works in practice with a few examples." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186209888 :tutorial/content "Let $X$ and $Y$ be discrete random variables, where $Y$ takes values $\alpha$ and $\beta$ with probabilities $0.4$ and $0.6,$ respectively. Suppose we are given the following conditional expectations:

- $\textrm{E}[X \mid Y = \alpha] = 7$

- $\textrm{E}[X \mid Y = \beta] = 3$

Let's compute $\textrm{E}[X]$ using the law of total expectation.

The law of total expectation states

$$
\textrm{E}[X]= \sum_y \textrm{E} [X \mid Y = y] \cdot P(Y=y).
$$

In this problem, $Y$ takes two values:

- $Y = \alpha$ with probability $0.4,$ and $\textrm{E}[X \mid Y = \alpha] = 7$

- $Y = \beta$ with probability $0.6,$ and $\textrm{E}[X \mid Y = \beta] = 3$

So, we calculate our expected value as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =\text{E}[X∣Y=\alpha ]\cdot P(Y=\alpha )+\text{E}[X∣Y=\beta ]\cdot P(Y=\beta ) \\  & =7\cdot 0.4+3\cdot 0.6 \\  & =2.8+1.8 \\  & =4.6\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186209885 :tutorial/content "We’ve seen that the law of total expectation allows us to compute the expected value of a random variable $X$ by conditioning on another variable $Y.$ This idea extends naturally to a more general and elegant identity called the **tower property**:

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \textrm{E}[\textrm{E}[X \mid Y]]
$$

At first glance, this may look abstract, so let’s unpack what it means.

The inner term $\textrm{E}[X \mid Y]$ is itself a *random variable*—its value depends on the outcome of $Y.$ The outer expectation then takes the average of that conditional expectation over all possible values of $Y.$

In other words, we are averaging $X$ in two stages:

- Within each scenario (for each possible value of $Y$), we find the expected value of $X.$

- Across all scenarios, we take the weighted average of those conditional expectations, where the weights are the probabilities of each $Y.$

Let’s explore a few examples to build some intuition." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186209955 :tutorial/content "Let $X$ and $Y$ be discrete random variables, and suppose 

$$
\textrm{E}[X \mid Y] = \sqrt{3}\,Y + 1.
$$

If $\textrm{E}[Y] = \sqrt3,$ let's compute $\textrm{E}[X]$. 

This is a direct application of the tower property, which states that

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \textrm{E}[\textrm{E}[X \mid Y]].
$$

So, we substitute the given expression for the inner expectation:

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \textrm{E}\left[\sqrt{3}\,Y + 1\right]
$$

Now, we apply the linearity of expectation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =\text{E}[\sqrt{3}\,Y+1] \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \text{E}[Y]+\text{E}[1] \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \sqrt{3}+1 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186209886 :tutorial/content "Let $X$ and $Y$ be discrete random variables, and suppose $Y$ takes only two values $y_1$ and $y_2.$  We want to show that the *law of total expectation* holds in this simple case:

$$
\mathbb{E}[X] = \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y = y_1] \cdot P(Y = y_1) + \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y = y_2] \cdot P(Y = y_2)
$$

We start with the definition of expectation, given by

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \sum_x x \cdot P(X = x).
$$

Next, we express $P(X = x)$ using the law of total probability:

$$
P(X = x) = P(X = x \mid Y = y_1) \cdot P(Y = y_1) + P(X = x \mid Y = y_2) \cdot P(Y = y_2)
$$

Substituting this expression into the expectation formula, we get

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \sum_x x \left( P(X = x \mid Y = y_1) \cdot P(Y = y_1) + P(X = x \mid Y = y_2) \cdot P(Y = y_2) \right).
$$

We can now distribute the sum across the two terms

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = P(Y = y_1) \cdot \sum_x x \cdot P(X = x \mid Y = y_1) + P(Y = y_2) \cdot \sum_x x \cdot P(X = x \mid Y = y_2).
$$

But each of the sums above is just a conditional expectation according to the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{x}x\cdot P(X=x∣Y={y}_{1}) & =\text{E}[X∣Y={y}_{1}] \\ {\sum }_{x}x\cdot P(X=x∣Y={y}_{2}) & =\text{E}[X∣Y={y}_{2}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we conclude that

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\textrm{E}[X] = \textrm{E}[X \mid Y = y_1] \cdot P(Y = y_1) + \textrm{E}[X \mid Y = y_2] \cdot P(Y = y_2)},
$$

as required.

We can use a similar argument to prove the more general case, where $Y$ takes more than two values." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186209889 :tutorial/content "Let $X$ and $Y$ be discrete random variables. Now, we want to prove that the tower property holds:

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \textrm{E}[\textrm{E}[X \mid Y]]
$$

We start with the definition of expectation

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \sum_x x \cdot P(X = x).
$$

Next, we apply the law of total probability to express $P(X = x)$ in terms of $Y.$  Let $S_Y$ denote the support of $Y.$ Then, we have

$$
P(X = x) = \sum_{y \in S_Y} P(X = x \mid Y = y) \cdot P(Y = y).
$$

Substituting this into the expectation formula, we get

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \sum_x x \left( \sum_{y \in S_Y} P(X = x \mid Y = y) \cdot P(Y = y) \right).
$$

We can now switch the order of summation:

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \sum_{y \in S_Y} P(Y = y) \cdot \sum_x x \cdot P(X = x \mid Y = y)
$$

Each inner sum is just the conditional expectation $\textrm{E}[X \mid Y = y]{:}$

$$
\sum_x x \cdot P(X = x \mid Y = y) = \textrm{E}[X \mid Y = y]
$$

So, we conclude that

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \sum_{y \in S_Y} \textrm{E}[X \mid Y = y] \cdot P(Y = y).
$$

But this expression is just the definition of $\textrm{E}[\textrm{E}[X \mid Y]]$ for discrete $Y{:}$

$$
\textrm{E}[\textrm{E}[X \mid Y]] = \sum_{y \in S_Y} \textrm{E}[X \mid Y = y] \cdot P(Y = y)
$$

Therefore, we have shown that

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\textrm{E}[X] = \textrm{E}[\textrm{E}[X \mid Y]]},
$$

as required." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186208871 :activity/expected-seconds 1140.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186173356 :answer-field/choices 17592186173360] [:db/retract 17592186173356 :answer-field/choices 17592186173361] [:db/retract 17592186173356 :answer-field/choices 17592186173357] [:db/retract 17592186173356 :answer-field/choices 17592186173358] [:db/retract 17592186173356 :answer-field/choices 17592186173359] [:db/retract 17592186173344 :answer-field/choices 17592186173345] [:db/retract 17592186173344 :answer-field/choices 17592186173346] [:db/retract 17592186173344 :answer-field/choices 17592186173347] [:db/retract 17592186173344 :answer-field/choices 17592186173348] [:db/retract 17592186173344 :answer-field/choices 17592186173349] {:db/id 17592186175965 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-c3cbf898-5adf-5f1a-9995-178ecdb7db19"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186175964 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-551dfc8f-f76b-5f91-a118-1f244aa7dd9d"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176183 :question/worked-solution "The position of a point in cylindrical polar coordinates is written as $(r,\theta ,z),$ where

Again, recall that for a point $(r,\theta,z)$ in cylindrical polar coordinates,

- $r\geq 0$ and $\theta\in [0,2\pi)$ are the usual plane polar coordinates, and

- $z\in (-\infty, \infty)$ is the usual Cartesian $z$-coordinate.

With that in mind, let's examine our equation:

$$
z^2=r^2
$$

This equation requires that the square of the distance from any point on the surface to the $xy$-plane equals the square of the distance from that point to the $z$-axis.
In other words, the tangent of the angle between any position vector on the surface and the $z$-axis, which is given by $\dfrac{r}{z}$, must be equal to

$$
\dfrac{r}{z} =\pm \sqrt{\dfrac{r^2}{z^2}} = \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{r^2}{r^2}} = \pm1.
$$

On the other hand, $\theta$ can vary arbitrarily in its domain. 

- For $\dfrac{r}{z} = 1,$ the angle between the position vector of any point on the surface and the $z$-axis must be equal $\dfrac{\pi}{4}.$ This corresponds to a *half-cone* for positive $z{:}$

![](images/18/1841d50bb07c0e6787f4824af0e13516912fb9ad77fac0515f00c243899eb18e.png)

 

- On the other hand, for $\dfrac{r}{z} = -1,$ the angle between the position vector of any point on the surface and the $z$-axis must be equal $\dfrac{3\pi}{4}.$ This corresponds to a *half-cone* for negative $z{:}$

![](images/e3/e32b1b4ba84faea7a4dc536e0f49bcda9295a4a42790162b3b9bad06db39a908.png)

![](images/45/452f0482708656146b2e5cd7f58832250fc95e25707cacb66800255aee977b21.png)" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186085290 :answer-field/correct 17592186085294 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-6bfc4a3c-5e7b-532b-95bd-4e49a1efa533" :question/id #uuid "6bfc4a3c-5e7b-532b-95bd-4e49a1efa533" :question/math-academy-id "q-26914" :question/problem "Which of the following is the graph of $y=4({2}^{x})+4?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we plot the graph of $y={2}^{x}:$

![](images/6d/6d5b359544227b89d1dc5ca9967c9dfcda84bf5345184063a1d0deef994c3692.png)

Therefore, our function takes the form

$$
y=k({10}^{x})-3.
$$

We can solve for $k$ by finding a point on the graph and substituting for $x$ and $y.$ The labeled point on the graph is $(0,1),$ so we substitute $x=0$ and $y=1$ into the function and solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =k({10}^{x})-3 \\ 1 & =k({10}^{0})-3 \\ 1 & =k(1)-3 \\ 1 & =k-3 \\ 4 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our function takes the form

$$
y=k({2}^{x})+1.
$$

We can solve for $k$ by finding a point on the graph and substituting for $x$ and $y.$ The labeled point on the graph is $(0,3.5),$ so we substitute $x=0$ and $y=3.5$ into the function and solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =k({2}^{x})+1 \\ 3.5 & =k({2}^{0})+1 \\ 3.5 & =k(1)+1 \\ 3.5 & =k+1 \\ 2.5 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curve is $y=2.5({2}^{x})+1.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d29ba8d5-82d0-52b6-939b-119fe78d8db4"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d29ba8d5-82d0-52b6-939b-119fe78d8db4" :answer-field/id #uuid "d29ba8d5-82d0-52b6-939b-119fe78d8db4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-71407824-a8ad-5e1e-b6fe-b9ba8075671b" :answer-field/choices ["answer-e50c8d48-2425-5e73-bd1c-d2a842248e31" "answer-b1e9d21b-a213-54e5-93ab-0172b47154ba" "answer-4b2740d1-15f5-5c10-9d5d-f42781190300" "answer-71407824-a8ad-5e1e-b6fe-b9ba8075671b" "answer-40cd7eb5-26eb-5f47-9864-d179eee20251"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e50c8d48-2425-5e73-bd1c-d2a842248e31" :answer/id #uuid "e50c8d48-2425-5e73-bd1c-d2a842248e31" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "y=0.5({2}^{x})+1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b1e9d21b-a213-54e5-93ab-0172b47154ba" :answer/id #uuid "b1e9d21b-a213-54e5-93ab-0172b47154ba" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "y=1.5({2}^{x})+1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4b2740d1-15f5-5c10-9d5d-f42781190300" :answer/id #uuid "4b2740d1-15f5-5c10-9d5d-f42781190300" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "y=1.5({2}^{x})+2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-71407824-a8ad-5e1e-b6fe-b9ba8075671b" :answer/id #uuid "71407824-a8ad-5e1e-b6fe-b9ba8075671b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "y=2.5({2}^{x})+1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-40cd7eb5-26eb-5f47-9864-d179eee20251" :answer/id #uuid "40cd7eb5-26eb-5f47-9864-d179eee20251" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "y=2.5({2}^{x})-2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186088868 :tutorial/content "Adding a value to $y=2^x$ will **translate** (shift) the exponential function up or down the $y$-axis. 

For instance, adding $3$ to $y=2^x$ will move each point on the exponential function $3$ units up.

![](images/c8/c89fd5fdcdc3773143a5f14ecb20f5bd2917bce20ece18a7dc70631bf358a0e8.png)

Note the following points:

1\. The $y$-intercept $(0,1)$ has moved up $3$ units to the point $(0,4).$

2\. The horizontal asymptote $y=0$ has moved up $3$ units to $y=3.$

As a second example, let's consider the function $y=2^x-3.$ In this case, the graph of $y=2^x$ is shifted *down* by $3$ units.

![](images/84/84987b3e9138a2e7e8afe70a7aa28a1cd81e081033aa2a766773e63cb8f41da5.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186087901 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166890 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-957651b3-45e4-5a93-853b-1785322d0942"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-957651b3-45e4-5a93-853b-1785322d0942" :question/id #uuid "957651b3-45e4-5a93-853b-1785322d0942" :question/math-academy-id "q-138022" :question/problem "Find the maximum value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}$ given that $‖x‖=1.$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that ${x}_{2}^{2}\ge 0.$ So, we have that

$$
-{x}_{2}^{2}\le {x}_{2}^{2}.
$$

As a result,  

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & \le {x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $‖x‖=1$ is equivalent to ${x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}=1.$ So,  in turn, $Q(x)\le 1.$

So, the value of $Q(x)$ can be no greater than $1.$ But before we conclude that $1$ is the maximum, we need to find a vector such that $Q(x)=1.$

Notice that when $x={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =(1)^{2}-(0)^{2} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, given that $‖x‖=1,$ the maximum value of $Q(x)$ is equal to $1.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields "3e4f6268-3e58-5684-9bea-f874fd53aaf3" :question/math-academy-id "q-138069" :question/problem "Find the minimum value of $Q(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}$ given that $‖x‖=1.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of the matrix $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -6 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)(\lambda -3) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =-2,\,3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}=-2.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-55b2d835-40d6-572d-8824-c8db3cfc4a3b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Find the arc length of the polar curve $r={e}^{\theta }$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}$ (shown in blue in the diagram above)." :question/worked-solution "The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={e}^{\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }={e}^{\theta }.
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{({e}^{\theta })}^{2}+{({e}^{\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{e}^{2\theta }+{e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{2{e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{e}^{\theta }{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}({e}^{\pi /2}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =\sqrt{2}({e}^{\pi /2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186091738 :answer-field/correct "answer-ad493751-d3c8-5246-8a30-3a2a4aefa677" :answer-field/choices ["answer-635d1f78-1ff1-548c-b1d2-727e82d8d662" "answer-b6a466dc-34ab-5292-b042-6078d2d70c1f" "answer-ad493751-d3c8-5246-8a30-3a2a4aefa677" "answer-d7923dd0-6a1a-51d5-bb60-8f501bdb44b0"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-635d1f78-1ff1-548c-b1d2-727e82d8d662" :answer/id #uuid "635d1f78-1ff1-548c-b1d2-727e82d8d662" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\sqrt{2}({e}^{\pi /2}-1)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b6a466dc-34ab-5292-b042-6078d2d70c1f" :answer/id #uuid "b6a466dc-34ab-5292-b042-6078d2d70c1f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\sqrt{2}({e}^{\pi /2}-{e}^{-\pi /2})" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ad493751-d3c8-5246-8a30-3a2a4aefa677" :answer/id #uuid "ad493751-d3c8-5246-8a30-3a2a4aefa677" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{2}({e}^{\pi /2}-1)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d7923dd0-6a1a-51d5-bb60-8f501bdb44b0" :answer/id #uuid "d7923dd0-6a1a-51d5-bb60-8f501bdb44b0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{2}{e}^{\pi /2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186100942 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-2014fae0-a89c-5d1e-8735-16f0159dd06c"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-2014fae0-a89c-5d1e-8735-16f0159dd06c" :question/id #uuid "2014fae0-a89c-5d1e-8735-16f0159dd06c" :question/math-academy-id "q-119283" :question/problem "The growth rate of a watermelon production $P(t)$ in a certain land is jointly proportional to the watermelon production at time $t,$ measured in months, and the difference between the land's carrying capacity and the watermelon production. If the constant of proportionality is $0.2$ and the maximum possible watermelon production is $1\,800,$ which differential equation could be used to model $P(t)?$" :question/worked-solution "Since the watermelon production growth rate is *jointly* proportional to the watermelon production at time $t$ and the difference between the carrying capacity and the watermelon production, the watermelon production follows a logistic growth model.

A logistic growth equation has the form

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=kP(a-P),
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a>P$ is the carrying capacity.

In this case, the constant of proportionality is $k=0.2,$ and the carrying capacity is $a=1\,800.$ Therefore, the watermelon production is given by the equation

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=0.2P(1\,800-P).
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-bb8637b4-c23b-5591-8ea3-4b43b99fdc95"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "42788b85-30ff-5f36-a9fd-86e424b97617" :question/math-academy-id "q-138980" :question/problem "Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={cos}^{3}⁡t,\,y={sin}^{3}⁡t,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?" :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({cos}^{3}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({sin}^{3}⁡t)=3{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{3}⁡t\sqrt{{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t)}^{2}+{(3{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{3}⁡t\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{4}⁡t+9{sin}^{4}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{3}⁡t\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the identity ${sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t=1,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{3}⁡t\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{3}⁡t\sqrt{(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{3}⁡t\cdot |3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t|\,\text{d}t \\  & =6\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{3}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =6\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{4}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-632462c4-14ed-5c49-b96d-6314fe36a641"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "The exact global minimum value of the function $f(x)={x}^{2}-4x+5$ on the closed interval $0\le x\le 5$ is{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's apply the candidates test step by step.

**Step 1**: We find the critical points. Taking the derivative of $f(x)={x}^{2}-4x+5,$ we get

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=2x-4.
$$

Solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-4 & =0 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the critical points are $x=2$ and the endpoints $x=0,5$ (since the derivative is not defined at the endpoints)

**Step 2**: We evaluate $f(x)$ at the critical points.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0) & ={0}^{2}-4(0)+5=5 \\ f(2) & ={2}^{2}-4(2)+5=1 \\ f(5) & ={5}^{2}-4(5)+5=10\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: We compare all of the values found in step $2.$

- The smallest value is $f(2)=1,$ so the global minimum is $1.$

- The greatest value is $f(5)=10,$ so the global maximum is $10.$

Remember that a parallelogram is a quadrilateral with $2$ pairs of parallel sides.

With that in mind, let's look at each shape in turn.

- The shape $P$ is a parallelogram since it has $2$ pairs of parallel sides.

- The shape $Q$ is a square. Therefore, its opposite sides are parallel, so it is a parallelogram.

- The shape $R$ is a rhombus. Since the opposite sides of a rhombus are parallel, it is a parallelogram.

- The shape $S$ is a kite. It has no pairs of opposite sides that are parallel, therefore, it is not a parallelogram.

Therefore, shapes $P,$ $Q,$ and $R$ are parallelograms. :question/problem "$(-5)(2x+3y)-5y=$"] ["question-dcca9682-5c6e-581c-bcc3-60c96a3dddcd" :question/worked-solution "First, we distribute the $(-5)$ over each of the terms in parentheses.

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}(-5)(2x+3y)-5y & = \\ (-5)\cdot 2x+(-5)\cdot 3y-5y & = \\ (-10x)+(-15y)-5y & = \\ -10x-15y-5y\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we collect like terms.

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}-10x-15y-5y & = \\ -10x+(-15y-5y) & = \\ -10x-20y\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-dcca9682-5c6e-581c-bcc3-60c96a3dddcd" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-add26c3a-8ea0-579d-b7c2-eb977845c92f" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "A water tank with a capacity of $5,000$ liters is filled with water to $42.5%$ of its capacity. How much water is in the tank?"] ["question-aeb2c9f4-4f11-5f7d-ac23-e92ca6ecec4e" :question/worked-solution "To solve this problem, we can use the formula:

$$
\text{part}=\text{percentage}\times \text{whole}
$$

In our case, the whole is the capacity of the tank, which is $5,000$ liters. The percentage is $42.5%,$ and the part is the amount of water in the tank.

**Method 1**

First, we convert the percentage to a decimal:

$$
42.5%=42.5÷100=0.425
$$

Applying our formula, we have:

$$

So the ratio of triangles to hexagons is $2:10.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,2 &  & : & \,\,\,\, & \,\,\,10 &  \\ \,\,↓÷\,\,2 &  &  &  & \,\,\,↓÷\,\,2 &  \\ \,\,1 &  & : &  & \,\,\,5 & \end{aligned}
$$

- $-\frac{3}{4}$ is a rational number. It can be written as $\frac{(-3)}{4}.$

- $\frac{3}{4}$ is a rational number.

- $5$ is a rational number. It can be written as $\frac{5}{1}.$

II. $532$

III. $501$"] ["question-cca0b3f3-f64a-53b6-8329-0c693549bc28" :question/worked-solution "To check if a number is divisible by $7,$ double the last digit, subtract the result from the remaining digits, and then check if the difference is divisible by $7.$

- For the number $523,$ we have that 

$$
52-2(3)=52-6=46
$$

which is not divisible by $7.$ Therefore, $523$ is not divisible by $7.$

- For the number $532,$ we have that 

$$
53-2(2)=53-4=49
$$

which is divisible by $7.$ Therefore, $532$ is divisible by $7.$

- For the number $501,$ we have that 

$$
50-2(1)=50-2=48
$$

which is not divisible by $7.$ Therefore, $501$ is not divisible by $7.$

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={2}^{\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }={2}^{\theta }\operatorname{ln}⁡2.
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{({2}^{\theta })}^{2}+{({2}^{\theta }\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{2}^{2\theta }+{2}^{2\theta }{ln}^{2}⁡2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(1+{ln}^{2}⁡2){2}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{1+{ln}^{2}⁡2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{2}^{\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{1+{ln}^{2}⁡2}\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\cdot {2}^{\theta }{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{ln}^{2}⁡2}\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\cdot ({2}^{\pi /2}-{2}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{1+{ln}^{2}⁡2}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}({2}^{\pi /2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-da080066-6980-5e46-a310-b96dc7f7120c" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-2a4caf7b-52fc-5e88-b891-82cc9a3a2cf7" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-a1c1460f-c5a2-5e99-b7f7-17db73e707c6" :question/worked-solution "The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{(1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{2-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-a1c1460f-c5a2-5e99-b7f7-17db73e707c6" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-452ad711-f8a6-5c7b-b980-01feac5bbbde" :answer-field/id #uuid Find the arc length $L$ of the polar curve $r=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ for $\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{5\pi }{6}$ (shown in blue in the diagram above). Do not round the answer.

$L=$
{{field-1}}"] ["question-a9290c4e-ece3-5a58-aecc-bb62b4894116" :question/worked-solution "The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6}\sqrt{{(3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6}\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +9{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6}\sqrt{9}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6}3\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /6} \\  & =3(\frac{5\pi }{6}-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-a9290c4e-ece3-5a58-aecc-bb62b4894116" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-3487b8fc-2024-52a0-8191-9d6c368ac790" :answer-field/id #uuid "3487b8fc-2024-52a0-8191-9d6c368ac790"] ["answer-901a723b-e6e5-572f-9b48-3f4f2a4dea43" :answer/id #uuid "901a723b-e6e5-572f-9b48-3f4f2a4dea43"] ["answer-901a723b-e6e5-572f-9b48-3f4f2a4dea43" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-901a723b-e6e5-572f-9b48-3f4f2a4dea43" :answer/value "\pi"] ["answer-field-3487b8fc-2024-52a0-8191-9d6c368ac790" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-3487b8fc-2024-52a0-8191-9d6c368ac790" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-3487b8fc-2024-52a0-8191-9d6c368ac790" :answer-field/correct "answer-901a723b-e6e5-572f-9b48-3f4f2a4dea43"] ["answer-field-3487b8fc-2024-52a0-8191-9d6c368ac790" :answer-field/choices "answer-901a723b-e6e5-572f-9b48-3f4f2a4dea43"] ["question-a9290c4e-ece3-5a58-aecc-bb62b4894116" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-3487b8fc-2024-52a0-8191-9d6c368ac790"] [17592186092374 :knowledge-point/questions "question-a9290c4e-ece3-5a58-aecc-bb62b4894116"] ["question-6ddfe515-d085-541a-8dab-b3a5ab40f555" :question/id #uuid "6ddfe515-d085-541a-8dab-b3a5ab40f555"] ["question-6ddfe515-d085-541a-8dab-b3a5ab40f555" :question/math-academy-id "q-353601"] ["question-6ddfe515-d085-541a-8dab-b3a5ab40f555" :question/problem "![](images/ec/ec0b88ec00ef7e7061af0b08761eb73f05a5f669208babacbd4eb86736019230.png)

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=18{e}^{3\theta }.

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{{(6{e}^{3\theta })}^{2}+{(18{e}^{3\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{36{e}^{6\theta }+324{e}^{6\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{360{e}^{6\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =6\sqrt{10}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}{e}^{3\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =6\sqrt{10}{[\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3\theta }]}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =2\sqrt{10}{[{e}^{3\theta }]}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =2\sqrt{10}({e}^{\pi }-{e}^{0}) \\  & =2\sqrt{10}({e}^{\pi }-1).\end{aligned}

Now, we must determine the temperature during the month of January. Since we know that the temperature decreases on average by ${3.2}^{∘}\,\text{C}$ compared to December, we subtract the variation in temperature from the average temperature in December. This gives

$$
-{0.5}^{∘}\,\text{C}-{3.2}^{∘}\,\text{C}=-{3.7}^{∘}\,\text{C}.
$$

Therefore, the average temperature in Toronto in January is $-{3.7}^{∘}\,\text{C}.$"] ["question-aab3a1fe-f42d-5861-9d8c-8da472abefec" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["question-25541256-5bc3-5680-8cfb-415ab2841d24" :question/math-academy-id "q-2343"] ["question-25541256-5bc3-5680-8cfb-415ab2841d24" :question/problem "Find the values of $c$ that satisfy the mean value theorem for 
 $f(x)=2\sqrt{x}$ on the interval $[0,4].$"] ["question-25541256-5bc3-5680-8cfb-415ab2841d24" :question/worked-solution "The function $f(x)$ is continuous on $[0,4]$ and differentiable on $(0,4),$ hence we can apply the mean value theorem. 

So, the mean value theorem states that there exists a $c\in (0,4)$ such that

$$
{f}^{′}(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}.
$$

Plugging in $a=0$ and $b=4$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(c) & =\frac{f(4)-f(0)}{4-0} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{4}-2\sqrt{0}}{4} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt{x})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$

</tbody></table>"] ["question-dac59390-e4c1-5a03-ac45-73be8ac0d42f" :question/worked-solution "Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $f(y)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}+{y}_{2}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}+{y}_{2}^{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{y}_{1} & 1 \\ 1 & 2{y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${y}_{0}=y({x}_{0})=[\begin{aligned}2(1) \\ 1-3(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $y$ with respect to $x$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}(2{x}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}(2{x}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{2}-3{x}_{1}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{2}-3{x}_{1})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x)){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 9 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-dac59390-e4c1-5a03-ac45-73be8ac0d42f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-3703a9d4-39d0-52e0-b2bc-ee344c22c3a9" :answer-field/id #uuid
