</tbody></table>"] ["question-5bd6ce37-dfc0-53de-b48f-f0c1cbf86c1e" :question/worked-solution "Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $f(y)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}(2{y}_{1}+4{y}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}(2{y}_{1}+4{y}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}^{2}+8{y}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}^{2}+8{y}_{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 2{y}_{1} & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${y}_{0}=y({x}_{0})=[\begin{aligned}{1}^{2}+{0}^{2} \\ {1}^{2}-{0}^{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 2 & 8\end{aligned}].
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $y$ with respect to $x$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{2}^{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1} & 2{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{1} & -2{x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x)){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 2 & 8\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}12 & 0 \\ 20 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-5bd6ce37-dfc0-53de-b48f-f0c1cbf86c1e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-4bc9ae22-cb20-510a-b7a2-e6f0d1758238" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ 0 & -4 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

</tbody></table>"] ["question-fdb98924-99f5-55a4-8e7e-a090dae96539" :question/worked-solution "Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $f(y)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}(2{y}_{1}{y}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}(2{y}_{1}{y}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}^{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}^{3})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{y}_{2} & 2{y}_{1} \\ 3{y}_{1}^{2} & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${y}_{0}=y({x}_{0})=[\begin{aligned}2(1) \\ 3(-1)^{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}6 & 4 \\ 12 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $y$ with respect to $x$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}(2{x}_{1}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}(2{x}_{1}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}(3{x}_{2}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}(3{x}_{2}^{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 6{x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x)){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 4 \\ 12 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}12 & -24 \\ 24 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-fdb98924-99f5-55a4-8e7e-a090dae96539" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-0ca9696c-ed27-5b5d-bd05-4135421712bd" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(z(y(x)))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}z}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $z\in {R}^{2}$ by multiplying it by $C$ and outputs a vector $f(z)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}z}=C.
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{z}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{z}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{z}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{z}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ {y}_{2} & {y}_{1}\end{aligned}].
$$

Evaluating at ${y}_{0}=A{x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{2}$ by multiplying it by $A$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=A.
$$

In a previous lesson, we saw that the derivative of $f(\mathbf{y}(x))$ with respect to $x$ is given by the multivariable chain rule.

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d}x}= \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y_1} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y_1}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y_2} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y_2}{\partial x} + \dots + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y_n} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y_n}{\partial x}
$$

This can be written as a product of matrices as follows:

![](images/14/1482285b6db08d8b944fd98871736ffebd912d78842ceac6fbad959b9b9e9e6d.svg)

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d}x}
= \underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}\mathbf y}}_{1\times n} \cdot \underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf y}{\textrm{d}x}}_{n\times 1}
$$

where

- $\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}\mathbf y}$ is the *total derivative* of $f$ with respect to $\mathbf y$, which is a row vector of size $1\times n$, and

- $\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf y}{\textrm{d}x}$ is the *total derivative* of $\mathbf y$ with respect to $x$, which is a column vector of size $n\times 1.$

</tbody></table>"] ["question-3234de52-8801-51a2-806f-23f965c5de2f" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

The forcing term

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2}+t+3 \\ -{t}^{2}+2t\end{aligned}]
$$

of the inhomogeneous system of ODEs is polynomial of degree $2.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also polynomial of degree $2,$ i.e.

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}{t}^{2}+{b}_{1}t+{c}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}{t}^{2}+{b}_{2}t+{c}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{aligned}]{t}^{2}+[\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]t+[\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

where ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{c}_{1},{c}_{2}$ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the derivative of ${x}_{p}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{x}_{p}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ 2{a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the unknown constants, we substitute ${x}_{p}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}$ into our system:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}2{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ 2{a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}{t}^{2}+{b}_{1}t+{c}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}{t}^{2}+{b}_{2}t+{c}_{2}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2}+t+3 \\ -{t}^{2}+2t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ 2{a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-({a}_{2}{t}^{2}+{b}_{2}t+{c}_{2}) \\ {a}_{1}{t}^{2}+{b}_{1}t+{c}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2}+t+3 \\ -{t}^{2}+2t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0{t}^{2}+2{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ 0{t}^{2}+2{a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}(-{a}_{2}+2){t}^{2}+(-{b}_{2}+1)t+(-{c}_{2}+3) \\ ({a}_{1}-1){t}^{2}+({b}_{1}+2)t+{c}_{1}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding coefficients of like powers of $t,$ we get the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-{a}_{2}+2=0 \\ -\,{b}_{2}+1=2{a}_{1} \\ -\,{c}_{2}+3={b}_{1} \\ {a}_{1}-1=0 \\ {b}_{1}+2=2{a}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}={b}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first and fourth equations, we get

$$
{a}_{2}=2,\,{a}_{1}=1.
$$

Substituting these into the second and fifth equations, and solving for ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2},$ we get

$$
{b}_{2}=-1,\,{b}_{1}=2.
$$

Finally, substituting these last values into the third and sixth equations, and solving for ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we have

$$
{c}_{2}=1,\,{c}_{1}=-1.
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}+2t-1 \\ 2{t}^{2}-t+1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{t}^{2}+[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]t+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$"] ["question-3234de52-8801-51a2-806f-23f965c5de2f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-2933141c-2169-5b87-8fb5-b8ed2e025c9c" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

The forcing term

$$
{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]
$$

of the inhomogeneous system of ODEs is exponential. Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also exponential, i.e.

$$
{x}_{p}(t)={e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}],
$$

where $a,b$  are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the derivative of ${x}_{p}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{x}_{p}^{′}(t)=-3{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the unknown constants, we substitute ${x}_{p}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}$ into our system:

$$
\begin{aligned}-3{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot {e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]+{e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\ -3[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-3a \\ -3b\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2b \\ 2a\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-3a \\ -3b\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2b+1 \\ 2a+5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-2b+1=-3a \\ 2a+5=-3b\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get 

$$
-2b+1=-3a\,⇒\,a=\frac{2b-1}{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $b,$ we have

$$
2(\frac{2b-1}{3})+5=-3b\,⇒\,4b-2+15=-9b\,⇒\,b=-1.
$$

So,

$$
a=\frac{2(-1)-1}{3}=\frac{-2-1}{3}=-1.
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{x}_{p}(t)={e}^{-3t}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$"] ["question-2e73d348-8d9b-5a9f-8dbf-5305290f7f53" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-6c17466c-b8ca-50c3-9f75-a6a53610a6c3" :answer-field/id #uuid </tbody></table>"] [17592186167169 :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

The forcing term

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2t+1\end{aligned}]
$$

of the inhomogeneous system of ODEs is polynomial of degree $1.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also polynomial of degree $1,$ i.e.

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{aligned}]t+[\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

where ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{b}_{1},{b}_{2}$  are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the derivative of ${x}_{p}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{x}_{p}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the unknown constants, we substitute ${x}_{p}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}$ into our system:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]([\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{aligned}]t+[\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}])+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2t+1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}+3{a}_{2} \\ {a}_{1}-{a}_{2}\end{aligned}]t+[\begin{aligned}{b}_{1}+3{b}_{2} \\ {b}_{1}-{b}_{2}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2t+1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0t+{a}_{1} \\ 0t+{a}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}({a}_{1}+3{a}_{2})t+({b}_{1}+3{b}_{2}+1) \\ ({a}_{1}-{a}_{2}-2)t+({b}_{1}-{b}_{2}+1)\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{a}_{1}+3{a}_{2}=0 \\ {a}_{1}-{a}_{2}-2=0 \\ {b}_{1}+3{b}_{2}+1={a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}-{b}_{2}+1={a}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first two equations, we get 

$$
{a}_{1}=\frac{3}{2},\,{a}_{2}=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

 
Substituting these into the third and fourth equations, and solving for ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2},$ we have

$$
{b}_{1}=-1,\,{b}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

 

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=[\begin{aligned}3/2 \\ -1/2\end{aligned}]t+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1/2\end{aligned}].
$$"] [17592186167169 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-68397710-f20c-5389-86e2-ff7174f9153b" :answer/id #uuid "68397710-f20c-5389-86e2-ff7174f9153b"] ["answer-68397710-f20c-5389-86e2-ff7174f9153b" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-68397710-f20c-5389-86e2-ff7174f9153b" :answer/value "-1"] [17592186164048 :answer-field/correct "answer-68397710-f20c-5389-86e2-ff7174f9153b"] [17592186164048 :answer-field/choices "answer-68397710-f20c-5389-86e2-ff7174f9153b"] ["answer-168093fa-9a63-55ce-a515-83e652a3a0ce" :answer/id #uuid "168093fa-9a63-55ce-a515-83e652a3a0ce"] ["answer-168093fa-9a63-55ce-a515-83e652a3a0ce" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-168093fa-9a63-55ce-a515-83e652a3a0ce" :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}"] [17592186164047 :answer-field/correct "answer-168093fa-9a63-55ce-a515-83e652a3a0ce"] [17592186164047 :answer-field/choices "answer-168093fa-9a63-55ce-a515-83e652a3a0ce"] [17592186167990 :tutorial/content "Consider an **inhomogeneous** linear system of ordinary differential equations in component form:

Since the region lies to the left of the $y$-axis, the width of the cylindrical shells is given by $f(y)=0-(-\sqrt{y}+y)=\sqrt{y}-y.$ Using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}yf(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y(\sqrt{y}-y)\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{3/2}-{y}^{2})\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi ({\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{3/2}\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =2\pi ({\frac{2{y}^{5/2}}{5}|}_{0}^{1}-{\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{1}) \\  & =2\pi ((\frac{2}{5}-0)-(\frac{1}{3}-0)) \\  & =2\pi (\frac{2}{5}-\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{15}\end{aligned}

{{field-1}}"] ["question-2d1d4e63-93d8-5dc2-a21f-3d16bb6f6063" :question/worked-solution "First, we determine the points where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation for $y:$

The solutions are $y=0$ and $y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}.$ So, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}.$

{{field-1}}"] ["question-69689ccc-dfd4-5812-991b-d48dbc7eafee" :question/worked-solution "First, we determine the points where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}5y-5{y}^{4} & =0 \\ 5y(1-{y}^{3}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions are $y=0$ and $y=1.$ So, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=1.$ 

Using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}yf(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y(5y-5{y}^{4})\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(5{y}^{2}-5{y}^{5})\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi (5{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y-5{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{5}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =2\pi (\frac{5}{3}{y}^{3}\,{|}_{0}^{1}-\frac{5}{6}{y}^{6}\,{|}_{0}^{1}\,) \\  & =2\pi (\frac{5}{3}(1-0)-\frac{5}{6}(1-0)) \\  & =2\pi (\frac{5}{3}-\frac{5}{6}) \\  & =2\pi \cdot \frac{5}{6} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-69689ccc-dfd4-5812-991b-d48dbc7eafee" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-a692812a-555a-5732-b8c5-43f45d5cfb92" :answer-field/id #uuid "a692812a-555a-5732-b8c5-43f45d5cfb92"] ["answer-1b2bc8ac-9cce-5432-82e4-a0d93044820f" :answer/id #uuid "1b2bc8ac-9cce-5432-82e4-a0d93044820f"] ["answer-1b2bc8ac-9cce-5432-82e4-a0d93044820f" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-1b2bc8ac-9cce-5432-82e4-a0d93044820f" :answer/value "\frac{5\pi}{3}"] ["answer-field-a692812a-555a-5732-b8c5-43f45d5cfb92" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-a692812a-555a-5732-b8c5-43f45d5cfb92" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-a692812a-555a-5732-b8c5-43f45d5cfb92" :answer-field/correct "answer-1b2bc8ac-9cce-5432-82e4-a0d93044820f"] ["answer-field-a692812a-555a-5732-b8c5-43f45d5cfb92" :answer-field/choices "answer-1b2bc8ac-9cce-5432-82e4-a0d93044820f"] ["question-69689ccc-dfd4-5812-991b-d48dbc7eafee" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-a692812a-555a-5732-b8c5-43f45d5cfb92"] [17592186068815 :knowledge-point/questions "question-69689ccc-dfd4-5812-991b-d48dbc7eafee"] [17592186069988 :tutorial/content "Consider the plane region enclosed by the curve $x=f(y),$ the $y$-axis, and the horizontal lines $y=c$ and $y=d,$ as shown below. If we rotate this region $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis, we get a solid of revolution.

![](images/19/1927064dcef318f2c0490ff071532b024da30a328b2752c28e197171eeec6b5f.png)

One way of computing the volume of the solid is to divide the interval from $y=c$ to $y=d$ on the $y$-axis to get horizontal slices. This approach is called the **shell method**.

Consider one such slice of height $\Delta{y},$ as shown in the picture below (on the left). When this rectangle is rotated about the $x$-axis, it forms a solid **shell** (i.e., the skin of a cylinder).

![](images/25/2561448ab909594dda427b76860fcdda5147f8966fec9e20958d1c5fca11b536.png)

Since we assume that $\Delta{y}$ is very small, the outer radius of the shell approximately equals the inner radius $y.$ The thickness of the shell is $\Delta{y}$ and its height is $x=f(y)$.

Imagine we cut this shell and unfold it to obtain a rectangular solid, as shown below. Its width is $x=f(y)$, its thickness is $\Delta{y},$ and its height is $2\pi y$ (the circumference of the shell).

![](images/03/03030fb80f0aa51c637e6d39b4f763e8d7fc89abd111a012d3e560a952cfba99.png)

The volume of the shell approximately equals the volume of the rectangular solid:

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}_{\text{shell}} & ≈{V}_{\text{rec}} \\  & =2\pi y\cdot x\cdot Δy \\  & =2\pi yf(y)Δy\end{aligned}
$$

The sum over all the shells will approximate the total volume that we want. This approximation becomes more accurate as $\Delta{y} \to 0$. Therefore, the volume $V$ of the solid is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}yx\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}y\,f(y)\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186069989 :tutorial/content "One of the advantages of using the shell method versus other methods is that the resulting integral can be much simpler to evaluate. This is often true when we want to rotate a curve of the form $x = f(y)$ about the $x$-axis.

For example, suppose we want to compute the volume generated when the region below is rotated about the $x$-axis:

![](images/1d/1d23dde2cdd557feb50f82f72f4ff09174d5fb9a0c94e7810a6c06acb95a13d0.png)

According to the shell method, the volume $V$ is given by the following straightforward integral: 

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}yf(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y(2y-2{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}-2{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now compare this to the disc method.

To determine this volume using the disc method, we'd first need to express our curve as two separate functions of $x,$ one for the lower part and one for the upper part, as follows:

![](images/d9/d957a8e263db8ddd8ad3e5fa37f63b0cdbb47e706c367350c3ff6b8ff90294ff.svg)

![](images/f4/f416ab43297265aec4836eca2020d8f08976852cc025ad4d3a0766023187adef.png)

The required volume is equal to the difference between the volumes generated when the upper and lower curves are rotated about the $x$-axis. Thus, according to the disc method, the required volume is given by

$$
V = \pi \int_{0}^{1/2} \left( \left[ \dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{1-2x} \right]^2 - \left[ \dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{1-2x} \right]^2 \right) \textrm{d}x.
$$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4x+3y=5 \\ -x-6y=4\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the elimination method to solve the system. Notice that if we multiply the first equation by $2,$ then we will get a $6y$ term that can cancel with the $-6y$ in the second equation:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4x+3y=5 & |\,\times 2 \\ -x-6y=4 & \end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}8x+6y=10 \\ -x-6y=4\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations eliminates the $y$-variable and allows us to solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}8x+\cancel{6y} & =10 \\ -x-\cancel{6y} & =4 \\ (8x-x) & =(10+4) \\ 7x & =14 \\ x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can substitute $x=2$ into the equation $4x+3y=5$ to solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4x+3y & =5 \\ 4(2)+3y & =5 \\ 8+3y & =5 \\ 3y & =-3 \\ y & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system is $x=2,\,y=-1.$ So the coordinates of the point of intersection are $(2,-1).$"] ["question-3f0c0760-2f71-5da7-a09a-417c59aab4e2" :question/difficulty "question-6f0810d4-95d5-5ec1-a80a-fff5b7ccd8fa"] [17592186070021 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find the point of intersection between the two lines $y = x + 2$ and $y = 2x + 1.$ A sketch of The point $P$ consists of the coordinates $(x,y)$ that satisfy both equations $y=x+2$ and $y=2x+1.$ So, to find the coordinates of $P$ we need to solve the system of equations consisting of the two lines:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=x+2 \\ y=2x+1\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this system by substitution. Substituting the first equation $y=x+2$ into the second equation $y=2x+1$ gives an equation that we can solve for $x\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2 & =2x+1 \\ x+1 & =2x \\ 1 & =x\end{aligned}
$$

This is the $x$-coordinate of the point of intersection. To find the $y$-coordinate, we substitute $x = 1$ back into one of the equations, say $y=x+2,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =x+2 \\  & =1+2 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

"29e3e5d7-28ea-5e8a-b874-caa92a5ebba1"] ["question-29e3e5d7-28ea-5e8a-b874-caa92a5ebba1" :question/math-academy-id "q-336597"] ["question-29e3e5d7-28ea-5e8a-b874-caa92a5ebba1" :question/problem "$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x(t)+\overset{f(t)}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}]}},\,Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t} & {e}^{2t} \\ 0 & -2{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the system of differential equations and the fundamental matrix of the corresponding homogeneous system above. Using the method of variation of parameters, compute ${Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)$ and the particular solution ${x}_{p}(t)$ of the system.

<td align="center"></td>

</tbody></table>"] ["question-29e3e5d7-28ea-5e8a-b874-caa92a5ebba1" :question/worked-solution "We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t} & {e}^{2t} \\ 0 & -2{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{4t}\cdot (-2{e}^{2t})-0\cdot {e}^{2t}}[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{-{e}^{-6t}}{2}[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{-4t} & {e}^{-4t} \\ 0 & -{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}]. \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{-4t} & {e}^{-4t} \\ 0 & -{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{-4t} \\ -2{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}-{e}^{-4t} \\ -2{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int -{e}^{-4t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -2{e}^{-2t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-4t} \\ {e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t} & {e}^{2t} \\ 0 & -2{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-4t} \\ {e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{4} \\ -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-29e3e5d7-28ea-5e8a-b874-caa92a5ebba1" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-57ab610c-28ab-5d09-83f7-d68b274b353d" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-59d9272b-7eb2-549a-868b-86d14c7fdef5" :question/math-academy-id "q-336703"] ["question-59d9272b-7eb2-549a-868b-86d14c7fdef5" :question/problem "Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into the {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation."] ["question-59d9272b-7eb2-549a-868b-86d14c7fdef5" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L2},$ and $\text{L3}.$ Let's substitute ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$ from $\text{L1}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into $\text{initial system of ODEs}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{pre-multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-59d9272b-7eb2-549a-868b-86d14c7fdef5" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-dfeef9c0-222d-580e-9176-2a58212a74b2" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

$$

$$

$$

Since $Y$ is uniformly distributed on $\{1, 2, \dots, 201\},$ we compute

$$
\textrm{E}[Y] = \frac{1 + 201}{2} = 101.
$$

["question-d15a80b9-3b38-5de0-953c-45a827aaaf2b" :question/math-academy-id "q-275580"] ["question-d15a80b9-3b38-5de0-953c-45a827aaaf2b" :question/problem "A robotic arm randomly selects a box in a warehouse containing $n$ items from $1$ to $150,$ with each value equally likely. The arm then randomly picks one of these $n$ items and scans its position number (from $1$ to $n,$ each value equally likely).

What is the expected position number scanned?

The expected position number scanned is
{{field-1}}."] ["question-d15a80b9-3b38-5de0-953c-45a827aaaf2b" :question/worked-solution "This is a two-step random process: first, a box is selected containing $n$ items uniformly from $1$ through $150,$ and then an item is chosen uniformly in one of the positions numbered $1$ through $n.$

- Let $Y$ be the number of items in the box. Since this is an integer selected uniformly from $1$ to $150,$ we have $Y∼U\{1,2,…,150\}.$

- Let $X$ be the position number scanned, an integer selected uniformly from $1$ to $Y.$

We are asked to compute $\text{E}[X].$ Since the distribution of $X$ depends on $Y,$ we apply the tower property:

$$
\text{E}[X]=\text{E}[\text{E}[X∣Y]]
$$

Given $Y=n,$ the number $X$ is chosen uniformly from $1$ to $n.$ So, we have that

$$
\text{E}[X∣Y=n]=\frac{n+1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$"] [17592186208946 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-630c2241-afa1-5bd5-9578-2f06d9c7212c" :answer/id #uuid "630c2241-afa1-5bd5-9578-2f06d9c7212c"] ["answer-630c2241-afa1-5bd5-9578-2f06d9c7212c" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-630c2241-afa1-5bd5-9578-2f06d9c7212c" :answer/value "125.75"] [17592186205427 :answer-field/correct "answer-630c2241-afa1-5bd5-9578-2f06d9c7212c"] [17592186205427 :answer-field/choices "answer-630c2241-afa1-5bd5-9578-2f06d9c7212c"] [17592186209887 :tutorial/content "Recall that if $X$ is a discrete random variable, the expected value of $X$ is given by

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \sum_{x} x\cdot P(X = x).
$$

There is an alternative method for computing $\textrm{E}[X],$ which allows us to compute the expected value of a random variable by conditioning on another variable.  

Suppose another discrete random variable $Y$ takes on a set of possible values. If we know $\textrm{E}[X \mid Y = y]$ for each value $y,$ then the **law of total expectation** states

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \sum_{y} \textrm{E}[X \mid Y = y] \cdot P(Y = y).
$$

 

Conceptually, this tells us that $\textrm{E}[X]$ is just a weighted average of the conditional expectations $\textrm{E}[X \mid Y = y],$ where each weight is the probability $P(Y = y).$  

In many problems, directly computing $\textrm{E}[X]$ from the definition can be difficult. It turns out that breaking $\textrm{E}[X]$ up into conditional pieces often simplifies things. The law of total expectation is especially useful when $X$ depends on an underlying condition $Y,$ and each conditional case is easier to analyze than the full distribution of $X.$

Let’s see how this works in practice with a few examples."] [17592186209888 :tutorial/content "Let $X$ and $Y$ be discrete random variables, where $Y$ takes values $\alpha$ and $\beta$ with probabilities $0.4$ and $0.6,$ respectively. Suppose we are given the following conditional expectations:

- $\textrm{E}[X \mid Y = \alpha] = 7$

- $\textrm{E}[X \mid Y = \beta] = 3$

Let's compute $\textrm{E}[X]$ using the law of total expectation.

The law of total expectation states

$$
\textrm{E}[X]= \sum_y \textrm{E} [X \mid Y = y] \cdot P(Y=y).
$$

In this problem, $Y$ takes two values:

- $Y = \alpha$ with probability $0.4,$ and $\textrm{E}[X \mid Y = \alpha] = 7$

- $Y = \beta$ with probability $0.6,$ and $\textrm{E}[X \mid Y = \beta] = 3$

So, we calculate our expected value as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =\text{E}[X∣Y=\alpha ]\cdot P(Y=\alpha )+\text{E}[X∣Y=\beta ]\cdot P(Y=\beta ) \\  & =7\cdot 0.4+3\cdot 0.6 \\  & =2.8+1.8 \\  & =4.6\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186209885 :tutorial/content "We’ve seen that the law of total expectation allows us to compute the expected value of a random variable $X$ by conditioning on another variable $Y.$ This idea extends naturally to a more general and elegant identity called the **tower property**:

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \textrm{E}[\textrm{E}[X \mid Y]]
$$

At first glance, this may look abstract, so let’s unpack what it means.

The inner term $\textrm{E}[X \mid Y]$ is itself a *random variable*—its value depends on the outcome of $Y.$ The outer expectation then takes the average of that conditional expectation over all possible values of $Y.$

In other words, we are averaging $X$ in two stages:

- Within each scenario (for each possible value of $Y$), we find the expected value of $X.$

- Across all scenarios, we take the weighted average of those conditional expectations, where the weights are the probabilities of each $Y.$

Let’s explore a few examples to build some intuition."] [17592186209955 :tutorial/content "Let $X$ and $Y$ be discrete random variables, and suppose 

$$
\textrm{E}[X \mid Y] = \sqrt{3}\,Y + 1.

If $\textrm{E}[Y] = \sqrt3,$ let's compute $\textrm{E}[X]$.

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \textrm{E}[\textrm{E}[X \mid Y]].
$$

So, we substitute the given expression for the inner expectation:

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \textrm{E}\left[\sqrt{3}\,Y + 1\right]

\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =\text{E}[\sqrt{3}\,Y+1] \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \text{E}[Y]+\text{E}[1] \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \sqrt{3}+1 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186209886 :tutorial/content "Let $X$ and $Y$ be discrete random variables, and suppose $Y$ takes only two values $y_1$ and $y_2.$  We want to show that the *law of total expectation* holds in this simple case:

$$
\mathbb{E}[X] = \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y = y_1] \cdot P(Y = y_1) + \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y = y_2] \cdot P(Y = y_2)

$$

Next, we express $P(X = x)$ using the law of total probability:

$$

We can now distribute the sum across the two terms

\textrm{E}[X] = P(Y = y_1) \cdot \sum_x x \cdot P(X = x \mid Y = y_1) + P(Y = y_2) \cdot \sum_x x \cdot P(X = x \mid Y = y_2).

as required.

We can use a similar argument to prove the more general case, where $Y$ takes more than two values."] [17592186209889 :tutorial/content "Let $X$ and $Y$ be discrete random variables. Now, we want to prove that the tower property holds:

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \textrm{E}[\textrm{E}[X \mid Y]]

We start with the definition of expectation

$$

Next, we apply the law of total probability to express $P(X = x)$ in terms of $Y.$  Let $S_Y$ denote the support of $Y.$ Then, we have

$$

Substituting this into the expectation formula, we get

$$

We can now switch the order of summation:

$$

So, we conclude that

$$

Again, recall that for a point $(r,\theta,z)$ in cylindrical polar coordinates,

- $r\geq 0$ and $\theta\in [0,2\pi)$ are the usual plane polar coordinates, and

- $z\in (-\infty, \infty)$ is the usual Cartesian $z$-coordinate.

With that in mind, let's examine our equation:

$$
z^2=r^2
$$

This equation requires that the square of the distance from any point on the surface to the $xy$-plane equals the square of the distance from that point to the $z$-axis.
In other words, the tangent of the angle between any position vector on the surface and the $z$-axis, which is given by $\dfrac{r}{z}$, must be equal to

$$
\dfrac{r}{z} =\pm \sqrt{\dfrac{r^2}{z^2}} = \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{r^2}{r^2}} = \pm1.
$$

On the other hand, $\theta$ can vary arbitrarily in its domain. 

- For $\dfrac{r}{z} = 1,$ the angle between the position vector of any point on the surface and the $z$-axis must be equal $\dfrac{\pi}{4}.$ This corresponds to a *half-cone* for positive $z{:}$

![](images/18/1841d50bb07c0e6787f4824af0e13516912fb9ad77fac0515f00c243899eb18e.png)

 

- On the other hand, for $\dfrac{r}{z} = -1,$ the angle between the position vector of any point on the surface and the $z$-axis must be equal $\dfrac{3\pi}{4}.$ This corresponds to a *half-cone* for negative $z{:}$

![](images/e3/e32b1b4ba84faea7a4dc536e0f49bcda9295a4a42790162b3b9bad06db39a908.png)

Therefore, combining the two half cones, the equation $z^2 = r^2$ defines the *cone* shown below.

$$

$$

"question-8412e9ee-2ea9-5393-944f-a1233b5c49f8"] [17592186088868 :tutorial/content "Adding a value to $y=2^x$ will **translate** (shift) the exponential function up or down the $y$-axis. 

For instance, adding $3$ to $y=2^x$ will move each point on the exponential function $3$ units up.

![](images/c8/c89fd5fdcdc3773143a5f14ecb20f5bd2917bce20ece18a7dc70631bf358a0e8.png)

Note the following points:

1\. The $y$-intercept $(0,1)$ has moved up $3$ units to the point $(0,4).$

2\. The horizontal asymptote $y=0$ has moved up $3$ units to $y=3.$

As a second example, let's consider the function $y=2^x-3.$ In this case, the graph of $y=2^x$ is shifted *down* by $3$ units.

![](images/84/84987b3e9138a2e7e8afe70a7aa28a1cd81e081033aa2a766773e63cb8f41da5.png)"] [17592186087901 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0] ["question-957651b3-45e4-5a93-853b-1785322d0942" :question/id #uuid "957651b3-45e4-5a93-853b-1785322d0942"] ["question-957651b3-45e4-5a93-853b-1785322d0942" :question/math-academy-id "q-138022"] ["question-957651b3-45e4-5a93-853b-1785322d0942" :question/problem "Find the maximum value of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}$ given that $‖x‖=1.$"] ["question-957651b3-45e4-5a93-853b-1785322d0942" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that ${x}_{2}^{2}\ge 0.$ So, we have that

$$
-{x}_{2}^{2}\le {x}_{2}^{2}.
$$

As a result,  

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & \le {x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $‖x‖=1$ is equivalent to ${x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}=1.$ So,  in turn, $Q(x)\le 1.$

So, the value of $Q(x)$ can be no greater than $1.$ But before we conclude that $1$ is the maximum, we need to find a vector such that $Q(x)=1.$

Notice that when $x={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =(1)^{2}-(0)^{2} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, given that $‖x‖=1,$ the maximum value of $Q(x)$ is equal to $1.$"] ["question-957651b3-45e4-5a93-853b-1785322d0942" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] :question/problem "Find the minimum value of $Q(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}$ given that $‖x‖=1.$"] ["question-3e4f6268-3e58-5684-9bea-f874fd53aaf3" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of the matrix $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -6 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)(\lambda -3) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =-2,\,3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
min\{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1\}=-2.
$$"] ["question-3e4f6268-3e58-5684-9bea-f874fd53aaf3" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-55b2d835-40d6-572d-8824-c8db3cfc4a3b" :answer-field/id #uuid Find the arc length of the polar curve $r={e}^{\theta }$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}$ (shown in blue in the diagram above)."] [17592186092923 :question/worked-solution "The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={e}^{\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }={e}^{\theta }.
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{({e}^{\theta })}^{2}+{({e}^{\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{e}^{2\theta }+{e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{2{e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{e}^{\theta }{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}({e}^{\pi /2}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =\sqrt{2}({e}^{\pi /2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186092923 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-635d1f78-1ff1-548c-b1d2-727e82d8d662" :answer/id #uuid "635d1f78-1ff1-548c-b1d2-727e82d8d662"] "2014fae0-a89c-5d1e-8735-16f0159dd06c"] ["question-2014fae0-a89c-5d1e-8735-16f0159dd06c" :question/math-academy-id "q-119283"] ["question-2014fae0-a89c-5d1e-8735-16f0159dd06c" :question/problem "The growth rate of a watermelon production $P(t)$ in a certain land is jointly proportional to the watermelon production at time $t,$ measured in months, and the difference between the land's carrying capacity and the watermelon production. If the constant of proportionality is $0.2$ and the maximum possible watermelon production is $1\,800,$ which differential equation could be used to model $P(t)?$"] ["question-2014fae0-a89c-5d1e-8735-16f0159dd06c" :question/worked-solution "Since the watermelon production growth rate is *jointly* proportional to the watermelon production at time $t$ and the difference between the carrying capacity and the watermelon production, the watermelon production follows a logistic growth model.

A logistic growth equation has the form

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=kP(a-P),
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a>P$ is the carrying capacity.

In this case, the constant of proportionality is $k=0.2,$ and the carrying capacity is $a=1\,800.$ Therefore, the watermelon production is given by the equation

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=0.2P(1\,800-P).
$$"] ["question-2014fae0-a89c-5d1e-8735-16f0159dd06c" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-bb8637b4-c23b-5591-8ea3-4b43b99fdc95" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={cos}^{3}⁡t,\,y={sin}^{3}⁡t,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?"] ["question-42788b85-30ff-5f36-a9fd-86e424b97617" :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({cos}^{3}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({sin}^{3}⁡t)=3{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{3}⁡t\sqrt{{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t)}^{2}+{(3{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{3}⁡t\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{4}⁡t+9{sin}^{4}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{3}⁡t\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the identity ${sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t=1,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{3}⁡t\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{3}⁡t\sqrt{(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{3}⁡t\cdot |3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t|\,\text{d}t \\  & =6\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{3}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =6\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{4}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-42788b85-30ff-5f36-a9fd-86e424b97617" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-632462c4-14ed-5c49-b96d-6314fe36a641" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "Let's apply the candidates test step by step.

**Step 1**: We find the critical points. Taking the derivative of $f(x)={x}^{2}-4x+5,$ we get

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=2x-4.
$$

Solving ${f}^{′}(x)=0,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-4 & =0 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the critical points are $x=2$ and the endpoints $x=0,5$ (since the derivative is not defined at the endpoints)

**Step 2**: We evaluate $f(x)$ at the critical points.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0) & ={0}^{2}-4(0)+5=5 \\ f(2) & ={2}^{2}-4(2)+5=1 \\ f(5) & ={5}^{2}-4(5)+5=10\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: We compare all of the values found in step $2.$

- The smallest value is $f(2)=1,$ so the global minimum is $1.$

- The greatest value is $f(5)=10,$ so the global maximum is $10.$

Notice that our solid can be written as the type I region

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,y)\in D,\,\,0\le z\le 4-x-2y},
$$

where

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le 1}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](images/65/65c61ad7dc2964cd0de9a6bbdf259fcf3388e25da4eaabf155d58ff0c05c8d55.png)

$$
f(\mathbf y) = f(y_1,y_2, \ldots, y_n)
$$

with $n$ independent variables, and $\mathbf{y}: \mathbb R \to \mathbb R^n$, defined by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}y_{1}(x) \\ y_{2}(x) \\ ⋮ \\ y_{n}(x)\end{bmatrix}
$$

which is a vector-valued function of a variable $x$.

In a previous lesson, we saw that the derivative of $f(\mathbf{y}(x))$ with respect to $x$ is given by the multivariable chain rule.

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d}x}= \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y_1} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y_1}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y_2} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y_2}{\partial x} + \dots + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y_n} \cdot \dfrac{\partial y_n}{\partial x}
$$

This can be written as a product of matrices as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂y_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂y_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂y_{n}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Now, notice that this can be written as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d}x} = \underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}\mathbf y}}_{1\times n} \cdot \underbrace{\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf y}{\textrm{d}x}}_{n\times 1}
$$

where

- $\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}\mathbf y}$ is the *total derivative* of $f$ with respect to $\mathbf y$, which is a row vector of size $1\times n$, and
- $\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf y}{\textrm{d}x}$ is the *total derivative* of $\mathbf y$ with respect to $x$, which is a column vector of size $n\times 1$.

$$

$$

Here, the dot denotes matrix multiplication. The inner matrix dimensions match, so this is a valid matrix product.

**Watch Out!** When applying the chain rule for total derivatives, the *order of multiplication matters!* For example, if we swap the order of the matrix products, we'd get an incorrect result:

{{field-1}}."] [17592186209887 :tutorial/content "Recall that if $X$ is a discrete random variable, the expected value of $X$ is given by

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \sum_{x} x\cdot P(X = x)
$$

There is an alternative method for computing $\textrm{E}[X]$, which allows us to compute the expected value of a random variable by conditioning on another variable.

Suppose another discrete random variable $Y$ takes on a set of possible values. If we know

$$
\textrm{E}[X \mid Y = y]
$$

for each value $y$, then the **law of total expectation** states

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \sum_{y} \textrm{E}[X \mid Y = y] \cdot P(Y = y)
$$

Conceptually, this tells us that $\textrm{E}[X]$ is just a weighted average of the conditional expectations

$$
\textrm{E}[X \mid Y = y]
$$

where each weight is the probability

$$
P(Y = y)
$$

In many problems, directly computing $\textrm{E}[X]$ from the definition can be difficult. It turns out that breaking $\textrm{E}[X]$ up into conditional pieces often simplifies things. The law of total expectation is especially useful when $X$ depends on an underlying condition $Y$, and each conditional case is easier to analyze than the full distribution of $X$.

Let’s see how this works in practice with a few examples."] [17592186209888 :tutorial/content "Let $X$ and $Y$ be discrete random variables, where $Y$ takes values $\alpha$ and $\beta$ with probabilities $0.4$ and $0.6$, respectively. Suppose we are given the following conditional expectations:

- $\textrm{E}[X \mid Y = \alpha] = 7$
- $\textrm{E}[X \mid Y = \beta] = 3$

Let's compute $\textrm{E}[X]$ using the law of total expectation.

The law of total expectation states

$$
\textrm{E}[X]= \sum_y \textrm{E} [X \mid Y = y] \cdot P(Y=y)
$$

In this problem, $Y$ takes two values:

- $Y = \alpha$ with probability $0.4$, and $\textrm{E}[X \mid Y = \alpha] = 7$
- $Y = \beta$ with probability $0.6$, and $\textrm{E}[X \mid Y = \beta] = 3$

So, we calculate our expected value as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[X] &= E[X∣Y = α] \cdot P(Y = α) + E[X∣Y = β] \cdot P(Y = β) \\
&= 7 \cdot 0.4 + 3 \cdot 0.6 \\
&= 2.8 + 1.8 \\
&= 4.6
\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186209885 :tutorial/content "We’ve seen that the law of total expectation allows us to compute the expected value of a random variable $X$ by conditioning on another variable $Y$. This idea extends naturally to a more general and elegant identity called the **tower property**:

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \textrm{E}[\textrm{E}[X \mid Y]]
$$

At first glance, this may look abstract, so let’s unpack what it means.

The inner term $\textrm{E}[X \mid Y]$ is itself a *random variable*—its value depends on the outcome of $Y$. The outer expectation then takes the average of that conditional expectation over all possible values of $Y$.

In other words, we are averaging $X$ in two stages:

- Within each scenario (for each possible value of $Y$), we find the expected value of $X$.
- Across all scenarios, we take the weighted average of those conditional expectations, where the weights are the probabilities of each $Y$.

\textrm{E}[X] = \textrm{E}[\textrm{E}[X \mid Y]]
$$

So, we substitute the given expression for the inner expectation:

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \textrm{E}\left[\sqrt{3}\,Y + 1\right]
$$

Now, we apply the linearity of expectation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[X] &= E[\sqrt{3}Y + 1] \\
&= \sqrt{3} \cdot E[Y] + E[1] \\
&= \sqrt{3} \cdot \sqrt{3} + 1 \\
&= 4
\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186209886 :tutorial/content "Let $X$ and $Y$ be discrete random variables, and suppose $Y$ takes only two values $y_1$ and $y_2$. We want to show that the *law of total expectation* holds in this simple case:

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

We can now distribute the sum across the two terms

$$

$$

$$
P(X = x)
$$

in terms of $Y$. Let $S_Y$ denote the support of $Y$. Then, we have

$$

$$

$$

$$

Again, recall that for a point $(r,\theta,z)$ in cylindrical polar coordinates,

- $r\geq 0$ and $\theta\in [0,2\pi)$ are the usual plane polar coordinates, and

- $z\in (-\infty, \infty)$ is the usual Cartesian $z$-coordinate.

With that in mind, let's examine our equation:

$$
z^2=r^2
$$

This equation requires that the square of the distance from any point on the surface to the $xy$-plane equals the square of the distance from that point to the $z$-axis.
In other words, the tangent of the angle between any position vector on the surface and the $z$-axis, which is given by $\dfrac{r}{z}$, must be equal to

$$
\dfrac{r}{z} =\pm \sqrt{\dfrac{r^2}{z^2}} = \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{r^2}{r^2}} = \pm1.
$$

On the other hand, $\theta$ can vary arbitrarily in its domain. 

- For $\dfrac{r}{z} = 1,$ the angle between the position vector of any point on the surface and the $z$-axis must be equal $\dfrac{\pi}{4}.$ This corresponds to a *half-cone* for positive $z{:}$

![](images/18/1841d50bb07c0e6787f4824af0e13516912fb9ad77fac0515f00c243899eb18e.png)

- On the other hand, for $\dfrac{r}{z} = -1,$ the angle between the position vector of any point on the surface and the $z$-axis must be equal $\dfrac{3\pi}{4}.$ This corresponds to a *half-cone* for negative $z{:}$

![](images/e3/e32b1b4ba84faea7a4dc536e0f49bcda9295a4a42790162b3b9bad06db39a908.png)

Therefore, combining the two half cones, the equation $z^2 = r^2$ defines the *cone* shown below.

![](images/84/84737b12a1689fe2ac03ab09572e4c396d35493f55df5d65af80eeb8c5ae5676.png)

Suppose we remove the restriction $\theta\in[0,2\pi)$ so that it can be any number. What would the surface look like then?

If we remove the restriction on $\theta,$ we obtain more spirals. For example, the diagram below shows $r=\theta$ for $\theta \in [0, 4\pi).$

So, let's find where they intersect.\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2} & =3-2{y}^{2} \\\\ 3{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2} & =3\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, the projection of the intersection in the $yz$-plane is an ellipse.\n\nNotice that our solid can be written as a type II region: \n\n$$\nR=\\{(x,y,z)\\,:\\,(y,z)\\in D,\\,\\,{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2}\\le x\\le 3-2{y}^{2}\\},\n$$\n\nwhere $D$ is the interior of the ellipse $3{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2}=3.$ \n\nAs a result, the volume of $R$ is given by \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\\text{d}V \\\\  & ={∬}_{D}[{\\int }_{{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2}}^{3-2{y}^{2}}\\text{d}x]\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={∬}_{D}(3-2{y}^{2})-({y}^{2}+2{z}^{2})\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={∬}_{D}3-3{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}\\,\\text{d}A.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, notice that the boundary of $D$ consists of \n\n- the lower part $z=-\\sqrt{\\frac{3(1-{y}^{2})}{2}},$ and\n\n- the upper part $z=\\sqrt{\\frac{3(1-{y}^{2})}{2}},$\n\nfor $-1\\le y\\le 1.$ \n\nTherefore, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}3-3{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}\\,\\text{d}A & ={\\int }_{-1}^{1}{\\int }_{-\\sqrt{3(1-{y}^{2})/2}}^{\\sqrt{3(1-{y}^{2})/2}}\\,3-3{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}\\,dz\\,dy.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n \n\nFinally, \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}+f & ={(-\\sqrt{\\frac{3(1-{y}^{2})}{2}})}^{2}+{(\\sqrt{\\frac{3(1-{y}^{2})}{2}})}^{2}+(3-3{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}) \\\\  & =\\frac{3(1-{y}^{2})}{2}+\\frac{3(1-{y}^{2})}{2}+(3-3{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}) \\\\  & d A\n$$\n\nWe have a similar result for triple integrals:\n\n*If $R$ is a region in three-dimensional space, then the volume of $R$ is given by*\n\n$$\n\\textrm{Volume}(R) = \\iiint\\limits_{R} \\textrm{d}V.\n$$\n\nIn other words, the volume of $R$ equals the triple integral of the function $f(x,y,z)=1$ over $R.$ \n\nFor example, let's use triple integrals to find the volume of the rectangular prism shown below.\n\n![](images/8f/8f9ab5db03f1cdf84ef484aca1ab89995237e7ef333c9b7c563d0080d317e981.png)\n\n \n\nNotice that our solid can be written in set-builder notation as\n\n$$\nR = \\big\\{ (x,y,z) \\: : \\: 0 \\leq x \\leq 1, \\:\\: 0 \\leq y \\leq 2, \\:\\: 0 \\leq z \\leq 3 \\big\\}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, the volume of $R$ is \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\\text{d}V \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{1}{\\int }_{0}^{2}{\\int }_{0}^{3}dz\\,dy\\,dx \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{1}dx\\cdot {\\int }_{0}^{2}dy\\cdot {\\int }_{0}^{3}dz \\\\  & =(1-0)\\cdot (2-0)\\cdot (3-0) \\\\  & =6.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Note:** We get the same value using the formula for the volume of a rectangular prism:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}V & =\\text{length}\\cdot \\text{width}\\cdot \\text{height} $D\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\textrm{Area}\\ \\!(D) = \\displaystyle \\iint\\limits_{D} 1 \\cdot \\textrm d A = \\displaystyle \\iint\\limits_{D}  \\ \\textrm d A\n$$\n\nWe have a similar result for triple integrals:\n\n*If $R$ is a region in three-dimensional space, then the volume of $R$ is given by*\n\n$$\n\\textrm{Volume}(R) = \\iiint\\limits_{R} \\textrm{d}V.\n$$\n\nIn other words, the volume of $R$ equals the triple integral of the function $f(x,y,z)=1$ over $R.$ \n\nFor example, let's use triple integrals to find the volume of the rectangular prism shown below.\n\n![](images/8f/8f9ab5db03f1cdf84ef484aca1ab89995237e7ef333c9b7c563d0080d317e981.png)\n\n \n\nNotice that our solid can be written in set-builder notation as\n\n$$\nR = \\big\\{ (x,y,z) \\: : \\: 0 \\leq x \\leq 1, \\:\\: 0 \\leq y \\leq 2, \\:\\: 0 \\leq z \\leq 3 \\big\\}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, the volume of $R$ is \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\\text{d}V \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{1}{\\int }_{0}^{2}{\\int }_{0}^{3}dz\\,dy\\,dx \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{1}dx\\cdot {\\int }_{0}^{2}dy\\cdot {\\int }_{0}^{3}dz \\\\  & =(1-0)\\cdot (2-0)\\cdot (3-0) \\\\  & =6.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Note:** We get the same value using the formula for the volume of a rectangular prism:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}V & =\\text{length}\\cdot \\text{width}\\cdot \\text{height} \\\\  & =1\\cdot 2\\cdot 3 \\\\  & =6\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nLet's see some more examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "8b8f4748-190d-5fda-9a83-139e6a994d94" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4911 :tutorial/title :question/worked-solution "Notice that our solid can be written as a type II region: \n\n$$\nR=\\{(x,y,z)\\,:\\,0\\le y\\le 2,\\,\\,0\\le z\\le 1,\\,\\,-2\\le x\\le {z}^{2}+y\\}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\\text{d}V \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{2}{\\int }_{0}^{1}{\\int }_{-2}^{{z}^{2}+y}\\,dx\\,dz\\,dy \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{2}{\\int }_{0}^{1}[x]_{x=-2}^{x={z}^{2}+y}\\,dz\\,dy \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{2}{\\int }_{0}^{1}{z}^{2}+y-(-2)\\,dz\\,dy \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{2}{\\int }_{0}^{1}{z}^{2}+y+2\\,dz\\,dy \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{2}{[\\frac{1}{3}{z}^{3}+(y+2)z]}_{z=0}^{z=1}\\,dy \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{2}\\frac{1}{3}+y+2\\,dy \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{2}\\frac{7}{3}+y\\,dy \\\\  & ={[\\frac{7}{3}y+\\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\\\  & =\\frac{7}{3}\\cdot 2+\\frac{1}{2}\\cdot {2}^{2}-0 \\\\  & =\\frac{20}{3}\\end{aligned}\n$$"} :step/id #uuid an ellipse.\n\nNotice that our solid can be written as a type II region: \n\n$$\nR=\\{(x,y,z)\\,:\\,(y,z)\\in D,\\,\\,{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2}\\le x\\le 3-2{y}^{2}\\},\n$$\n\nwhere $D$ is the interior of the }_{{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2}}^{3-2{y}^{2}}\\text{d}x]\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={∬}_{D}(3-2{y}^{2})-({y}^{2}+2{z}^{2})\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={∬}_{D}3-3{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}\\,\\text{d}A.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, notice that the boundary of $D$ consists of \n\n- the lower part $z=-\\sqrt{\\frac{3(1-{y}^{2})}{2}},$ and\n\n- the upper part $z=\\sqrt{\\frac{3(1-{y}^{2})}{2}},$\n\nfor $-1\\le y\\le 1.$ \n\nTherefore, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}3-3{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}\\,\\text{d}A & ={\\int }_{-1}^{1}{\\int }_{-\\sqrt{3(1-{y}^{2})/2}}^{\\sqrt{3(1-{y}^{2})/2}}\\,3-3{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}\\,dz\\,dy.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n \n\nFinally, \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}+f & ={(-\\sqrt{\\frac{3(1-{y}^{2})}{2}})}^{2}+{(\\sqrt{\\frac{3(1-{y}^{2})}{2}})}^{2}+(3-3{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}) \\\\  & =\\frac{3(1-{y}^{2})}{2}+\\frac{3(1-{y}^{2})}{2}+(3-3{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}) \\\\  & integrals, as follows:\n\n$$\nV={\\int }_{-1}^{1}{\\int }_{a(y)}^{b(y)}\\,f(y,z)\\,dz\\,dy\n$$\n\nWhat is ${a}^{2}+{b}^{2}+f?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to determine the projection of the intersection of our surfaces onto the $yz$-plane. So, let's find where they intersect.\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2} & =3-2{y}^{2} \\\\ 3{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2} & =3\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, the projection of the intersection in the $yz$-plane is an ellipse.\n\nNotice that our solid can be written as a type II region: \n\n$$\nR=\\{(x,y,z)\\,:\\,(y,z)\\in D,\\,\\,{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2}\\le x\\le 3-2{y}^{2}\\},\n$$\n\nwhere $D$ is the interior of the ellipse $3{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2}=3.$ \n\nAs a result, the volume of $R$ is given by \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\\text{d}V \\\\  & ={∬}_{D}[{\\int }_{{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2}}^{3-2{y}^{2}}\\text{d}x]\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={∬}_{D}(3-2{y}^{2})-({y}^{2}+2{z}^{2})\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={∬}_{D}3-3{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}\\,\\text{d}A.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, notice that the boundary of $D$ consists of \n\n- the lower part $z=-\\sqrt{\\frac{3(1-{y}^{2})}{2}},$ and\n\n- the upper part $z=\\sqrt{\\frac{3(1-{y}^{2})}{2}},$\n\nfor $-1\\le y\\le 1.$ \n\nTherefore, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}3-3{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}\\,\\text{d}A & ={\\int }_{-1}^{1}{\\int }_{-\\sqrt{3(1-{y}^{2})/2}}^{\\sqrt{3(1-{y}^{2})/2}}\\,3-3{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}\\,dz\\,dy.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n \n\nFinally, \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}+f & ={(-\\sqrt{\\frac{3(1-{y}^{2})}{2}})}^{2}+{(\\sqrt{\\frac{3(1-{y}^{2})}{2}})}^{2}+(3-3{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}) \\\\  & =\\frac{3(1-{y}^{2})}{2}+\\frac{3(1-{y}^{2})}{2}+(3-3{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}) \\\\  & =6-6{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} :step/id #uuid "fe1c9984-4492-5bc7-9f8a-f367a564a7b2" :step/next {:db/id 17592186433114}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid All its sides are congruent and the opposite sides are parallel, so it is a rhombus.\n\n- The shape $R$ is a trapezoid. Since it has only one pair of parallel sides, it is not a rhombus.\n\n- The shape $S$ is an isosceles trapezoid.  Since it has only one pair of parallel sides, it is not a rhombus.\n\nTherefore, shape $Q$ is a rhombus. So, it is not always necessary to draw both inequalities and find the overlap. In this lesson, we will learn how to calculate the percentage of a whole number in real-world situations.\n\nFor example, suppose Daniel and Luisa traveled $200$ kilometers in their car. If Luisa drove $40 \\%$ of the way, how many kilometers did she drive?\n\nTo solve this problem, we can use the following formula:\n\n$$\n\\textrm{part} = \\textrm{percentage} \\times \\textrm{whole}\n$$\n\nIn this case, the whole is the number of kilometers traveled, which is $200$ kilometers. The percentage is $40 \\%,$ and the part is the distance Luisa drove.\n\nAs usual, we can use two methods to solve this problem:\n\n**Method 1**\n\nFirst, we convert the percentage to a decimal: \n\n$$\n40 \\% = 40 \\div 100  = 0.4\n$$\n\nApplying our formula, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\text{part} & =\\text{percentage}\\times \\text{whole} \\\\  & =40%\\times 200 \\\\  & =0.4\\times 200 \\\\  & =80.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo Luisa drove $80$ kilometers.\n\n**Method 2**\n\nFirst, we convert the percentage to a fraction:\n\n$$\n40 \\% = \\dfrac{40}{100} = \\dfrac{40 \\div 20}{100 \\div 20} = \\dfrac{2}{5}\n$$\n\nApplying the formula, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\text{part} & =\\text{percentage}\\times \\text{whole} \\\\  & =40%\\times 200 \\\\  & =\\frac{2}{5}\\times 200 \\\\  & =\\frac{400}{5} \\\\  & =80.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nAgain, we find that Luisa drove $80$ kilometers." :tutorial/id #uuid "b32fe964-00bc-58b8-8e13-0ebde913bd87" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2080 :step/content {:db/id 17592186148699 :tutorial/content "Percentages are *very* common in everyday life. For example, they are used in retail, finance, and sports! In this lesson, we will learn how to calculate the percentage of a whole number in real-world situations.\n\nFor example, suppose Daniel and Luisa traveled $200$ kilometers in their car. If Luisa drove $40 \\%$ of the way, how many kilometers did she drive?\n\nTo solve this problem, we can use the following formula:\n\n$$\n\\textrm{part} = \\textrm{percentage} \\times \\textrm{whole}\n$$\n\nIn this case, the whole is the number of kilometers traveled, which is $200$ kilometers. The percentage is $40 \\%,$ and the part is the distance Luisa drove.\n\nAs usual, we can use two methods to solve this problem:\n\n**Method 1**\n\nFirst, we convert the percentage to a decimal: \n\n$$\n40 \\% = 40 \\div 100  = 0.4\n$$\n\nApplying our formula, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\text{part} & =\\text{percentage}\\times \\text{whole} \\\\  & =40%\\times 200 \\\\  & =0.4\\times 200 \\\\  & =80.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo Luisa drove $80$ kilometers.\n\n**Method 2**\n\nFirst, we convert the percentage to a fraction:\n\n$$\n40 \\% = \\dfrac{40}{100} = \\dfrac{40 \\div 20}{100 \\div 20} = \\dfrac{2}{5}\n$$\n\nApplying the formula, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\text{part} & =\\text{percentage}\\times \\text{whole} \\\\  & =40%\\times 200 \\\\  & =\\frac{2}{5}\\times 200 \\\\  & =\\frac{400}{5} \\\\  & =80.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nAgain, we find that Luisa drove $80$ kilometers." :tutorial/id #uuid "b32fe964-00bc-58b8-8e13-0ebde913bd87" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2080 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "6f30bc9e-6f94-5aa2-a2a2-62ed9c078df2" :step/math-academy-id 7956 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148562}} {:db/id 17592186148699 :tutorial/content "Percentages are *very* common in everyday life. \\left(\\sqrt{{\\color{red}10}^2}\\right)^2 = ({\\color{red}10})^2 = {\\color{blue}100}\n$$\n\nNotice that the squaring the square root gives the number under the square root:\n\n$$\n\\left( the following formula to compute the arc length bounded by a polar curve:\n\n$$\nL = \\int_{\\theta_1}^{\\theta_2} \\sqrt{ r^2 + \\left( \\frac{\\textrm{d}r}{\\textrm{d}\\theta} \\right)^2} \\:\\textrm{d}\\theta\n$$\n\nBut where does this formula come from? Let's start with the familiar formula for the arc length of a parametric curve:\n\n$$\nL = \\int_{t_1}^{t_2} \\sqrt{ \\left(\\frac{\\textrm{d}x}{\\textrm{d}t}\\right)^2 +\\left(\\frac{\\textrm{d}y}{\\textrm{d}t}\\right)^2 }\\textrm{d}t\n$$\n\nA polar curve is really just a parametric curve with parameter $\\theta$ and parametric equations given by\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}x & =r\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta ,\\,y=r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta .\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWriting the arc length formula for a parametric function with parameter $\\theta,$ we have\n\n$$\nL = \\int_{\\theta_1}^{\\theta_2} \\sqrt{ \\left(\\frac{\\textrm{d}x}{\\textrm{d}\\theta}\\right)^2 +\\left(\\frac{\\textrm{d}y}{\\textrm{d}\\theta}\\right)^2 }\\textrm{d}\\theta .\n$$\n\nSince $x = r \\cos \\theta,$ we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{\\text{d}x}{\\text{d}\\theta } & =\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}\\theta }(r\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta ) \\\\  & =\\frac{\\text{d}r}{\\text{d}\\theta }\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta +r\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}\\theta }(\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta ) \\\\  & =\\frac{\\text{d}r}{\\text{d}\\theta }\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta -r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta .\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nLikewise, since $y=r\\sin \\theta,$ we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{\\text{d}y}{\\text{d}\\theta } & =\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}\\theta }(r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta ) \\\\  & =\\frac{\\text{d}r}{\\text{d}\\theta }\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta +r\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}\\theta }(\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta ) \\\\  & =\\frac{\\text{d}r}{\\text{d}\\theta }\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta +r\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta .\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSubstituting the above into our expression for $L,$ we reach the desired formula:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}L & ={\\int }_{{\\theta }_{1}}^{{\\theta }_{2}}\\sqrt{{(\\frac{\\text{d}x}{\\text{d}\\theta })}^{2}+{(\\frac{\\text{d}y}{\\text{d}\\theta })}^{2}}\\,\\text{d}\\theta  \\\\  & ={\\int }_{{\\theta }_{1}}^{{\\theta }_{2}}\\sqrt{{(\\frac{\\text{d}r}{\\text{d}\\theta }\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta -r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta )}^{2}+{(\\frac{\\text{d}r}{\\text{d}\\theta }\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta +r\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta )}^{2}}\\,\\text{d}\\theta  \\\\  & ={\\int }_{{\\theta }_{1}}^{{\\theta }_{2}}\\sqrt{{(\\frac{\\text{d}r}{\\text{d}\\theta })}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta +{(\\frac{\\text{d}r}{\\text{d}\\theta })}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta +{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\\theta }\\,\\text{d}\\theta  \\\\  & ={\\int }_{{\\theta }_{1}}^{{\\theta }_{2}}\\sqrt{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta )+{(\\frac{\\text{d}r}{\\text{d}\\theta })}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta )}\\,\\text{d}\\theta  \\\\  & ={\\int }_{{\\theta }_{1}}^{{\\theta }_{2}}\\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\\frac{\\text{d}r}{\\text{d}\\theta })}^{2}}\\,\\text{d}\\theta .\\end{aligned}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1821e80d-8c1b-5d2f-88dd-c207d2c3d99f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1144 :tutorial/title "Derivation of the Main Formula"} :step/id #uuid :topic/math-academy-id 288} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186064988 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065346 :tutorial/content "The **mean value theorem** states that for any function that is continuous and differentiable on some interval, there is some point where the derivative of the function is equal to the slope between the endpoints. More precisely, that is:\n\n> *If $f(x)$ is a function that's continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$, then there exists a point $c\\in (a,b)$ such that*\n> \n> \n> $$\n> f'(c) = \\dfrac {f(b) - f(a)} {b-a}.\n> $$\n\nLet's illustrate this idea with an example. Consider the graph of the function \n\n$$\ny = f(x) = 6 - \\dfrac 4 x\n$$\n\nthat's defined on the closed interval $[1,4].$\n\n![](images/fd/fd4d75f2ed0db427c2e3bd41335ceb302c3126781f595c8c21ec914e50f82f64.png)\n\nThe line $l_1$ is the secant line that intersects the curve at the endpoints of the interval. The mean value theorem guarantees that there is some special point inside the interval where the tangent line has the same slope as $l_1.$ \n\nIn the diagram above, the special point is $(2,4),$ and the tangent line $l_2$ at this point is parallel to the secant line $l_1.$\n\nTo double-check that $l_1$ and $l_2$ are parallel, we can compute their slopes. The line $l_1$ passes through the points $(1,f(1))$ and $(4,f(4)),$ so its slope is given by \n\n$$\nm=\\dfrac{f(4)-f(1)}{4-1} =  \\dfrac{5-2}{4-1} = 1.\n$$\n\nOn the other hand, the slope of the line $l_2$ can be found by calculating $f'(2).$\n\n$$\nf'(x) = \\dfrac{4}{x^2}\\quad\\Longrightarrow\\quad f'(2) = 1\n$$\n\nSince the lines $l_1$ and $l_2$ have the same slope, they are parallel." Thus,\n$\\dfrac{\\textrm d\\mathbf y}{\\textrm d \\mathbf x} = \\mathbf{A}$.\n\nTherefore, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\left.\\frac{d}{dx}f(z(y(x)))\\right|_{x_{0}} &= :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186205055 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205190 :tutorial/content "Consider the multivariable function $f:\\mathbb R^n \\to\\mathbb R$, defined by\n\n$$\nf(\\mathbf y) = f(y_1,y_2, \\ldots, y_n)\n$$\n\nwith $n$ independent variables, and $\\mathbf{y}: \\mathbb R \\to \\mathbb R^n$, defined by\n\n$$\n\\begin{bmatrix}y_{1}(x) \\\\ y_{2}(x) \\\\ ⋮ \\\\ y_{n}(x)\\end{bmatrix}\n$$\n\nwhich is a vector-valued function of a variable $x$.\n\nIn a previous lesson, we saw that the derivative of $f(\\mathbf{y}(x))$ with respect to $x$ is given by the multivariable chain rule.\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\textrm{d} f}{\\textrm{d}x}= \\dfrac{\\partial f}{\\partial y_1} \\cdot \\dfrac{\\partial y_1}{\\partial x} + \\dfrac{\\partial f}{\\partial y_2} \\cdot \\dfrac{\\partial y_2}{\\partial x} + \\dots + \\dfrac{\\partial f}{\\partial y_n} \\cdot \\dfrac{\\partial y_n}{\\partial x}\n$$\n\nThis can be written as a product of matrices as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{bmatrix}\\frac{∂f}{∂y_{1}} & \\frac{∂f}{∂y_{2}} & ⋯ & \\frac{∂f}{∂y_{n}}\\end{bmatrix}\n$$\n\nNow, notice that this can be written as\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\textrm{d} f}{\\textrm{d}x} = \\underbrace{\\dfrac{\\textrm{d}f}{\\textrm{d}\\mathbf y}}_{1\\times n} \\cdot \\underbrace{\\dfrac{\\textrm{d}\\mathbf y}{\\textrm{d}x}}_{n\\times 1}\n$$\n\nwhere\n\n- $\\dfrac{\\textrm{d}f}{\\textrm{d}\\mathbf y}$ is the *total derivative* of $f$ with respect to $\\mathbf y$, which is a row vector of size $1\\times n$, and\n- $\\dfrac{\\textrm{d}\\mathbf y}{\\textrm{d}x}$ is the *total derivative* of $\\mathbf y$ with respect to $x$, which is a column vector of size $n\\times 1$.\n\nIn the next slides, we will apply this matrix formulation to a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "17350522-fdcb-5adf-a0e3-30fbe076474e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 12384 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "55b69b88-94a5-5e68-b80c-fdb21b7034b5" :step/math-academy-id 610762 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205056}} {:db/id 17592186205056 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205191 :tutorial/content "Let $\\mathbf{y}: \\mathbb{R}^n \\to \\mathbb{R}^q$ and $\\mathbf{f}: \\mathbb{R}^q \\to \\mathbb{R}^m$ be two differentiable vector-valued functions. We want to compute the derivative of the composition $\\mathbf{f}(\\mathbf{y}(\\mathbf{x}))$ with respect to $\\mathbf{x} \\in \\mathbb{R}^n$.\n\nThe **chain rule for total derivatives** tells us that\n\n$$\n\\underbrace{\\dfrac{\\textrm{d}\\mathbf{f}}{\\textrm{d} \\mathbf{x}}}_{m \\times n} = \\underbrace{\\dfrac{\\textrm{d}\\mathbf{f}}{\\textrm{d} \\mathbf{y}}}_{m \\times q} \\cdot \\underbrace{\\dfrac{\\textrm{d}\\mathbf{y}}{\\textrm{d} \\mathbf{x}}}_{q \\times n}\n$$\n\nHere, the dot denotes matrix multiplication. The inner matrix dimensions match, so this is a valid matrix product.\n\n**Watch Out!** When applying the chain rule for total derivatives, the *order of multiplication matters!* For example, if we swap the order of the matrix products, we'd get an incorrect result:\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\textrm{d}\\mathbf{f}}{\\textrm{d} \\mathbf{x}} = \\underbrace{\\dfrac{\\textrm{d}\\mathbf{y}}{\\textrm{d} \\mathbf{x}}}_{q \\times n} \\cdot \\underbrace{\\dfrac{\\textrm{d}\\mathbf{f}}{\\textrm{d} \\mathbf{y}}}_{m \\times q} \\qquad \\text{(WRONG!)}\n$$\n\nThis is incorrect because the inner matrix dimensions do not agree, making it an invalid matrix product.\n\nLet's take a look at a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "be71f9c1-7d65-5804-9536-88b35b9f95f5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 12385 :tutorial/title "The Chain Rule for Total Derivatives"} :step/id #uuid "c4066bbf-680a-5ee8-9250-732582cd85b8" :step/math-academy-id 610763 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205057}} {:db/id 17592186205057 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205198 :tutorial/content "Suppose we define\n$\\begin{bmatrix}y_{1} + y_{2} \\\\ y_{1} - 2y_{2}\\end{bmatrix}$\n\nThen, we have $\\mathbf{f}: \\mathbb{R}^2 \\to \\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\\mathbf{y}: \\mathbb{R}^2 \\to \\mathbb{R}^2$.\n\nLet's see how to compute the derivative for the composition $\\mathbf{f}(\\mathbf{y}(\\mathbf{x}))$.\n\nThe chain rule states that\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\textrm{d} \\mathbf{f}}{\\textrm{d} \\mathbf{x}} = \\dfrac{\\textrm{d}\\mathbf{f}}{\\textrm{d} \\mathbf{y}} \\cdot \\dfrac{\\textrm{d}\\mathbf{y}}{\\textrm{d} \\mathbf{x}}\n$$\n\nLet's consider each of the factors in turn.\n\n- The function $\\mathbf{f}$ acts on a vector $\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathbb{R}^2$ and outputs a vector $\\mathbf{f}(\\mathbf{y}) \\in \\mathbb{R}^2$. Thus, the total derivative of $\\mathbf{f}$ with respect to $\\mathbf{y}$ is a $2\\times 2$ matrix.\n- The function $\\mathbf{y}$ acts on a vector $\\mathbf{x} \\in \\mathbb{R}^2$ and outputs a vector $\\mathbf{y}(\\mathbf{x}) \\in \\mathbb{R}^2$. Thus, the total derivative of $\\mathbf{y}$ with respect to $\\mathbf{x}$ is also a $2\\times 2$ matrix.\n\nComputing our derivatives, we get\n$\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & -2\\end{bmatrix}$\n\nThen, by the chain rule, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\frac{df}{dx} &= \\frac{df}{dy} \\cdot \\frac{dy}{dx} \\\\\n&= \\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & -2\\end{bmatrix} \\cdot \\begin{bmatrix}2x_{1} & 0 \\\\ 0 & 2x_{2}\\end{bmatrix} \\\\\n&= \\begin{bmatrix}2x_{1} & 2x_{2} \\\\ 2x_{1} & -4x_{2}\\end{bmatrix}\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThis matrix gives us the total derivative of $\\mathbf f$ with respect to $\\mathbf x$." :tutorial/id #uuid "15c3d109-a5c5-5b01-a804-4e1b94e8269b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13107 :tutorial/title "A Concrete Example"} :step/id #uuid have the following differentiable functions:\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{y}: \\mathbb{R}^n \\to \\mathbb{R}^p, \\qquad \\mathbf{z}: \\mathbb{R}^p \\to \\mathbb{R}^q, \\qquad \\mathbf{f}: \\mathbb{R}^q \\to \\mathbb{R}^m\n$$\n\nThe chain rule can be extended in the natural way as follows:\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\textrm d}{\\textrm d \\mathbf x} \\mathbf{f}(\\mathbf{z}(\\mathbf{y}(\\mathbf x))) = \\underbrace{\\dfrac{\\textrm d\\mathbf f}{\\textrm d \\mathbf z}}_{m\\times q} \\cdot \\underbrace{\\dfrac{\\textrm d\\mathbf z}{\\textrm d \\mathbf y}}_{q\\times p} \\cdot \\underbrace{\\dfrac{\\textrm d\\mathbf y}{\\textrm d \\mathbf x}}_{p\\times n}\n$$\n\nLet's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "7e23add8-cf11-5e3b-9950-84e432ab21da" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13109 the previous slide is correct by computing the derivative directly.\n\nRecall that\n$\\begin{bmatrix}y_{1} + y_{2} \\\\ y_{1} - 2y_{2}\\end{bmatrix}$\n\nFirst, we substitute $\\mathbf{y}$ into $\\mathbf{f}$ to write $\\mathbf{f}$ explicitly in terms of $\\mathbf{x}{:}$\n$\\begin{bmatrix}x_{1}^{2} + x_{2}^{2} \\\\ x_{1}^{2} - 2x_{2}^{2}\\end{bmatrix}$\n\nNow, we compute the derivative of $\\mathbf f$ with respect to $\\mathbf x{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\frac{df}{dx} &= \\begin{bmatrix}\\frac{∂f_{1}}{∂x_{1}} & \\frac{∂f_{1}}{∂x_{2}} \\\\ \\frac{∂f_{2}}{∂x_{1}} & \\frac{∂f_{2}}{∂x_{2}}\\end{bmatrix} \\\\\n&= \\begin{bmatrix}2x_{1} & 2x_{2} \\\\ 2x_{1} & -4x_{2}\\end{bmatrix}\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThis agrees with the result we obtained using the chain rule."
