:step/math-academy-id 610802 :step/next {:db/id 17592186205058}} {:db/id 17592186205065 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205218 :tutorial/content "We can use the chain rule for functions that use matrices in their definition.\n\nFor example, consider the functions\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{y}(\\mathbf{x}) = \\mathbf{A}\\mathbf{x}\n$$\n\nand\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{f}(\\mathbf{y}) = \\mathbf{B}\\mathbf{y}\n$$\n\nwhere $\\mathbf x\\in \\mathbb R^3, \\mathbf y\\in\\mathbb R^2$, and the matrices $\\mathbf{A}$ and $\\mathbf{B}$ are given by\n$\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 \\\\ -1 & 3 & 4\\end{bmatrix}$\nWhat is\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\textrm d}{\\textrm d \\mathbf x} \\mathbf{f}(\\mathbf{y}(\\mathbf x))\n$$\n\nevaluated at\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{x}_0 = [2, \\, 0, \\, -1]^T\n$$\n\nUsing the chain rule, we have\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\textrm d}{\\textrm d \\mathbf x} \\mathbf{f}(\\mathbf{y}(\\mathbf x)) = \\dfrac{\\textrm d\\mathbf f}{\\textrm d \\mathbf y} \\cdot \\dfrac{\\textrm d\\mathbf y}{\\textrm d \\mathbf x}\n$$\n\nLet's consider each of the factors in turn.\n\n- The function $\\mathbf{f}$ acts on a vector $\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathbb{R}^2$ by multiplying it by $\\mathbf{B}$ and outputs a vector $\\mathbf{f}(\\mathbf{y}) \\in \\mathbb{R}^2$. Thus,\n$\\dfrac{\\textrm d\\mathbf f}{\\textrm d \\mathbf y} = \\mathbf{B}$.\n- The function $\\mathbf{y}$ acts on a vector $\\mathbf{x} \\in \\mathbb{R}^3$ by multiplying it by $\\mathbf{A}$ and outputs a vector $\\mathbf{y}(\\mathbf{x}) \\in \\mathbb{R}^2$. Thus,\n$\\dfrac{\\textrm d\\mathbf y}{\\textrm d \\mathbf x} = \\mathbf{A}$.\n\nSince these derivatives are constant matrices, the value at $\\mathbf{x}_0$ is simply their product. Therefore, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\frac{d}{dx}f(y(x)) &= \\frac{df}{dy} \\cdot \\frac{dy}{dx} \\\\\n&= BA \\\\\n&= \\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\\\ 1 & -1\\end{bmatrix}\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 \\\\ -1 & 3 & 4\\end{bmatrix} \\\\\n&= \\begin{bmatrix}1 & 6 & 14 \\\\ 2 & -3 & -2\\end{bmatrix}\n\\end{aligned}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1f342078-4ed2-5d64-9c73-2ad6cd06661f" \\mathbf{f}(\\mathbf{y}(\\mathbf x)) = \\dfrac{\\textrm d\\mathbf f}{\\textrm d \\mathbf y} \\cdot \\dfrac{\\textrm d\\mathbf y}{\\textrm d \\mathbf x}\n$$\n\nLet's consider each of the factors in So, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=1$.\n\nUsing the shell method, the volume of the solid can be found as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nV &= 2π\\int_{c}^{d}yf(y)dy \\\\\n&= 2π\\int_{0}^{1}y(2y - 2y^{2})dy \\\\\n&= 4π\\int_{0}^{1}(y^{2} - y^{3})dy \\\\\n&= 4π(\\int_{0}^{1}y^{2}dy - \\int_{0}^{1}y^{3}dy) \\\\\n&= \\left.4π(\\frac{y^{3}}{3}\\right|_{0}^{1} - \\left.\\frac{y^{4}}{4}\\right|_{0}^{1}) \\\\\n&= 4π((\\frac{1}{3} - 0) - (\\frac{1}{4} - 0)) \\\\\n&= 4π(\\frac{1}{3} - \\frac{1}{4}) \\\\\n&= \\frac{π}{3}\n\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186069108 :question/id #uuid "2b4ef651-870f-563d-9f71-2c08a3729984" :question/math-academy-id "q-17025"} {:db/id 17592186069109 :question/id #uuid "e38e1862-ade8-5d11-82c4-4c90c727b4f0" :question/math-academy-id "q-17027"} {:db/id 17592186068816 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068658 :question/id #uuid "77659797-1ecc-567e-b864-cfb39c21b0c0" :question/math-academy-id "e-8856"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "49361606-6120-5b9c-888f-0cdaf012f125" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049178} {:db/id 17592186050057} {:db/id 17592186050819}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069022 :question/id #uuid "f700586f-01f8-5e62-9795-305f22fa8179" :question/math-academy-id "q-11402"} {:db/id 17592186069023 :question/id #uuid "5e4f431c-c20b-5b36-b61b-0c45e3b37d9b" :question/math-academy-id "q-11403"}] :knowledge-point/title "Constructing an Integral Representing the Volume of a Solid"} {:db/id 17592186068658 :question/id #uuid "77659797-1ecc-567e-b864-cfb39c21b0c0" :question/math-academy-id "e-8856" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186068816 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "49361606-6120-5b9c-888f-0cdaf012f125" :knowledge-point/title "Constructing an Integral Representing the Volume of a Solid"}] :question/problem "![](images/cf/cf4e624293586613b00a7209cd40a89b5303f0495c2fba36d751660ae7f8a91b.png)\n\nConsider the finite region bounded by the curve $x=4y-y^2$ and the $y$-axis, as shown above. If we rotate this region $2\\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis, we get a solid of revolution.\n\n![](images/19/1927064dcef318f2c0490ff071532b024da30a328b2752c28e197171eeec6b5f.png)\n\nOne way of computing the volume of the solid is to divide the interval from $y=c$ to $y=d$ on the $y$-axis to get horizontal slices. This approach is called the **shell method**.\n\nConsider one such slice of height $\\Delta{y}$, as shown in the picture below (on the left). When this rectangle is rotated about the $x$-axis, it forms a solid **shell** (i.e., the skin of a cylinder).\n\n![](images/25/2561448ab909594dda427b76860fcdda5147f8966fec9e20958d1c5fca11b536.png)\n\nSince we assume that $\\Delta{y}$ is very small, the outer radius of the shell approximately equals the inner radius $y$. The thickness of the shell is $\\Delta{y}$ and its height is $x=f(y)$.\n\nImagine we cut this shell and unfold it to obtain a rectangular solid, as shown below. Its width is $x=f(y)$, its thickness is $\\Delta{y}$, and its height is $2\\pi y$ (the circumference of the shell).\n\n![](images/03/03030fb80f0aa51c637e6d39b4f763e8d7fc89abd111a012d3e560a952cfba99.png)\n\nThe volume of the shell approximately equals the volume of the rectangular solid:\n\n$$\nV_{shell} \\mid \\approx V_{rec}; = 2πy \\cdot x \\cdot Δy; = 2πyf(y)Δy\n$$\n\nThe sum over all the shells will approximate the total volume that we want. This approximation becomes more accurate as $\\Delta{y} \\to 0$. Therefore, the volume $V$ of the solid is given by\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nV &= 2π\\int_{c}^{d}yxdy \\\\\n&= 2π\\int_{c}^{d}yf(y)dy\n\\end{aligned}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6b39e027-cd9c-572b-9d98-e3b708e1b618" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5286 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "72547125-fabd-5779-a865-3e7942bbad99" :step/math-academy-id 33070 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069749}} {:db/id 17592186069747 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068815 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068657 :question/id #uuid "29e835eb-531e-5241-911f-45e2d686b183" :question/math-academy-id "e-8853"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "623f9081-96b8-53f5-8881-b17bea5d0316" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069108} {:db/id 17592186069109}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Volume of a Solid Using the Shell Method"} :step/id #uuid "7a174fca-da25-58a3-b88f-d062ddd5cad6" :step/math-academy-id 33074} {:db/id 17592186069748 :step/content {:db/id 17592186069989 :tutorial/content "One of the advantages of using the shell method versus other methods is that the resulting integral can be much simpler to evaluate. This is often true when we want to rotate a curve of the form $x = f(y)$ about the $x$-axis.\n\nFor example, suppose we want to compute the volume generated when the region below is rotated about the $x$-axis:\n\n![](images/1d/1d23dde2cdd557feb50f82f72f4ff09174d5fb9a0c94e7810a6c06acb95a13d0.png)\n\nAccording to the shell method, the volume $V$ is given by the following straightforward integral:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nV &= 2π\\int_{0}^{1}yf(y)dy \\\\\n&= 2π\\int_{0}^{1}y(2y - 2y^{2})dy \\\\\n&= 2π\\int_{0}^{1}2y^{2} - 2y^{3}dy\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nLet's now compare this to the disc method.\n\nTo determine this volume using the disc method, we'd first need to express our curve as two separate functions of $x$, one for the lower part and one for the upper part, as follows:\n\n$$\n{y = \\frac{1}{2} + \\frac{1}{2}\\sqrt{1 - 2x},\\begin{vmatrix}y \\ge \\frac{1}{2} \\\\ y = \\frac{1}{2} - \\frac{1}{2}\\sqrt{1 - 2x},\\end{vmatrix}y < \\frac{1}{2}\n$$\n\n![](images/f4/f416ab43297265aec4836eca2020d8f08976852cc025ad4d3a0766023187adef.png)\n\nThe required volume is equal to the difference between the volumes generated when the upper and lower curves are rotated about the $x$-axis. Thus, according to the disc method, the required volume is given by\n\n$$\nV = \\pi \\int_{0}^{1/2} \\left(\\left[ \\dfrac{1}{2}+\\dfrac{1}{2}\\sqrt{1-2x} \\right]^2 - \\left[ \\dfrac{1}{2}-\\dfrac{1}{2}\\sqrt{1-2x} \\right]^2 \\right) \\textrm{d}x\n$$\n\nAs we can see, this integral is a lot more complicated than the one we obtained using the shell method!" :tutorial/id #uuid "cb718bb7-7c09-555f-bd37-dadebd89ba90" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5292 :tutorial/title "Advantages of the Shell Method"} :step/id #uuid "4660fad3-185d-5d29-946d-ac581eb8d39f" :step/math-academy-id 33076 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069747}} {:db/id 17592186069749 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068816 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068658 :question/id #uuid "77659797-1ecc-567e-b864-cfb39c21b0c0" :question/math-academy-id "e-8856"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "49361606-6120-5b9c-888f-0cdaf012f125" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049178} {:db/id 17592186050057} {:db/id 17592186050819}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069022} {:db/id 17592186069023}] :knowledge-point/title "Constructing an Integral Representing the Volume of a Solid"} :step/id #uuid "b93bd632-6fba-5317-ad2d-eb331be9e45c" :step/math-academy-id 33082 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069748}}] :activity/title "The Shell Method: Rotating a Region About the X-Axis" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186068950} {:db/id 17592186069746 :step/content {:db/id 17592186069988 :tutorial/content "Consider the plane region enclosed by the curve $x=f(y)$, the $y$-axis, and the horizontal lines $y=c$ and $y=d$, as shown below. Therefore, the volume $V$ of the solid is given by\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nV &= 2π\\int_{c}^{d}yxdy \\\\\n&= 2π\\int_{c}^{d}yf(y)dy\n\\end{aligned}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6b39e027-cd9c-572b-9d98-e3b708e1b618" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5286 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186069749 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068816 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068658 :question/id #uuid "77659797-1ecc-567e-b864-cfb39c21b0c0" :question/math-academy-id "e-8856"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "49361606-6120-5b9c-888f-0cdaf012f125" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049178} {:db/id 17592186050057} {:db/id 17592186050819}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069022} {:db/id 17592186069023}] :knowledge-point/title "Constructing an Integral Representing the Volume of a Solid"} :step/id #uuid "b93bd632-6fba-5317-ad2d-eb331be9e45c" :step/math-academy-id 33082 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069748}} {:db/id 17592186069747 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068815 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068657 :question/id #uuid "29e835eb-531e-5241-911f-45e2d686b183" :question/math-academy-id "e-8853"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "623f9081-96b8-53f5-8881-b17bea5d0316" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069108} {:db/id 17592186069109}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Volume of a Solid Using the Shell Method"} :step/id #uuid "7a174fca-da25-58a3-b88f-d062ddd5cad6" :step/math-academy-id 33074} {:db/id 17592186069748 :step/content {:db/id 17592186069989 :tutorial/content "One of the advantages of using the shell method versus other methods is that the resulting integral can be much simpler to evaluate. This is often true when we want to rotate a curve of the form $x = f(y)$ about the $x$-axis.\n\nFor example, suppose we want to compute the volume generated when the region below is rotated about the $x$-axis:\n\n![](images/1d/1d23dde2cdd557feb50f82f72f4ff09174d5fb9a0c94e7810a6c06acb95a13d0.png)\n\nAccording to the shell method, the volume $V$ is given by the following straightforward integral:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nV &= 2π\\int_{0}^{1}yf(y)dy \\\\\n&= 2π\\int_{0}^{1}y(2y - 2y^{2})dy \\\\\n&= 2π\\int_{0}^{1}2y^{2} - 2y^{3}dy\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nLet's now compare this to the disc method.\n\nTo determine this volume using the disc method, we'd first need to express our curve as two separate functions of $x$, one for the lower part and one for the upper part, as follows:\n\n$$\n{y = \\frac{1}{2} + \\frac{1}{2}\\sqrt{1 - 2x},\\begin{vmatrix}y \\ge \\frac{1}{2} \\\\ y = \\frac{1}{2} - \\frac{1}{2}\\sqrt{1 - 2x},\\end{vmatrix}y < \\frac{1}{2}\n$$\n\n![](images/f4/f416ab43297265aec4836eca2020d8f08976852cc025ad4d3a0766023187adef.png)\n\nThe required volume is equal to the difference between the volumes generated when the upper and lower curves are rotated about the $x$-axis. Thus, according to the disc method, the required volume is given by\n\n$$\nV = \\pi \\int_{0}^{1/2} \\left(\\left[ \\dfrac{1}{2}+\\dfrac{1}{2}\\sqrt{1-2x} \\right]^2 - \\left[ \\dfrac{1}{2}-\\dfrac{1}{2}\\sqrt{1-2x} \\right]^2 \\right) \\textrm{d}x\n$$\n\nAs we can see, this integral is a lot more complicated than the one we obtained using the shell method!" :tutorial/id #uuid "cb718bb7-7c09-555f-bd37-dadebd89ba90" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5292 :tutorial/title "Advantages of the Shell Method"} :step/id #uuid "4660fad3-185d-5d29-946d-ac581eb8d39f" :step/math-academy-id 33076 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069747}} {:db/id 17592186069989 :tutorial/content "One of the advantages of using the shell method versus other methods is that the resulting integral can be much simpler to evaluate. So, we need to solve the system of equations consisting of the two lines:\n\n$$\n{y = 5x + 3; y = x - 1\n$$\n\nWe will use the substitution method to solve the system. Substituting the first equation\n\n$$\ny=5x+3\n$$\n\ninto the second equation $y=x-1$ gives an equation that we can solve for $x$:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\n5x + 3 &= x - 1 \\\\\n5x &= x - 4 \\\\\n4x &= -4 \\\\\nx &= -1\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThis is the $x$-coordinate of the point of intersection. To find the $y$-coordinate, we substitute $x = -1$ back into one of the equations, say $y=x-1$, as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\ny &= x - 1 \\\\\n&=-1 - 1 \\\\\n&=-2\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the solution to the system is\n\n$$\nx=-1, \\, y=-2\n$$\n\nSo, the coordinates of the intersection point are $(-1,-2)$."} {:db/id 17592186048826} {:db/id 17592186069112 :question/id #uuid "e5474d40-cfd8-5d52-b2b0-e62e8f7d76fc" :question/math-academy-id "q-208830" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186068713 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e122a1fe-f340-5af6-9908-68ad52f89731" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Intersection of Two Lines Given in Slope-Intercept Form"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/id #uuid "328893f1-1bfe-5d8b-b29a-5733b229fb9a" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186066105} {:answer-field/id #uuid "3c1bfb5b-8661-579d-bbb2-a888c6e3cec3" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186066106}] :question/problem "The point of intersection of the lines $y = 3x - equations\n\n$$\ny=x+2\n$$\n\nand\n\n$$\ny=2x+1\n$$\n\nSo, to find the coordinates of $P$ we need to solve the system of equations consisting of the two lines:\n\n$$\n{y = x + 2; y = 2x + 1\n$$\n\nWe can solve this system by substitution. Substituting the first equation\n\n$$\ny=x+2\n$$\n\ninto the second equation\n\n$$\ny=2x+1\n$$\n\ngives an equation that we can solve for $x$:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nx + 2 &= 2x + 1 \\\\\nx + 1 &= 2x \\\\\n1 &= x\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThis is the $x$-coordinate of the point of intersection. 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the standard Hermitian inner product $⟨\\,\\cdot \\,,\\,\\cdot \\,⟩$ over $C.$ \nWhich of the following statements are true?\n\nSelect all that apply.\n\n- **I.** $⟨ia,b⟩=i⟨a,b⟩$ for any $a,b\\in {C}^{n}$\n\n- **II.** $⟨a,\\overset{―}{\\alpha }b⟩=⟨\\alpha a,b⟩$ for any $a,b\\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\\alpha \\in C$\n\n- **III.** $⟨ia,a⟩\\in R$ for any $a\\in {C}^{n}$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the standard Hermitian inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties:\n\n- It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\\alpha \\in C,$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\\,$ and $\\,⟨\\alpha a,b⟩=\\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$\n\n- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\\alpha \\in C,$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\\,$ and $\\,⟨a,\\alpha b⟩=\\overset{―}{\\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$\n\n- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\\in {C}^{n},$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$\n\n- It is positive-definite. For any $a\\in {C}^{n},$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$\n\nWith that in mind, let's examine our statements. \n\n- Statement I is true.  Indeed, the inner product in ${C}^{n}$ is linear in the first argument. So, a constant multiple from the first argument can be factored out.\n\n- Statement II is true. By the antilinearity of a complex inner product in the second argument and linearity in the first argument, we have \n\n$$\n⟨a,\\overset{―}{\\alpha }b⟩=\\overset{―}{(\\overset{―}{\\alpha })}⟨a,b⟩=\\alpha ⟨a,b⟩=⟨\\alpha a,b⟩.\n$$\n\n- Statement III is false. Notice that $⟨a,a⟩\\in R$ for any $a\\in {C}^{n}.$ Therefore, if $a\\ne 0,$ then\n\n$$\n⟨ia,a⟩=i⟨a,a⟩\\notin R.\n$$\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is \"I and II only.\""} {:db/id 17592186360759 A complex number is equal to its conjugate if and only if it is a real number. The inner product over $C$  is a complex number in general.\n\n- Statement II is true. Indeed, by the antilinearity of a complex inner product in the second argument, we have \n\n$$\n⟨a,-ib⟩=\\overset{―}{(-i)}⟨a,b⟩=i⟨a,b⟩.\n$$\n\n- Statement III is false.  The inner product over $C$ is positive-definite. So, for any $a\\in {C}^{n},$ we have\n$\\,$ $⟨a,a⟩\\ge 0.$\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is \"II only.\""} {:db/id 17592186360784 :question/id #uuid "8247f7d2-00cd-54b9-9bd1-43c13383de3e" over $C$ satisfies the following properties. \n\n- It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\\alpha \\in C,$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\\,$ and $\\,⟨\\alpha a,b⟩=\\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$\n\n- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\\alpha \\in C,$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\\,$ and $\\,⟨a,\\alpha b⟩=\\overset{―}{\\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$\n\n- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\\in {C}^{n},$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$\n\n- It is positive-definite. For any $a\\in {C}^{n},$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$\n\nFirst, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ is antilinear in the second argument:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}⟨a,\\,b-(1+3\\text{i})c⟩ & =⟨a,b⟩-⟨a,(1+3\\text{i})c⟩ \\\\  & =⟨a,b⟩-(\\overset{―}{1+3\\text{i}})⟨a,c⟩ \\\\  & =⟨a,b⟩-(1-3\\text{i})⟨a,c⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ has conjugate symmetry:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}⟨a,b⟩-(1-3\\text{i})⟨a,c⟩ & =\\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}-(1-3\\text{i})⟨a,c⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we substitute the values for $⟨b,a⟩$ and $⟨a,c⟩:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}-(1-3\\text{i})⟨a,c⟩ & =\\overset{―}{1+\\text{i}}-(1-3\\text{i})\\cdot 2 \\\\  & =1-\\text{i}-2+6\\text{i} \\\\  & =-1+5\\text{i}\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186272228 :question/id #uuid \\,⟩$ is the standard Hermitian inner product over $C,$ find $⟨a,\\,(4-\\text{i})b+c⟩$ if  \n\n$\\,$ $⟨b,a⟩=-1-\\text{i}\\,$ and $\\,⟨a,c⟩=5.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties. \n\n- It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\\alpha \\in C,$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\\,$ and $\\,⟨\\alpha a,b⟩=\\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$\n\n- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\\alpha \\in C,$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\\,$ and $\\,⟨a,\\alpha b⟩=\\overset{―}{\\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$\n\n- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\\in {C}^{n},$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$\n\n- It is positive-definite. For any $a\\in {C}^{n},$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$\n\nFirst, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ is antilinear in the second argument:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}⟨a,\\,(4-\\text{i})b+c⟩ & =⟨a,(4-\\text{i})b⟩+⟨a,c⟩ \\\\  & =(\\overset{―}{4-\\text{i}})⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩ \\\\  & =(4+\\text{i})⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ has conjugate symmetry:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}(4+\\text{i})⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c\\text{ }⟩ & =(4+\\text{i})\\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}+⟨a,c⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we substitute the values for $⟨b,a⟩$ and $⟨a,c⟩:$  \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}(4+\\text{i})\\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}+⟨a,c⟩ & =(4+\\text{i})\\cdot (\\overset{―}{-1-\\text{i}})+5 \\\\  & =(4+\\text{i})\\cdot (-1+\\text{i})+5 \\\\  & =-5+3\\text{i}+5 \\\\  & =3\\text{i}\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186360769 :question/id #uuid "57383a07-e3d6-5131-921a-e0eecd15115d" :question/math-academy-id "q-97200"} For any $a,b,c\\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\\alpha \\in C,$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\\,$ and $\\,⟨a,\\alpha b⟩=\\overset{―}{\\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$\n\n- It has conjugate symmetry. argument: \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}⟨4a-b,\\,c⟩ & =⟨4a,c⟩-⟨b,c⟩ \\\\  & =4⟨a,c⟩-⟨b,c⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ has conjugate symmetry: \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}4⟨a,c⟩-⟨b,c⟩ & =4\\overset{―}{⟨c,a⟩}-⟨b,c⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we substitute the values for $⟨c,a⟩$ and $⟨b,c⟩:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}4\\overset{―}{⟨c,a⟩}-⟨b,c⟩ & :question/math-academy-id "q-141160" :question/problem "Consider the standard Hermitian inner product $⟨\\,\\cdot \\,,\\,\\cdot \\,⟩$ over $C.$ \nWhich of the following statements are true?\n\nSelect all that apply.\n\n- **I.** $⟨ia,b⟩=i⟨a,b⟩$ for any $a,b\\in {C}^{n}$\n\n- **II.** $⟨a,\\overset{―}{\\alpha }b⟩=⟨\\alpha a,b⟩$ for any $a,b\\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\\alpha \\in C$\n\n- **III.** $⟨ia,a⟩\\in R$ for any $a\\in {C}^{n}$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the standard Hermitian inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties:\n\n- It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\\alpha \\in C,$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\\,$ and $\\,⟨\\alpha a,b⟩=\\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$\n\n- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\\alpha \\in C,$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\\,$ and $\\,⟨a,\\alpha b⟩=\\overset{―}{\\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$\n\n- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\\in {C}^{n},$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$\n\n- It is positive-definite. For any $a\\in {C}^{n},$ we have\n\n$\\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$\n\nWith that in mind, let's examine our statements. \n\n- Statement I is true.  Indeed, the inner product in ${C}^{n}$ is linear in the first argument. So, a constant multiple from the first argument can be factored out.\n\n- Statement II is true. By the antilinearity of a complex inner product in the second argument and linearity in the first argument, we have \n\n$$\n⟨a,\\overset{―}{\\alpha }b⟩=\\overset{―}{(\\overset{―}{\\alpha })}⟨a,b⟩=\\alpha ⟨a,b⟩=⟨\\alpha a,b⟩.\n$$\n\n- Statement III is false. Notice that $⟨a,a⟩\\in R$ for any $a\\in {C}^{n}.$ Therefore, if $a\\ne 0,$ then\n\n$$\n⟨ia,a⟩=i⟨a,a⟩\\notin R.\n$$\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is \"I and II only.\""} :step/id #uuid A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. \n\n$\\text{L1}:\\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$\n\n$\\text{L2}:\\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$\n\n$\\text{L3}:\\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$\n\n$\\text{L4}:\\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$\n\n$\\text{L5}:\\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$\n\n$\\text{L6}:\\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$\n\n$\\text{L7}:\\,$ $u(t)=\\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\\,\\text{d}t$\n\n$\\text{L8}:\\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\\,\\text{d}t$\n\nSelect the correct options in the following reasoning.\n\n$\\,$ Line $\\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that {{field-1}} matrix.\n\n$\\,$ Line $\\text{L5}$ follows from lines {{field-2}} by substitution.\n\n$\\,$ Line $\\text{L7}$ follows from line $\\text{L6}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation.\n\n$\\,$ Line $\\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting {{field-4}} into $\\text{L1}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each statement in turn.\n\n- We first consider line $\\text{L4}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ i.e., by substituting any column $c(t)$ of $Φ$ into the homogeneous system, we get\n\n$$\n{c}^{′}(t)=Ac(t),\n$$\n\nwhere ${c}^{′}(t)$ is the corresponding column of derivatives in $Φ.$ As a result, this means that ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ.$ Therefore, $\\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that $Φ\\text{ is a fundamental}$ matrix.\n\n- Next, we consider lines $\\text{L3}$, $\\text{L4},$ and $\\text{L5}.$ Let's substitute ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$ from $\\text{L4}$ into $\\text{L3}:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t) \\\\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+\\cancel{AΦu(t)}=\\cancel{AΦu(t)}+f(t) \\\\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, $\\text{L5}$ follows from $\\text{L3}\\text{ and }\\text{L4}$ by substitution.\n\n- Next, we consider lines $\\text{L6}$ and $\\text{L7}.$ To get $\\text{L7},$ we are $\\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\\text{L6}:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\int {u}^{′}(t)\\,\\text{d}t & =\\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\\,\\text{d}t \\\\ u(t) & =\\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\\,\\text{d}t\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- Finally, we consider lines $\\text{L1},$ $\\text{L7},$ and $\\text{L8}.$ Substituting\n\n$$\nu(t)=\\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\\,\\text{d}t\n$$\n\nfrom $\\text{L7}$ into $\\text{L1},$ we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\\\  & =Φ\\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\\,\\text{d}t.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, $\\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\\text{L7}$ into $\\text{L1}.$"} Using the method of variation of parameters, the general solution of the equation can be written in the form\n\n<table align=\"l\" cellpadding=\"0\" rules=\"all\">\n<tbody><tr>\n<td align=\"center\" height=\"40px\" rowspan=\"2\">$x(t)={c}_{1}\\begin{bmatrix}1 \\\\ 2\\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}\\begin{bmatrix}2 \\\\ 1\\end{bmatrix}{e}^{t}+\\,\\,$</td>\n<td height=\"30px\" width=\"5px\"></td>\n<td align=\"center\">{{field-1}}</td>\n<td align=\"center\" width=\"5px\"></td>\n<td align=\"center\" height=\"40px\" rowspan=\"2\">.</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td height=\"30px\" width=\"5px\"></td>\n<td align=\"center\">$-12t-6$</td>\n<td align=\"center\"></td>\n</tr>\n</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as \n\n$$\nx(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)\n$$\n\nwhere ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.\n\nNotice that we are given that\n\n$$\n{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\\begin{bmatrix}1 \\\\ 2\\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}\\begin{bmatrix}2 \\\\ 1\\end{bmatrix}{e}^{t}.\n$$\n\nWe'll look for a particular solution in the form\n\n$$\n{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\\,u(t)\n$$\n\nwhere $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and\n\n$$\nu(t)=\\int {Φ}^{-1}\\,f(t)\\,\\text{d}t.\n$$\n\nIn our case,\n\n$$\nΦ=\\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{t} \\\\ 2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t}\\end{bmatrix},\\,f(t)=\\begin{bmatrix}12t \\\\ 0\\end{bmatrix}.\n$$\n\nSince $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\\frac{1}{{e}^{-2t}\\cdot {e}^{t}-2{e}^{t}\\cdot 2{e}^{-2t}}\\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & -2{e}^{t} \\\\ -2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-2t}\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =-\\frac{{e}^{t}}{3}\\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & -2{e}^{t} \\\\ -2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-2t}\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =-\\frac{1}{3}\\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -2{e}^{2t} \\\\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\\end{bmatrix} \\\\ {Φ}^{-1}\\,f(t) & =-\\frac{1}{3}\\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -2{e}^{2t} \\\\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\\end{bmatrix}\\begin{bmatrix}12t \\\\ 0\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}-4t{e}^{2t} \\\\ 8t{e}^{-t}\\end{bmatrix}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, using our formula for $u(t),$ we $\\mathbf{f}(t)$ is a forcing vector.\n\nIn this lesson, we'll derive the formula for the particular solution of the above system using the method of variation of parameters.\n\nRecall that the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous system is given by\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{x}_c(t)  = \\Phi \\, \\mathbf{c}\n$$\n\nwhere $\\mathbf{c}$ is a vector of constants, and $\\Phi$ is the fundamental matrix.\n\nAs usual, for the method of variation of parameters, we'll look for a particular solution of our inhomogeneous system by varying the constant parameters, i.e., in the form\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{x}_p(t)  = \\Phi \\, \\mathbf{u}(t)\n$$\n\nwhere $\\mathbf{u}(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined.\n\nDifferentiating $\\mathbf{x}_p(t)$ with respect to $t,$ we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =(Φ\\,u(t))^{′} \\\\  & =Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, since $\\mathbf{x}_p(t)$ is a solution, substituting it back into the initial system gives a true equation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\\\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, since $\\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix, $\\Phi' = A \\Phi.$ Substituting this into the equation simplifies it to the following:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Φ{u}^{′}(t)+AΦu(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t) \\\\ Φ{u}^{′}(t) & =f(t)\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThen, since $\\Phi$ is invertible, we can pre-multiply both sides by $\\Phi^{-1}{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\\cdot f(t) \\\\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we integrate both sides of the final equations (ignoring the constant term):\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\int {u}^{′}(t)\\,\\text{d}t & =\\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\\,\\text{d}t \\\\ u(t) & =\\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\\,\\text{d}t\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, our particular solution is\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{x}_p(t) = \\Phi \\displaystyle\\int \\Phi^{-1}\\mathbf{f}(t) \\, \\text{d}t.\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "99630576-f78f-593a-af83-87c98421e2c0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14396 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186167897 Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\\frac{1}{0\\cdot (-6{e}^{2t})-5{e}^{2t}\\cdot {e}^{-3t}}\\begin{bmatrix}-6{e}^{2t} & -5{e}^{2t} \\\\ -{e}^{-3t} & 0\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =-\\frac{{e}^{t}}{5}\\begin{bmatrix}-6{e}^{2t} & -5{e}^{2t} \\\\ -{e}^{-3t} & 0\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =-\\frac{1}{5}\\begin{bmatrix}-6{e}^{3t} & 6{e}^{t}\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}12{e}^{4t} \\\\ {e}^{-t}\\end{bmatrix}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\\int {Φ}^{-1}\\,f(t)\\,\\text{d}t \\\\  & =\\int \\begin{bmatrix}12{e}^{4t} \\\\ {e}^{-t}\\end{bmatrix}\\,\\text{d}t \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}\\int 12{e}^{4t}\\,\\text{d}t \\\\ \\int {e}^{-t}\\,\\text{d}t\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}3{e}^{4t} \\\\ -{e}^{-t}\\end{bmatrix}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, our particular solution is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & Using the method of variation of parameters, the general solution of the equation can be written in the form\n\n<table align=\"l\" cellpadding=\"0\" rules=\"all\">\n<tbody><tr>\n<td align=\"center\" height=\"40px\" rowspan=\"2\">$x(t)={c}_{1}\\begin{bmatrix}1 \\\\ 2\\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}\\begin{bmatrix}2 \\\\ 1\\end{bmatrix}{e}^{t}+\\,\\,$</td>\n<td height=\"30px\" width=\"5px\"></td>\n<td align=\"center\">{{field-1}}</td>\n<td align=\"center\" width=\"5px\"></td>\n<td align=\"center\" height=\"40px\" rowspan=\"2\">.</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td height=\"30px\" width=\"5px\"></td>\n<td align=\"center\">$-12t-6$</td>\n<td align=\"center\"></td>\n</tr>\n</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as \n\n$$\nx(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)\n$$\n\nwhere ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.\n\nNotice that we are given that\n\n$$\n{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\\begin{bmatrix}1 \\\\ 2\\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}\\begin{bmatrix}2 \\\\ 1\\end{bmatrix}{e}^{t}.\n$$\n\nWe'll look for a particular solution in the form\n\n$$\n{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\\,u(t)\n$$\n\nwhere $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and\n\n$$\nu(t)=\\int {Φ}^{-1}\\,f(t)\\,\\text{d}t.\n$$\n\nIn our case,\n\n$$\nΦ=\\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{t} \\\\ 2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t}\\end{bmatrix},\\,f(t)=\\begin{bmatrix}12t \\\\ 0\\end{bmatrix}.\n$$\n\nSince $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\\frac{1}{{e}^{-2t}\\cdot {e}^{t}-2{e}^{t}\\cdot 2{e}^{-2t}}\\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & -2{e}^{t} \\\\ -2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-2t}\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =-\\frac{{e}^{t}}{3}\\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t} & -2{e}^{t} \\\\ -2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-2t}\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =-\\frac{1}{3}\\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -2{e}^{2t} \\\\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\\end{bmatrix} \\\\ {Φ}^{-1}\\,f(t) & =-\\frac{1}{3}\\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t} & -2{e}^{2t} \\\\ -2{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\\end{bmatrix}\\begin{bmatrix}12t \\\\ 0\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}-4t{e}^{2t} \\\\ 8t{e}^{-t}\\end{bmatrix}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\\int {Φ}^{-1}\\,f(t)\\,\\text{d}t \\\\  & =\\int \\begin{bmatrix}-4t{e}^{2t} \\\\ 8t{e}^{-t}\\end{bmatrix}\\,\\text{d}t \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}\\int -4t{e}^{2t}\\,\\text{d}t \\\\ \\int 8t{e}^{-t}\\,\\text{d}t\\end{bmatrix}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nIntegrating the components by parts, we get the following:\n\n- For the first component, let $u=-4t$ and $\\text{d}v={e}^{2t}\\,\\text{d}t.$ Then, $\\text{d}u=-4\\,\\text{d}t$ and $v=\\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}.$ So,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\int -4t{e}^{2t}\\,\\text{d}t & =(-4t)\\cdot \\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\\int \\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}\\cdot (-4\\,\\text{d}t) \\\\  & =-2t{e}^{2t}+\\int 2{e}^{2t}\\,\\text{d}t \\\\  & =-2t{e}^{2t}+{e}^{2t} \\\\  & ={e}^{2t}(1-2t).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- For the second component, let $u=8t$ and $\\text{d}v={e}^{-t}\\,\\text{d}t.$ Then, $\\text{d}u=8\\,\\text{d}t$ and $v=-{e}^{-t}.$ So,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\int -4t{e}^{2t}\\,\\text{d}t & =8t\\cdot (-{e}^{-t})-\\int -{e}^{-t}\\cdot 8\\,\\text{d}t \\\\  & =-8t{e}^{-t}+\\int 8\\,{e}^{-t}\\text{d}t \\\\  & =-8t{e}^{-t}-8{e}^{2t} \\\\  & =-8{e}^{-t}(1+t).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, our particular solution is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\\,u(t) \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{t} \\\\ 2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{t}\\end{bmatrix}\\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t}(1-2t) \\\\ -8{e}^{-t}(1+t)\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}(1-2t)-16(1+t) \\\\ 2(1-2t)-8(1+t)\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}-18t-15 \\\\ -12t-6\\end{bmatrix}.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} :step/id #uuid values:\n\n- $Y = u$ with probability $0.2$, and $\\textrm{E}[X \\mid Y = u] = 6$\n- $Y = v$ with probability $0.5$, and $\\textrm{E}[X \\mid Y = v] = 9$\n- $Y = w$ with probability $0.3$, and \\cdot P(Y = w) \\\\\n&= 6 \\cdot 0.2 + 9 \\cdot 0.5 + 3 \\cdot 0.3 \\\\\n&= 1.2 + 4.5 + 0.9 \\\\\n&= 6.6\n\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186048872} {:db/id 17592186208940 :question/id #uuid This is a classic application of the law of total expectation, which allows us to calculate an overall expected value by conditioning on a related variable — in this case, the forest where the researcher is stationed.\n\nLet $X$ be the number of animal sightings in a day, and let $Y$ be the forest to which the researcher is assigned.\n\n- $Y = 1$ with probability $0.7$, and $\\textrm{E}[X \\mid Y = 1] = 6.2$.\n- $Y = 2$ with probability $0.3$, and $\\textrm{E}[X \\mid Y = 2] = 3.8$.\n\nSo, we calculate our expected value as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nE[X] &= E[X∣Y = 1] \\cdot P(Y = 1) + E[X∣Y = 2] \\cdot P(Y = 2) \\\\\n&= 6.2 \\cdot 0.7 + 3.8 \\cdot 0.3 \\\\\n&= 4.34 + 1.14 \\\\\n&= 5.48\n\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186208942 :question/id #uuid "ad5dd599-02f8-5a54-97a3-d02a13f8e9e6" :question/math-academy-id "q-275330"} {:db/id 17592186208943 :question/id #uuid "d5a708e9-c589-5fc2-b4d6-ac87be196ece" :question/math-academy-id "q-275331" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186208561 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "680dff97-3a2b-57ad-b234-c6184b9ef867" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating an Expectation in Context"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/id #uuid "a8515f8b-2618-5ee6-abbc-c44663bca517" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186205414}] :question/problem "A surveyor is sent to one of three cities: $A$, $B$, or $C$. [{:db/id 17592186209502 :step/content {:db/id 17592186209887 :tutorial/content "Recall that if $X$ is a discrete random variable, the expected value of $X$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\textrm{E}[X] = \\sum_{x} x\\cdot P(X = x)\n$$\n\nThere is an alternative method for computing $\\textrm{E}[X]$, which allows us to compute the expected value of a random variable by conditioning on another variable.\n\nSuppose another discrete random variable $Y$ takes on a set of possible values. If we know\n\n$$\n\\textrm{E}[X \\mid Y = y]\n$$\n\nfor each value $y$, then the **law of total expectation** states\n\n$$\n\\textrm{E}[X] = \\sum_{y} \\textrm{E}[X \\mid Y = y] \\cdot P(Y = y)\n$$\n\nConceptually, this tells us that $\\textrm{E}[X]$ is just a weighted average of the conditional expectations\n\n$$\n\\textrm{E}[X \\mid Y = y]\n$$\n\nwhere each weight is the probability\n\n$$\nP(Y = y)\n$$\n\nIn many problems, directly computing $\\textrm{E}[X]$ from the definition can be difficult. It turns out that breaking $\\textrm{E}[X]$ up into conditional pieces often simplifies things. The law of total expectation is especially useful when $X$ depends on an underlying condition $Y$, and each conditional case is easier to analyze than the full distribution of $X$.\n\nLet’s see how this works in practice with a few examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "48593a4b-9b04-583a-b9c6-5d781d9c5d4c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 12912 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "4ca67c7d-008b-5867-a495-27c33923a7f3" :step/math-academy-id 448840 :step/next {:db/id 17592186209503}} {:db/id 17592186209503 :step/content {:db/id 17592186209888 :tutorial/content "Let $X$ and $Y$ be discrete random variables, where $Y$ takes values $\\alpha$ and $\\beta$ with probabilities $0.4$ and $0.6$, respectively. Suppose we are given the following conditional expectations:\n\n- $\\textrm{E}[X \\mid Y = \\alpha] = 7$\n- $\\textrm{E}[X \\mid Y = \\beta] = 3$\n\nLet's compute $\\textrm{E}[X]$ using the law of total expectation.\n\nThe law of total expectation states\n\n$$\n\\textrm{E}[X]= \\sum_y \\textrm{E} [X \\mid Y = y] \\cdot P(Y=y)\n$$\n\nIn this problem, $Y$ takes two values:\n\n- $Y = \\alpha$ with probability $0.4$, and $\\textrm{E}[X \\mid Y = \\alpha] = 7$\n- $Y = \\beta$ with probability $0.6$, and $\\textrm{E}[X \\mid Y = \\beta] = 3$\n\nSo, we calculate our expected value as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nE[X] &= E[X∣Y = α] \\cdot P(Y = α) + E[X∣Y = β] \\cdot P(Y = β) \\\\\n&= 7 \\cdot 0.4 + 3 \\cdot 0.6 \\\\\n&= 2.8 + 1.8 \\\\\n&= 4.6\n\\end{aligned}\n$$" :tutorial/id 17592186209506}} {:db/id 17592186209506 :step/content {:db/id 17592186209885 :tutorial/content "We’ve seen that the law of total expectation allows us to compute the expected value of a random variable $X$ by conditioning on another variable $Y$. This idea extends naturally to a more general and elegant identity called the **tower property**:\n\n$$\n\\textrm{E}[X] = \\textrm{E}[\\textrm{E}[X \\mid Y]]\n$$\n\nAt first glance, this may look abstract, so let’s unpack what it means.\n\nThe inner term $\\textrm{E}[X \\mid Y]$ is itself a *random variable*—its value depends on the outcome of $Y$. The outer expectation then takes the average of that conditional expectation over all possible values of $Y$.\n\nIn other words, we are averaging $X$ in two stages:\n\n- Within each scenario (for each possible value of $Y$), we find the expected value of $X$.\n- Across all scenarios, we take the weighted average of those conditional expectations, where the weights are the probabilities of each $Y$.\n\nLet’s explore a few examples to build some intuition." :tutorial/id #uuid "bc773ad5-ce02-5722-96a2-08ef2c5ac53d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 12910 :tutorial/title "The Tower Property"} :step/id 17592186209887 :tutorial/content "Recall that if $X$ is a discrete random variable, the expected value of $X$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\textrm{E}[X] = \\sum_{x} x\\cdot P(X = x)\n$$\n\nThere is an alternative method for computing $\\textrm{E}[X]$, which allows us to compute the expected value of a random variable by conditioning on another variable.\n\nSuppose another discrete random variable $Y$ takes on a set of possible values. If we know\n\n$$\n\\textrm{E}[X \\mid Y = y]\n$$\n\nfor each value $y$, then the **law of total expectation** states\n\n$$\n\\textrm{E}[X] = \\sum_{y} \\textrm{E}[X \\mid Y = y] \\cdot P(Y = y)\n$$\n\nConceptually, this tells us that $\\textrm{E}[X]$ is just a weighted average of the conditional expectations\n\n$$\n\\textrm{E}[X \\mid Y = y]\n$$\n\nwhere each weight is the probability\n\n$$\nP(Y = y)\n$$\n\nIn many problems, directly computing $\\textrm{E}[X]$ from the definition can be difficult. It turns out that breaking $\\textrm{E}[X]$ up into conditional pieces often simplifies things. The law of total expectation is especially useful when $X$ depends on an underlying condition $Y$, and each conditional case is easier to analyze than the full distribution of $X$.\n\nLet’s see how this works in practice with a few examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "48593a4b-9b04-583a-b9c6-5d781d9c5d4c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 12912 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "4ca67c7d-008b-5867-a495-27c33923a7f3" :step/math-academy-id 448840 :step/next {:db/id 17592186209503}} {:db/id 17592186209887 :tutorial/content "Recall that if $X$ is a discrete random variable, the expected value of $X$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\textrm{E}[X] = \\sum_{x} x\\cdot P(X = x)\n$$\n\nThere is an alternative method for computing $\\textrm{E}[X]$, which allows us to compute the expected value of a random variable by conditioning on another variable.\n\nSuppose another discrete random variable $Y$ takes on a set of possible values. Suppose we are given the following conditional expectations:\n\n- $\\textrm{E}[X \\mid Y = \\alpha] = 7$\n- $\\textrm{E}[X \\mid Y = \\beta] = 3$\n\nLet's compute $\\textrm{E}[X]$ using the law of total expectation.\n\nThe law of total expectation states\n\n$$\n\\textrm{E}[X]= \\sum_y \\textrm{E} [X \\mid Y = y] \\cdot P(Y=y)\n$$\n\nIn this problem, $Y$ takes two values:\n\n- $Y = \\alpha$ with probability $0.4$, and $\\textrm{E}[X \\mid Y = \\alpha] = 7$\n- $Y = \\beta$ with probability $0.6$, and $\\textrm{E}[X \\mid Y = \\beta] = 3$\n\nSo, we calculate our expected value as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nE[X] &= E[X∣Y = α] \\cdot P(Y = α) + E[X∣Y = β] \\cdot P(Y = β) \\\\\n&= 7 \\cdot 0.4 + 3 \\cdot 0.6 \\\\\n&= 2.8 + 1.8 \\\\\n&= 4.6\n\\end{aligned}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "d728e35d-7ac2-5df5-a542-66e724725c43" :tutorial/math-academy-id 12913 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example of the Total Expectation"} :step/id #uuid "e48c6b64-85c3-54f7-b599-8bad2d53d91b" :step/math-academy-id 448841 :step/next {:db/id 17592186209504}} {:db/id 17592186209888 :tutorial/content "Let $X$ and $Y$ be discrete random variables, where $Y$ takes values $\\alpha$ and $\\beta$ with probabilities $0.4$ and $0.6$, respectively. from any point on the surface to the $xy$-plane equals the distance from that point to the $z$-axis. arbitrarily in its domain. \n\nTherefore, our surface is the half-cone shown below.\n\n![](images/69/69978d3f1026cf83019924c44d66f0e510ce8c84b35d10c77c270b87809b30aa.png)"} {:db/id 17592186176199 \n\nThe tangent of this angle equals the ratio between the distance $r$ from the point to the $z$-axis and the distance $z$ from the point to the $xy$-plane. :tutorial/content "Recall that for a point $(r,\\theta,z)$ in cylindrical polar coordinates,\n\n- $r\\geq 0$ and $\\theta\\in [0,2\\pi)$ are the usual plane polar coordinates, and\n\n- $z\\in (-\\infty, \\infty)$ is the usual Cartesian $z$-coordinate.\n\nWhen we fix one of these coordinates and allow the others to vary, we obtain some simple surfaces.\n\n- The equation \n\n$$\nr=c, \\qquad\n$$\n\n where $c\\geq 0$ requires that the distance from any point on the surface to the $z$-axis is fixed while $\\theta$ and $z$ can vary arbitrarily in their respective domains. So, we obtain a circular cylinder.\n\n![](images/72/728776f0f04642a1596df605968cb5dc5df22ea0a401cf9522ba1ff91839ff0e.png)\n\n- The equation \n\n$$\n\\theta=c\n$$\n\n where $c\\in [0,2\\pi)$ requires that if we project the vector $\\overrightarrow{OP}$ onto the $xy$-plane for every point $P$ on our surface, the resulting vector makes an angle of $c$ radians with the positive $x$-axis. This constructs a **half-plane** that passes through the $z$-axis.\n\n![](images/bd/bdc54b001fde4816ced9eff3a771bdd5900804f78b3bd5e9586db42bebe80297.png)\n\n- Finally, the equation \n\n$$\nz=c\n$$\n\n where $z\\in (-\\infty, \\infty)$ requires that the $z$-coordinate of any point on our surface is fixed while $\\theta$ and $z$ can vary arbitrarily in their respective domains. Therefore, this surface is a plane parallel to the $xy$-plane.\n\n![](images/c3/c3f0af5747690797f27e156aa281c0b24f600919961a63a0244febaca710fcbe.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid defined by the equation $z^2=r^2$ in cylindrical polar coordinates?\n\nAgain, recall that for a point $(r,\\theta,z)$ in cylindrical polar coordinates,\n\n- $r\\geq 0$ and $\\theta\\in [0,2\\pi)$ are the usual plane polar coordinates, and\n\n- $z\\in (-\\infty, \\infty)$ is the usual Cartesian $z$-coordinate.\n\nWith that in mind, let's examine our equation:\n\n$$\nz^2=r^2\n$$\n\nThis equation requires that the square of the distance from any point on the surface to the $xy$-plane equals the square of the distance from that point to the $z$-axis.\nIn other words, the tangent of the angle between any position vector on the surface and the $z$-axis, which is given by $\\dfrac{r}{z}$, must be equal to\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{r}{z} =\\pm \\sqrt{\\dfrac{r^2}{z^2}} = \\pm\\sqrt{\\dfrac{r^2}{r^2}} = \\pm1.\n$$\n\nOn the other hand, $\\theta$ can vary arbitrarily in its domain. \n\n- For $\\dfrac{r}{z} = 1,$ the angle between the position vector of any point on the surface and the $z$-axis must be equal $\\dfrac{\\pi}{4}.$ This corresponds to a *half-cone* for positive $z{:}$\n\n![](images/18/1841d50bb07c0e6787f4824af0e13516912fb9ad77fac0515f00c243899eb18e.png)\n\n- On the other hand, for $\\dfrac{r}{z} = -1,$ the angle between the position vector of any point on the surface and the $z$-axis must be equal $\\dfrac{3\\pi}{4}.$ This corresponds to a *half-cone* for negative $z{:}$\n\n![](images/e3/e32b1b4ba84faea7a4dc536e0f49bcda9295a4a42790162b3b9bad06db39a908.png)\n\nTherefore, combining the two half cones, the equation $z^2 = r^2$ defines the *cone* shown below.\n\n![](images/84/842f8cf967d10144e568804bdfb1aadf75f029cf87dd7b6785168a44a95d0615.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "795b19b5-f3e0-535a-99a9-cd09e1c2cb58" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5309 :tutorial/title {:db/id 17592186176987 :tutorial/content "So far, we have kept the domains of the plane polar coordinates restricted to $r\\geq 0$ and $\\theta\\in [0,2\\pi).$ What happens if we lift these restrictions?\n\nConsider the equation $r=\\theta$ with the domain restrictions $r\\geq 0$ and $\\theta\\in [0,2\\pi)$ which defines the surface shown below.\n\n![](images/84/84737b12a1689fe2ac03ab09572e4c396d35493f55df5d65af80eeb8c5ae5676.png)\n\nSuppose we remove the restriction $\\theta\\in[0,2\\pi)$ so that it can be any number. What would the surface look like then?\n\nIf we remove the restriction on $\\theta,$ we obtain more spirals. For example, the diagram below shows $r=\\theta$ for $\\theta \\in [0, 4\\pi).$\n\n![](images/56/568291daf47340265d97a121f0b7b927233f2698e87e0d5adebbba640ff20afe.png)\n\nWe can also lift the restriction $r \\geq 0$ so $r$ can take negative values. constraint. \n\nTherefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:\n\n$$\n∇f(x,y)=\\lambda ∇g(x,y),\\,g(x,y)=1\n$$\n\nWe start by solving the first equation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\\\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\\\ ⟨-1,-1⟩ & =\\lambda ⟨2x,2y⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNotice that we cannot have $\\lambda =0$ since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. Therefore, assuming $\\lambda \\ne 0,$ we have the following:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}-1 &=2\\lambda x \\\\ -1 &=2\\lambda y\\end{aligned}\\right.\\,⇒\\,\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}x &=-\\frac{1}{2\\lambda } \\\\ y &=-\\frac{1}{2\\lambda }\\end{aligned}\\right.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, we substitute our expressions for $x$ and $y$ into the condition $g(x,y)=1$ and solve for $\\lambda ,$ as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{4{\\lambda }^{2}}+\\frac{1}{4{\\lambda }^{2}} & =1 \\\\ \\frac{2}{4{\\lambda }^{2}} & =1 \\\\ {\\lambda }^{2} & =\\frac{1}{2} \\\\ \\lambda  & =\\pm \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe can now find $x$ and $y.$ This gives\n\n$$\nx=\\pm \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}},\\,y=\\pm \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points\n\n$$\n(-\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}},-\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}),\\,(\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}},\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}).\n$$\n\nWe evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:\n\n| $\\,(x,y)\\,$ | $\\,(-\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}},-\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}})\\,$ | $\\,(\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}},\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}})\\,$ |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| $\\,f(x,y)\\,$ | $\\,1+\\sqrt{2}\\,$ | $\\,1-\\sqrt{2}\\,$ |\n\n$$\n\n$$\n\nTherefore, the function reaches a maximum value at $(-\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}},-\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}),$ and its maximum value is ⟨2x,-2y⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, we have the following:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}2(x-1) &=2\\lambda x \\\\ 2y &=-2\\lambda constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. \n\nTherefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:\n\n$$\n∇f(x,y)=\\lambda ∇g(x,y),\\,g(x,y)=0\n$$\n\nWe start by solving the first equation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\\\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\\\ ⟨2x,2y+4⟩ & =\\lambda ⟨2x,4y⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, we have the following:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}2x &=2\\lambda x \\\\ 2y+4 &=4\\lambda y\\end{aligned}\\right.\\,⇒\\,\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}x(1-\\lambda ) &=0 \\\\ y(2\\lambda -1) &=2\\end{aligned}\\right.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTo solve this system, we break it up into several cases:\n\n- Assuming $x=0$ in the first equation of the system, the constraint condition ${x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-2=0$ implies\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}2{y}^{2}-2 & =0\\,⇒\\,y=\\pm 1.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThis gives the critical points $(0,-1),(0,1).$\n\n- Assuming $\\lambda =1$ in the first equation of the system, the second equation of the system implies\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}y(2(1)-1)=2\\,⇒\\,y=2.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThen, the constraint condition ${x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-2=0$ implies\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}=-6.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhich gives a contradiction.\n\nTherefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points\n\n$$\n(0,-1),\\,(0,1).\n$$\n\nWe evaluate $f$ at these points. These are given in the following table:\n\n| $(x,y)$ | $(0,-1)$ | $(0,1)$ |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| $f(x,y)$ | $1$ | $9$ |\n\nTherefore, the function reaches a maximum value at the point $(0,1)$ and the parabola ${x}^{2}-2y-4=0.$\n\n*Hint: You may assume that the global minimum of $f(x,y)$ exists on the parabola.*" :question/worked-solution "We must find the minimum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)={x}^{2}-2y-4=0.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:\n\n$$\n∇f(x,y)=\\lambda ∇g(x,y),\\,g(x,y)=0\n$$\n\nWe start by solving the first equation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\\\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\\\ ⟨2x,2y⟩ & =\\lambda ⟨2x,-2⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, we have the following:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}2x &=2\\lambda x \\\\ 2y &=-2\\lambda\\end{aligned}\\right.\\,⇒\\,\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}x(1-\\lambda ) &=0 \\\\ y &=-\\lambda\\end{aligned}\\right.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTo solve this system, we break it up into several cases:\n\n- Assuming $x=0$ in the first equation of the system, the constraint condition ${x}^{2}-2y-4=0$ implies\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}-2y-4 & =0\\,⇒\\,y=-2.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThis gives the critical point $(0,-2).$\n\n- Assuming $\\lambda =1$ in the first equation of the system, the second equation of the system implies\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}y=-1.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThen, the constraint condition ${x}^{2}-2y-4=0$ implies\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2-4 & =0\\,⇒\\,x=\\pm \\sqrt{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThis gives the critical points $(-\\sqrt{2},-1),(\\sqrt{2},-1).$\n\nTherefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points\n\n$$\n(0,-2),\\,(\\pm \\sqrt{2},-1).\n$$\n\nWe evaluate $f$ at these points. These are given in the following table:\n\n| $(x,y)$ | $(0,-2)$ | $(\\pm \\sqrt{2},-1)$ |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| $f(x,y)$ | $4$ | $3$ |\n\nTherefore, the function reaches a minimum value at the points $(\\pm \\sqrt{2},-1)$ and its minimum value is $3.$"} {:db/id 17592186048972} {:db/id 17592186050688} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "fa485803-94c1-5d4d-81e7-ca9b8b7a3998" :topic/math-academy-id 1948} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125553 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125845 :tutorial/content "Suppose we would like to find the minimum and maximum values of the function\n\n$$\nf(x,y) = 2x^2+4y^2\n$$\n\nsubject to constraint $g(x,y) = x^2+y^2=1.$ In other words, we wish to find the global extrema of $f(x,y)$ defined on the circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin, as shown below.\n\n![](images/39/39893af9755488d142116370d451b7a3d92b334c27f983eb302492b0d516c41c.png)\n\nFirst, let's draw our constraint circle ($x^2+y^2=1$) and consider the level curves of $f(x,y).$ These level curves are ellipses of the form\n\n$$\nf(x,y) = 2x^2+4y^2 = k.\n$$\n\nAs we increase the parameter $k,$ we get ellipses with larger and larger axes, as shown below. \n\n![](images/d5/d59d566c9cf7e252884a1397eb4ac0c8f85b290790e9063be2ff6eb4a4aff04a.png)\n\nAs we continue to increase $k,$ a level curve will touch the circle at the points $(\\pm 1, 0)$ for some value of $k.$ The value of $k$ corresponding to that level curve gives us the *smallest* possible value of $f(x,y)$ on our circle $x^2+y^2=1.$\n\nIncreasing $k$ even further, we'll get another value of $k$ for which the corresponding level curve touches the circle at the points $(0, \\pm 1),$ as shown below. This value of $k$ gives us the *largest* possible value of the function $f(x,y)$ on our circle.\n\n![](images/48/48f71f5aa237936be24ccba572fb650b0d477c252d8338549a33cfea4874cbad.png)\n\nNotice that the corresponding level curves touch the circle in both cases (the minimum and the maximum). So, the level curve $f(x,y)=k$ and the circle $g(x,y)=1$ have a common tangent at these points. This means that the *gradients* of both curves must be parallel at these points. Therefore, at the extreme points, we must have\n\n$$\n\\nabla f(x,y) = \\lambda \\nabla g(x,y),\n$$\n\nwhere $\\lambda$ is some real number. The number $\\lambda$ is called a **Lagrange multiplier**.\n\nWe can now use these observations to write down a general method for optimizing a function subject to a constraint." :tutorial/id #uuid :step/content {:db/id 17592186125872 :tutorial/content "The **method of Lagrange multipliers** states that the extrema of a function $f(x,y)$ subject to constraint $g(x,y)=c$ can be found by solving the system\n\n$$\n\\nabla f(x,y) = \\lambda \\nabla g(x,y), \\qquad g(x,y)=c.\n$$\n\nThe method of Lagrange multipliers assumes that $\\nabla g \\neq \\mathbf{0}$ on the curve $g(x,y)=c.$\n\nNote that solutions to this system do not always exist! For example, the function $f(x,y)=x+y$ does not have a minimum (or maximum) on the hyperbola $x^2-y^2=1.$\n\nHowever, we can use the following theorem to guarantee the existence of solutions in some cases:\n\n*If $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint function $g(x,y) = c$ is closed and bounded, then $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint.*" :tutorial/id #uuid 17592186125553 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125845 :tutorial/content "Suppose we would like to find the minimum and maximum values of the function\n\n$$\nf(x,y) = 2x^2+4y^2\n$$\n\nsubject to constraint $g(x,y) = x^2+y^2=1.$ In other words, we wish to find the global extrema of $f(x,y)$ defined on the circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin, as shown below.\n\n![](images/39/39893af9755488d142116370d451b7a3d92b334c27f983eb302492b0d516c41c.png)\n\nFirst, let's draw our constraint circle ($x^2+y^2=1$) and consider the level curves of $f(x,y).$ These level curves are ellipses of the form\n\n$$\nf(x,y) = 2x^2+4y^2 = k.\n$$\n\nAs we increase the parameter $k,$ we get ellipses with larger and larger axes, as shown below. \n\n![](images/d5/d59d566c9cf7e252884a1397eb4ac0c8f85b290790e9063be2ff6eb4a4aff04a.png)\n\nAs we continue to increase $k,$ a level curve will touch the circle at the points $(\\pm 1, 0)$ for some value of $k.$ The value of $k$ corresponding to that level curve gives us the *smallest* possible value of $f(x,y)$ on our circle $x^2+y^2=1.$\n\nIncreasing $k$ even further, we'll get another value of $k$ for which the corresponding level curve touches the circle at the points $(0, \\pm 1),$ as shown below. This value of $k$ gives us the *largest* possible value of the function $f(x,y)$ on our circle.\n\n![](images/48/48f71f5aa237936be24ccba572fb650b0d477c252d8338549a33cfea4874cbad.png)\n\nNotice that the corresponding level curves touch the circle in both cases (the minimum and the maximum). So, the level curve $f(x,y)=k$ and the circle $g(x,y)=1$ have a common tangent at these points. This means that the *gradients* of both curves must be parallel at these points. Therefore, at the extreme points, we must have\n\n$$\n\\nabla f(x,y) = \\lambda \\nabla g(x,y),\n$$\n\nwhere $\\lambda$ is some real number. The number $\\lambda$ is called a **Lagrange multiplier**.\n\nWe can now use these observations to write down a general method for optimizing a function subject to a constraint." :tutorial/id #uuid "932667c3-77f7-56cb-ae08-dd6835e29462" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5109 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "639b5b29-18f2-5454-b193-c76dd6a45f3a" :step/math-academy-id 32055 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125627}} {:db/id 17592186125845 :tutorial/content "Suppose we would like to find the minimum and maximum values of the function\n\n$$\nf(x,y) = 2x^2+4y^2\n$$\n\nsubject to constraint $g(x,y) = x^2+y^2=1.$ In other words, we wish to find the global extrema of $f(x,y)$ defined on the circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin, as shown below.\n\n![](images/39/39893af9755488d142116370d451b7a3d92b334c27f983eb302492b0d516c41c.png)\n\nFirst, let's draw our constraint circle ($x^2+y^2=1$) and consider the level curves of $f(x,y).$ These level curves are ellipses of the form\n\n$$\nf(x,y) = 2x^2+4y^2 = k.\n$$\n\nAs we increase the parameter $k,$ we get ellipses with larger and larger axes, as shown below. \n\n![](images/d5/d59d566c9cf7e252884a1397eb4ac0c8f85b290790e9063be2ff6eb4a4aff04a.png)\n\nAs we continue to increase $k,$ a level curve will touch the circle at the points $(\\pm 1, 0)$ for some value of $k.$ The value of $k$ corresponding to that level curve gives us the *smallest* possible value of $f(x,y)$ on our circle $x^2+y^2=1.$\n\nIncreasing $k$ even further, we'll get another value of $k$ for which the corresponding level curve touches the circle at the points $(0, \\pm 1),$ as shown below. constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. \n\nTherefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:\n\n$$\n∇f(x,y)=\\lambda ∇g(x,y),\\,g(x,y)=1\n$$\n\nWe start by solving the first equation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\\\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\\\ ⟨-1,-1⟩ & =\\lambda ⟨2x,2y⟩\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNotice that we cannot have $\\lambda =0$ since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. Therefore, assuming $\\lambda \\ne 0,$ we have the following:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}-1 &=2\\lambda x \\\\ -1 &=2\\lambda y\\end{aligned}\\right.\\,⇒\\,\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}x &=-\\frac{1}{2\\lambda } \\\\ y &=-\\frac{1}{2\\lambda }\\end{aligned}\\right.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, we substitute our expressions for $x$ and $y$ into the condition $g(x,y)=1$ and solve for $\\lambda ,$ as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{4{\\lambda }^{2}}+\\frac{1}{4{\\lambda }^{2}} & =1 \\\\ \\frac{2}{4{\\lambda }^{2}} & =1 \\\\ {\\lambda }^{2} & =\\frac{1}{2} \\\\ \\lambda  & =\\pm \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe can now find $x$ and $y.$ This gives\n\n$$\nx=\\pm \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}},\\,y=\\pm \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points\n\n$$\n(-\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}},-\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}),\\,(\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}},\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}).\n$$\n\nWe evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:\n\n| $\\,(x,y)\\,$ | $\\,(-\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}},-\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}})\\,$ | $\\,(\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}},\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}})\\,$ |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| $\\,f(x,y)\\,$ | $\\,1+\\sqrt{2}\\,$ | $\\,1-\\sqrt{2}\\,$ |\n\n$$\n\n$$\n\nTherefore, the function reaches a maximum value at $(-\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}},-\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}),$ and its maximum value is "The graph below shows $y=k(6^{x})+c.$ Determine the values of $k$ and $c$ and find the equation of the curve.\n\n![](images/de/deb7e20658882229a3653f4058c787bf2a5c4a26c5f2982406a2dba34c2d5846.png)" :question/worked-solution "The horizontal asymptote of the curve $y=k(6^{x})+c$ is $y=c.$ In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is $y=4$, so $c=4.$\n\nTherefore, our function takes the form\n\n$$\ny=k(6^{x})+4.\n$$\n\nWe can solve for $k$ by finding a point on the graph and substituting for $x$ and $y.$ The labeled point on the graph is $(0,6),$ so we substitute $x=0$ and $y=6$ into the function and solve for $k\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}y & =k({6}^{x})+4 \\\\ 6 & =k({6}^{0})+4 \\\\ 6 & =k(1)+4 \\\\ 6 & =k+4 \\\\ 2 & =k\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the curve is $y=2(6^{x})+4.$"} {:db/id 17592186513313} {:db/id 17592186088061 :question/id #uuid "0f849808-e14b-5ed1-9f45-9decbc5d48b1" :question/math-academy-id "q-18518"} {:db/id 17592186088062 :question/id :topic/math-academy-id 817} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186088728 :step/content {:db/id 17592186088868 :tutorial/content "Adding a value to $y=2^x$ will **translate** (shift) the exponential function up or down the $y$-axis. \n\nFor instance, adding $3$ to $y=2^x$ will move each point on the exponential function $3$ units :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: \n\n- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$\n\n$$\nmax{Q(x)\\,|\\,‖x‖=1}={\\lambda }_{\\text{max}}\n$$\n\n- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$\n\n$$\nmin{Q(x)\\,|\\,‖x‖=1}={\\lambda }_{\\text{min}}\n$$\n\nFirst, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:\n\n$$\nA=\\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 & -1 \\\\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\\\ -1 & 0 & 3\\end{bmatrix}\n$$\n\nNow, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of the matrix $A:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}|A-\\lambda I| & =0 \\\\ \\begin{vmatrix}3-\\lambda  & 0 & -1 \\\\ 0 & 1-\\lambda  & 0 \\\\ -1 & 0 & 3-\\lambda \\end{vmatrix} & =0 \\\\ (1-\\lambda )\\begin{vmatrix}3-\\lambda  & -1 \\\\ -1 & 3-\\lambda \\end{vmatrix} & =0 \\\\ (1-\\lambda )((3-\\lambda )(3-\\lambda )-1) & =0 \\\\ (1-\\lambda )({\\lambda }^{2}-6\\lambda +8) & =0 \\\\ (1-\\lambda )(\\lambda -4)(\\lambda -2) & =0 \\\\ \\lambda  & =4,\\,2,\\,1\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n \n\nTherefore, we have\n\n$$\nmax{Q(x)\\,|\\,‖x‖=1}=4.\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186269172 :question/id #uuid "7affa7e5-177d-56c4-b158-cb7cb8121dd7" image of $S$ under the counterclockwise rotation ${R}_{{270}^{∘}}$ by an angle of ${270}^{∘}$ about the origin?\n- **I.** $(0,0)$\n- **II.** $(2,-2)$\n- **III.** $(-2,0)$\n\nSelect all that apply." :question/worked-solution "The counterclockwise rotation ${R}_{{270}^{∘}}$ by an angle of ${270}^{∘}$ is given by the matrix\n\n$$\nR=\\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\\\ -1 & 0\\end{bmatrix}.\n$$\n\nTo find the image of $S$ under the action of ${R}_{{270}^{∘}},$ we first create a matrix $X$ containing all of the vertices of $S:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}X & =\\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 & 2 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 2\\end{bmatrix}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, we compute the image of $X$ under ${R}_{{270}^{∘}}$ by calculating the matrix product $RX:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}RX & =\\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\\\ -1 & 0\\end{bmatrix}\\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 & 2 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 2\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 & 2 \\\\ 0 & -2 & -2\\end{bmatrix}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the coordinates of the respective vertices of ${S}^{′}$ are $(0,0),(0,-2),(2,-2).$\n\nSo, the correct answer is \"I and II only.\""} {:db/id 17592186354300 :question/id #uuid "393a348f-a234-528b-b073-1f1b828e454e" formula\n\n$$\nS=\\int 2\\pi x\\,\\text{d}s.\n$$\n\nSince our curve is given in parametric form, we have\n\n$$\n\\text{d}s=\\sqrt{{(\\frac{\\text{d}x}{\\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\\frac{\\text{d}y}{\\text{d}t})}^{2}}\\,\\text{d}t.\n$$\n\nTherefore, we will use\n\n$$\nS=2\\pi {\\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\\sqrt{{(\\frac{\\text{d}x}{\\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\\frac{\\text{d}y}{\\text{d}t})}^{2}}\\,\\text{d}t.\n$$\n\nWe are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\\sqrt[4]{6}.$ \n\nComputing the derivatives, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{\\text{d}x}{\\text{d}t} & =\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}t}({t}^{2})=2t, \\\\ \\frac{\\text{d}y}{\\text{d}t} & =\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}t}(\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{3}}{t}^{4})=\\frac{4}{\\sqrt{3}}{t}^{3}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}S & =2\\pi {\\int }_{0}^{\\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+{(\\frac{4}{\\sqrt{3}}{t}^{3})}^{2}}\\,\\text{d}t \\\\  & =2\\pi {\\int }_{0}^{\\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+\\frac{16}{3}{t}^{6}}\\,\\text{d}t \\\\  & =2\\pi {\\int }_{0}^{\\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\\sqrt{4{t}^{2}(1+\\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4})}\\,\\text{d}t \\\\  & =2\\pi {\\int }_{0}^{\\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\\cdot 2|t|\\sqrt{1+\\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4}}\\,\\text{d}t \\\\  & =4\\pi {\\int }_{0}^{\\sqrt[4]{6}}\\sqrt{1+\\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4}}\\cdot {t}^{3}\\,\\text{d}t.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=1+\\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4}.$ The critical points are our \"candidates.\"\n\n- If the function is defined on a closed interval $[a,b],$ then we must remember to include the endpoints as well.\n\n- If the function is defined on an open interval $(a,b),$ then we do not include the endpoints.\n\n**Step 2**: Determine the value of the function at each of the critical points.\n\n**Step 3**: Compare all the values of $f$ found in step $2.$ The greatest of these values is the global maximum value, and the least is the global minimum value." :tutorial/id #uuid "e714b234-f163-5ae5-a064-6bef2d3b9fc1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2667 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "9b5f6fdc-d0a8-5c91-a879-4f798a936a36" :step/math-academy-id 12797 :step/next {:db/id 17592186064995}} {:db/id 17592186065348 :tutorial/content "We know how to use the first derivative test to find the local extrema of a continuous function. If the constant of proportionality is $0.2,$ which differential equation could be used to model $P(t)?$" :question/worked-solution "Since the growth rate of infected trees is *jointly* proportional to the number of trees that are infected at time $t,$ and the number of uninfected trees, the number of infected trees follows a logistic growth model.\n\nA logistic growth equation has the form\n\n$$\n\\frac{dP}{dt}=kP(a-P),\n$$\n\nwhere $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a>P$ is the carrying capacity.\n\nIn this case, the constant of proportionality is $k=0.2,$ and the carrying capacity is $a=300.$ Therefore, the number of trees that are infected is given by the equation\n\n$$\n\\frac{dP}{dt}=0.2P(300-P).\n$$"} :step/id #uuid "4245bf2c-f044-5000-a8dc-9e8cf792d0e0"} [{:db/id 17592186130300 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130449 :tutorial/content "Recall that when we rotate a curve by $2\\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis, the area generated by this surface of revolution is given by\n\n$$\nS =  \\int 2\\pi y \\, \\textrm{d}s.\n$$\n\nNow suppose we have a parametrically defined curve: \n\n$$\nx = x(t), \\qquad\ny = y(t), \\qquad\nt \\in Building on the analytical framework established in the first course, students study orthogonality, multivariable integration, vector calculus theorems, and advanced methods for differential equations.\nThe course emphasizes mathematical structures that arise naturally in physics, including inner product spaces, orthogonal projections, integral theorems of vector calculus, and transform methods for solving differential equations. Students study norms, inner products, orthogonality, and orthogonal complements in vector spaces over the real and complex numbers. Techniques such as orthogonal projections, the Gram–Schmidt process, and QR factorization allow vectors to be decomposed into orthogonal components. These ideas play a role in Fourier analysis, signal decomposition, and numerical methods used in physical simulations.\nStudents then explore quadratic forms and the diagonalization of symmetric matrices. The spectral theorem provides a geometric interpretation of symmetric transformations and leads to techniques for analyzing energy functions and stability in physical systems. Singular value decomposition is also introduced as a powerful matrix factorization with applications in numerical modeling and data analysis.\nApplications of linear algebra follow, including least-squares methods for solving overdetermined systems. \\\\  & =80.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo Luisa drove $80$ kilometers.\n\n**Method 2**\n\nFirst, we convert the percentage to a fraction:\n\n$$\n40 \\% = \\dfrac{40}{100} = \\dfrac{40 \\div 20}{100 \\div
